. How dare you, Mr. Newcomb, in my own home, speak so slightingly of my brother? Why have you turned against him? When he was first accused of the crime, you acted as his friend. Since his escape, you never lose an opportunity to taunt me with his downfall.
Because the evidence against him has strengthened.

Mr. Newcomb, you call yourself friend. I do not believe you. Roger is as innocent of that crime as I am, and you know it. Not content with attempting to overturn my faith in my brother, you have spared no time or trouble to turn the colonel against him. He believes in your friendship so thoroughly, he never thinks to doubt your word.
That is as it should be, Mrs. Graham. And, I hope, some day, the colonel's wife will favor me with her confidence.

Never. Your very presence is hateful to me, and could I have my wish you would never again cross this threshold. The time will come when Roger's innocence will be proved, and woe to those who are his accusers.
If you please, Mrs. Graham, the colonel is asking for you.
Very well, Polly.
I fear the walk has been too much for the colonel. Will you excuse me?
Certainly.

It will be a long time before that day, my dear Mrs. Graham. The plot cannot so easily be unravelled. Suspects some foe of the colonel's, does she? She shall have a better cause. The shot will be more telling next time.
Is the colonel at home?

parts.direction: NEW. _turns, sees_ GIBBS, _and gives a surprised whistle_; GIBBS _looks at_ NEW., _and whistles_.

parts.say:
. What business brings you here?
GIBBS
. To inquire after the colonel's health.
I can give you full information. He has quite recovered, and is to rejoin his regiment to-day. What next?
To ascertain if he has ever found a clew to the perpetrator of the foul outrage.
If not, to turn traitor.

lines.source:
(_Enter_ DOR. _in house gown, and sees_ NEW. _and_ GIBBS. _She is about
  to retire, but stops upon hearing_ GIBBS'S _speech_.)

parts.say: Yes, for I can give him the name of the man who planned his murder.

parts.direction: DOR. _crosses to stage_ C. _and hides behind portière_.

parts.say: And what do you expect to get for this startling piece of news?
Well, say fifty dollars.

I will give you a hundred to say nothing about it, on one condition, that you yourself try your hand. That man Dowling was worse than nothing. It was a bad shot; we need better marksmen in our armies.
You are bound to murder him?

Murder? no indeed. “All's fair in love and war.” Are we not enemies? Is he not the invader of the sacred soil that was my birthplace? Has he not won the heart of the woman I once loved? That affection is now dead, and hatred has risen from the ashes. She scorned me once, and I shall not rest until her happiness is wrecked.
Then that explains your treachery towards her brother, Roger Carruth.

What do you know of Roger Carruth? The world looks upon him as a criminal; he is beyond recall and as good as dead.
GIBBS
. You are sure?
Yes, I am confident of that.
And the family; do they not suspect?
Suspect? not much; they are too simple for that. You are still in the colonel's regiment?
Yes. What are your orders?
Are you at any time placed as sentinel near the colonel's quarters?
Yes, any night may find me there.
Well, I must take my chances. To inquire after the colonel's health is sufficient excuse for my appearance in camp at any time. The colonel has given me a standing invitation.
Which you will have no hesitation in accepting, I see.
What time are you placed there on guard?
Just before taps.
Good, just the thing. After taps will be the time. Lights out, everything quiet. Can I depend upon you, Gibbs?
You have my word, sir.
Ha, ha! word? do you think that yours is worth anything?
Sometime I hope it will be.
Remember, you owe much to me. Should you turn traitor, your reckoning will be a sorry one.
I shall not forget all that you have done for me. Some day I will pay it back with interest.

I wonder if I can trust him? He seems docile enough; but sometimes I fancy there's a look in his eye—pshaw! what nonsense. Newcomb, my boy, a clever trick, a bold scheme; but you will win it, never fear.
. What do I hear? A scheme to take the colonel's life, and by his best friend too.

There he goes, oh, the hypocrite. Now I know why I hate him so. With all his fine manners, I have not been deceived. Ugh! I hate even to shake hands with him. Oh dear, if I were only a man, that I might be near the colonel. Whom shall I tell? Who will help me? Ruth must not know, she has enough to bear.

parts.direction: Goes to mantel and takes_ ROGER'S _picture; music_.

parts.say: They call me gay, Roger, frivolous and heartless. Perhaps I am, but if they could only look down deep into my heart, they would find the love for you, burning a strong and steadfast flame.

parts.direction: Places picture on mantel and stands looking at it.

parts.say: O, Roger, why did you leave me? We all believed in your innocence and could have helped you bear the burden, which now alone must be so heavy. Oh, if you were only here to help me now.

parts.direction: Bows head on hands and stands weeping; music ceases. Enter_ BIJAH _and_ POLLY.

parts.say:
That was the best piece of pie, Polly. If I could only have my knapsack as a receptacle for such samples of your cooking, I wouldn't need drum and fife to spur me on.
POLLY
. Hush, Bijah, Miss Dorothy is here.
. A visitor, Polly?
Yes ma'am. A friend from Oldtown; and only think, Miss Dorothy, he knows your Mr. Roger.
Knows my Roger?
Oh, tell me of him; where is he?
That I cannot tell you
, but here is a letter, which he bade me give you should I ever come to Baltimore.

lines.source:
(DOR. _takes letter; breaks seal_. BIJAH _and_ POLLY _retire to window;
music_.)

parts.say: . MY DARLING DOROTHY.—That you still have faith in me I have no doubt. Your heart is too pure for anything else. I have enlisted in the army, and only as private will serve my country with heart and soul. When the war is over, I will return to you; my innocence established, and the foe, not only my country's but my own, defeated and trodden under foot. Bijah Bright, the bearer of this letter, is a true and loyal friend. He is worthy of your greatest respect, for he stood by me in my darkest hours. My love to dear sister Ruth. Until we meet again, yours in life or in death.
. Mr. Bright, I am more than grateful to you for bringing this letter; it fills my heart with renewed hope. Believe me
, your loyalty to Roger makes us warm and steadfast friends.
I shall see him again, Miss Dorothy, and, when I do, I shall say to him, that the stars in heaven never shone brighter than the love in your eyes when you spoke his name.
You are a true knight. Will you take an answer to this letter?
Indeed, I will.
Thank you so much.
No thanks, Miss Dorothy, the pleasure's mine.
Isn't she just sweet, Bijah?

You've hit it this time; were it not for the dazzling brightness of the orbs of fascinating Miss Polly Primrose the palpitation of my heart would be greatly increased; as it is—
There's only one maid, and Polly's her name, Of my love, my heart, she surely makes game; But some time or other, so sorry she'll be, She'll sigh for her Bijah, the bear of Old T.

Indeed, I won't.
There's plenty of fish in the sea, Mr. B., Who'd bite at my hook with the greatest of glee: You think, as you've writ, sir, my heart is your own, That over your absence I sigh and I moan, Indeed, I do not, sir; pray hear me aright, I wouldn't give that
, sir, to be Mrs. Bright.
Ha, ha, Polly, that wee brain of yours isn't an idle one. It won't do for us to separate, but make a stock company and spring our poetic effusions upon the public together.
Is Miss Dorothy at home?
Why—Mr. Roger here?
Land of living! Where did you come from?
Was marching by; could not resist the temptation of a stolen glance at Dorothy.
Have just given her your letter, and she is now writing one in answer.
But I must see her.
Then I won't wait for that answer. And, as I know the sensations of a fluttering heart, I'll step out and let you flutter alone.
All right, Bijah. Where are you going?

Back to camp. I've had a taste of Polly's pies. That's joy enough for one day.
ROGER
. Take these to the captain, and I will soon follow.
All right.
Polly, should I on the cold earth lie, remember this—I loved your pie.
Pity sakes alive! Mr. Roger, how shall I break the news to Miss Dorothy?
Your wits were always lively, Polly. I shall leave it to you.
Dear me, she may come at any moment. Here, hide behind this.
Oh, dear, every idea in my brain is playing tag with the other. Such a horrid sensation I feel, as if some one had proposed and I had said “No,” when I meant “Yes.”
Shade of my departed grandsire, aid me.

parts.direction: Draws herself up, makes to door_ R., _exits calling_, “_Miss Dorothy, Miss Dorothy_.”

parts.say: ROGER
. Oh, how good to be in my own home again. They say that stolen goods are always the sweetest; one look and kiss from Dorothy will indeed be worth the stealing—hark, they are coming.

What is the matter, Polly? From the vigorous manner in which you called my name, I should think the house was on fire, or besieged by burglars.
POLLY
. Hush, Miss Dorothy, it ain't a fire—it's worse—it's burglars.
. Oh!
Don't, Miss Dorothy; some one entered the house while you were in your room, and has stolen something.
Stolen something! What?
Something that belongs to you. It is very precious.
. My rings are all here.
Oh,—no—not that, something worse;
it's your heart.

Polly, tell me instantly, what do you mean?
POLLY
. I mean—I mean—no, I don't mean, yes—I do—
Polly, if you can talk sensibly, pray do, and not as if your brain were congested.
Indeed, Miss Dorothy, my brain is all right—but look
behind that portière.
What is it? You make my very blood run cold.
Behind that portière

parts.direction: goes to it, draws it aside, disclosing_ ROGER

parts.say: , is—is—
Roger!
My own dear Dorothy.
Oh, Polly, you frightened me so.
Thank heaven, that's over—it's worse than having a tooth pulled.
You did nobly, Polly. Will you tell Mrs. Graham that I am here?
Indeed I will.
Oh. Roger, I have wanted you so much.
What do you think of me? my lonely hours so far away from you all.
But where have you been? Tell me, Roger.
Hush, Ruth is coming. I will tell you both together.
Roger, my dear brother.
Why this long silence? this uniform? What does it all mean?

lines.source:
(RUTH _and_ DOROTHY _both seated_. ROGER'S _hand on_ RUTH'S _shoulder,
the other holding_ DOROTHY'S _hand_.)

parts.say: It means, dear sister, that my heart responded to my country's call, and I could not stay away.
But why did you not confide in us? we all believed in your innocence.

All?
RUTH

. Yes, all; for at heart the colonel believes in your honor. He must, but his friend Newcomb has so woven his influence about him, that the poison has done its work. Oh, Roger, that man, how I despise and fear him.

And well you may. Never mind, Ruth, some day my name will stand without a blemish, and the colonel will be made to forget his doubts. Now, I shall serve my country with my heart and soul, believing and trusting that justice in good time will right my wrongs.
COLONEL
. Yes, major, a capital plan.
The colonel! he must not see you. I fear he may forget that you are my brother.
Never mind, Ruth, his words cannot hurt me.

lines.source:
(_Enter_ COLONEL _leaning upon arm of_ POTTS, _who carries the_
COLONEL'S _cloak and hat_.)

parts.say: Ruth, dear, I am quite myself again. The major's active brain has helped to clear my cobwebbed intellect, and our united forces have conceived a most brilliant scheme.
Roger Carruth, what are you doing here?
Calling upon my sister and my fiancée.

And do you think, sir, that I, their only protector, will allow one whose name is sullied to hold an interview with them?
RUTH
. Gordon, you forget that you are speaking to my brother.
. And please remember, Gordon, that this man I love and honor above all others.

Stop, I say. In my own house, I will speak my mind. Roger Carruth, leave this house. All here bear honored names. We do not associate with dishonest men.
RUTH
. Gordon, how can you be so cruel?

Colonel Graham, you forget to whom you are speaking. We once called ourselves brothers; that tie remains. We shall both fight for our country's honor. Mine will be a double duty. My good name shall stand again, and you, who spurn me now, shall live to crave my pardon. Farewell, Dorothy.
Gordon, you have broken my heart.
You call yourself a soldier. If I were your country, I would disown you.
Hush, Ruth, don't condemn me. Dorothy, I have done what seemed my duty.
There are some duties it is wiser to overlook.

parts.direction: COLONEL _and_ RUTH _stand talking together_; DOROTHY _drags_ POTTS _down front_.

parts.say: Pinky, what do you think of all this?
A downright dirty piece of business, but don't blame the colonel. Newcomb is at the bottom of this.
Newcomb? Oh, yes. Pinky, what do you think? I overheard him talking to one of the colonel's men, and he's plotting
murder.
What! Murder? Who is the victim?
The colonel. That shot in the back was a first attempt, and he is going to try it again.
Not by a large majority.
You must help him in some way.
I'll do my best; and if Newcomb isn't “laid out” before we're done with him, my name isn't Pinkerton Potts.
Find Roger; he will help you. He's too loyal to harbor the Colonel's words when his life is in danger.

lines.source:
(_Sound of fife and drum. Troops pass window, as at opening._ POLLY
_enters, goes to window_.)

parts.say:
Come, Ruth, my cloak and hat.
RUTH
. Must you leave me?

. Ruth, dearest, you are a soldier's wife, remember. Forgive my harsh words to Roger, but by the fireside or on the battle-field, our honor must be upheld. When the bugle calls me to active service, with heart and soul to lead my men in battle, it calls you to be brave and to conquer all fears, giving inspiration to those who march to meet the foe, and waiting with patient love and hope our safe return.
Good-by, Dorothy. Come, major.
Major, watch over him and bring him back to me.
I will do my best, Mrs. Graham.
Good-by, major; don't forget the sacred trust imposed upon you. Care for them both.

Ruth, dear, be brave. Roger will be near Gordon, I know. He has suffered much, but he will forget his own wrongs. We have faith in him and know him to be steadfast and true. Some time the world will know it. Keep hope alive in your heart, and believe with me, that Roger will some day make that shot in the back rebound, and the traitor will meet his just deserts.

lines.source:
(_Tableau._ RUTH _in_ DOROTHY'S _arms_. POLLY _at window waving
handkerchief_.)

SCENE I.—_Encampment of Union troops at Harrison's Landing one week
  later; time, noon. View of James River at back._ COLONEL GRAHAM'S
  _tent_, L.C., _opening facing audience. Trees_ R. _and_ L.; _fallen
  log_ R. _Campstool outside tent; inside, table, stools, couch. In
  one corner, banjo; old army coat, hanging. Sentinel pacing at back.
  Soldiers grouped about; wooden table_ C., _at which are seated
  soldiers playing cards_. KILROY _on log_ R.; BIJAH BRIGHT _standing
  back of table. Soldiers laugh as curtain is raised._

parts.say: Wal, that's a true story, and don't you forget it.
Faith, it's an injy rubber memory yees have any way. An' divil a bit does it trouble yees to stretch it. Be jabers! it makes me dhry to listen to yees.

parts.direction: Drinks from canteen, then looks at watch.

parts.say: Shure, it's toime I was on watch.

lines.source:
(_Enter_ COLONEL GRAHAM _and_ MAJOR POTTS. _Soldiers rise, salute, and
disperse._)

parts.say: Ah, major, already new life fills my veins; to know that I am with my men again. That seven days' fight is over at last; poor fellows! how many have answered their last call, and lie with white faces upturned to the sky; only the heavy dew for a winding-sheet; while the wounded are waiting for transports to take them back to Washington.
Those were hard days, colonel; but we

succeed in the end. When we have gained the victory, some of those brave fellows, whose souls are as white as their faces, will, if they can look down upon their country, rejoice that they gave their lives for so glorious a cause.
Halt! who comes there?
Friend.
Advance, friend, and give the countersign.

lines.source:
(GUARD _gives the countersign in whisper_; KILROY _takes sentinel's
place. The relieved sentinel falls behind guard and marches off._)

parts.say: Any orders, colonel?
No, major, go amongst the men if you will, and speak words of encouragement; I shall be my old self to-morrow. (POTTS _salutes, and

lines.source: exit past_ KILROY, _who salutes_. COLONEL _enters tent and writes at

parts.say: table_. KILROY,

parts.direction: pacing to and fro, suddenly starts and lowers musket

parts.say: Halt! who comes there?
Plague take it! only the wind.

parts.direction: PETE _appears, crawling on hands and knees_.

parts.say:
Halt! who comes there? Advance, and give the countersign.
PETE
. 'Deed I can't sign nuffin, massa.
. Well, by the powers, if it ain't a shmall nagur.
'Deed, massa, I done mean no harm; I's scared blue, I is.
Blue, is it? faith it must be navy blue thin, wid a coat of tan outshide it. Phat are yees doing here?
I's only come to find my mammy.
Foind yees mammy. It's a foine place yees come to luk for her; p'raps yees thinks she's a bowld sojer by in petticoats, ha, ha!
Please, massa, I tought maybe, when she runned away, der Union men would be good to her, and let her stay wid dem.

Bliss his heart, a good bit of faith he has thin, and Patrick Kilroy is the last man, though he has an Irish heart, that would lit any harm come to this shmall spal-peen. Corporal of the guard, post four.
. Look here, sir. See what I've found crossing the line. Shure it's a bit of ould Africa.
All right, I'll show him to the colonel.

parts.direction: KILROY _resumes march_; CORPORAL _leads_ PETE _to_ COLONEL'S _tent and salutes_.

parts.say: Well, what is it?
A contraband discovered crossing the lines.
Very well, leave him to me.
. My fine fellow, what is your name?
Dey neber done gib me one, massa, only Pete.

How old are you?
PETE
. Dunno, 'specs I'se purty old; I'se had heaps of fun.

Where did you come from?
PETE
. Ober dere. Powerful hard time I'se had too, massa. I'se runned away.
Why did you come here?
Ole massa, he sold my brudder, an' I jest feared he'd make me gwine too. An' I knowed der Union men was heaps good to de poor niggers, an' I tought p'raps yer might tell me whar my mammy is.
No, Pete, my boy, I don't know where your mammy is.

What are you going to do?
PETE
. Dunno!

parts.direction: Thinks a moment, then looks brightly into_ COLONEL'S _face_.

parts.say: 'Specs I should jes lub to stay wid you.

parts.direction: seating himself on stool, outside tent

parts.say: . Stay with me? What could you do?

I can brack yer boots, massa. An' oh, massa Colonel, I do so lub a horse! Let me take care ob yours. I can handle 'em, massa, if dey be eber so debblesome. Please jes try me; an' I do eberyting yer axes me, sho's yer born.
I havn't a horse, Pete; but you look like a pretty good boy. I think I can trust you. Yes, I will give you a trial.
Yer really means it?
Ki-yi!

Ha, ha! I'll make you my bodyguard.
PETE
. I ain't got no uniform, massa; 'specs I needs a sword for dat.
That is a ragged coat you have on for this time of year.

parts.direction: Goes into tent and brings out old army coat with gold stripes and buttons

parts.say: . Here, put this on. You won't grow to it this year

, but it is better than nothing.
PETE

parts.direction: delighted; changes coat and walks about, admiring himself

parts.say: . I jes wish my ole mammy see me now, she'd be proud, she'd be.
Pete, you are to take good care of everything that belongs to me; and some day, when the war is over, we will go North and try to find your mammy.
Has you a mammy, Massa Colonel?
No, Pete; she died long ago; but a dear wife and sister are praying for a safe return.
Massa Colonel, I'll do jes de bery bes I knows.
Well said, Pete. Now go into my tent and put it in order.
All right, massa.

parts.direction: Salutes and enters tent; enter_ POTTS _and_ BIJAH.

parts.say:
Ah, major! Whom have we here?
POTTS
. Bijah Bright, the standard-bearer of your regiment.
A grave duty, Mr. Bright. May it not be trodden beneath your feet.
Wal, I guess not, colonel: not while this right arm is strong. Jest feel that muscle.
Ha, ha! There's no doubt about that, or your heart either.
Only one corner reserved; the rest belongs to my country.
And may I ask who possesses so great a treasure?
Why, don't you know? My Polly, your Polly.
My Polly? Ah, I see. You mean Polly Primrose. Mr. Bright, you are to be congratulated; she's a treasure.
Don't be in a hurry with good wishes, sir. She's on the wing, and my shot has not yet brought her down.
On the anxious seat, are you?

I can at least wish you success.
BIJAH
. Thank you, sir.
Major, if you see a small darky about here, it is all right. He crossed the lines, and I will take care of him.
Very well, sir. He shall not be molested.

parts.direction: POTTS _and_ BIJAH _salute as_ COLONEL _exits past guard, who salutes_; MAJOR _seats himself on end of log_ R.; BIJAH _walks up and down_.

parts.say: But tell me more of this Newcomb, Bijah. What can be his motive in planning the colonel's death?

Wal, before Mr. Roger's sister married Colonel Graham, Newcomb was all-fired gone on her. I know, for I was about Baltimore at the time and heard no end of gossip. You see, Mrs. Graham didn't take to him, and snubbed him on all occasions. By Jiminy, wasn't he mad! The whole truth of the matter is, he's bound to be revenged, and takes what's nearest and dearest. He was the means of the colonel's injury, and I'm scared blue for fear that he will try it again. Roger Carruth has his eye on him, for he has a double debt to pay.
What's this?

parts.direction: Goes to tent and brings_ PETE, _holding banjo, down stage_; BIJAH _follows_.

parts.say: Who are you?
Please; massa, I's only Pete.
Where did you come from?
Ober dar, massa, and de colonel he's gwine to let me stay wid him.

Well, give us a tune.
PETE
. Deed, massa, dis yer belongs to de colonel; 'specs he wouldn't like to hab me gib yer dat.
Yes, he will; I can answer for that.
All right, massa. I'll play de bes I know.
Good, and here's a quarter for inspiration.

lines.source:
(PETE _salutes, takes coin, and seats himself on floor_ C. POTTS _sits
on camp-stool_; PETE _plays and sings a negro melody_; SOLDIERS _appear
and group at back, listening_.)

parts.say: Bravo, bravo!

I tell you what, Bijah, music and a song like that cheer a man up. If we have many more days of dead calm and quiet, I shall be tempted to desert the cause and soothe my troubled spirit with the society of some fair maiden.
BIJAH
. You're a great one, you are. Where did you get that coat?
Massa Colonel gib me dat; he's heaps good to me, he is. I takes care ob eberyting, and I's his guard.
His what? Guard? Oh, ho! You mean body-guard.
Wal, I vum, here's an idea. We'll work him.
Go back to your work, Pete.
Major, I have an idea.

parts.direction: POTTS _comes down front_; BIJAH _takes his arm_.

parts.say: Isn't it rather dangerous to give it away?

How can we look out for the colonel? We can't always be at his side, or he will suspect something. He must not be warned, his health won't stand that. That small specimen of black humanity calls himself the colonel's guard; body-guard, he means. Now, why can't he be warned of the colonel's danger, and I'll trust him for the rest? He's mightily taken with the colonel, and you know what a darky's devotion is.
Bijah, you're a trump! If that is a specimen of your stock of ideas, you are a valuable man. Pete, come here.
Come here; we wish to talk with you.
I's all ready, sar; bof years wide open.
That's all right. Keep your mouth shut.
You like the colonel pretty well, don't you?
Like him, massa? Deed I does. He's heaps good ter me. Look at des yer cloe's.

You can pay him back for them, if you will.
PETE

parts.direction: putting hands in pockets; turns them wrong side out; looks at them dolefully, then at_ POTTS

parts.say:
. Please, massa, I can't gib yer nuffin.
POTTS
. I don't mean money.
Does yer mean I can do somefin for him?
Yes, that's jest the pint.
Deed, I'd just like dat. Does yer know what he's gwine ter do for me? When dis yer war is ober he's gwine to help me find my mammy. Don't yer tink I 'specs him for dat?

Gad, you're a lucky fellow to find such a friend as that. I wish the colonel would help me find a sweetheart.
PETE
. 'Specs for such a fine-lookin gennleman as you is, massa, de colonel would not have to work bery hard.
Thank you, Pete. That's praise worth having.
I say, Pete, there's some one in this world, that
love the colonel: you must take good care of him. One of these fine days some one will try to shoot him.
Shoot massa Colonel? Not if Pete can help it.
Mind, you keep both eyes wide open.
Deed I will, massa.

Pete, my boy, the colonel is one of my dearest friends. I promised his wife that I would take good care of him, but I may be called away at any moment. I commend him to your care. And remember, the trust is a sacred one.
PETE

parts.direction: salutes; wipes eyes on sleeves, and stands looking after him

parts.say: . I'll do de bes I knows. Golly, 'specs I didn't jine de army for nuffin.

parts.direction: Goes into tent; brings out pail and exits_ R. _through the trees for water. Enter_ POLLY, _wearing cloak and poke bonnet, with basket covered with napkin on arm, leading_ DOR., _disguised as an old lady; bonnet with veil over face_.

parts.say: POLLY
. My gracious! thankful enough, I am, that we are out of sight of those horrid soldiers. One of them tried to kiss me. Ugh! it makes me shiver to think of it. Miss Dorothy, here we are at last.
. Indeed, I am thankful too. I am so tired.
Where are we, Polly?
Right in camp, miss; see that tent? I wonder who lives there? Let's look in and find out.

parts.direction: takes picture in frame from table

parts.say: . Look, Polly, Mrs. Graham's picture. It must be the colonel's.
Pity sakes alive! so it is. He must not see us here.

No indeed. I wonder how I can find Roger; ever since I overheard that plot, sleep has forsaken me.
POLLY

parts.direction: walking about, looking through trees_ R.

parts.say: . Some one is coming this way.
And I really believe it is Major Potts.
They say “Fortune favors the brave.” This is indeed a lucky find.
Why, Polly Primrose, what are you doing here?
Miss Dorothy, have you lost your senses? In camp! How did you enter?
Behold my disguise.

parts.direction: Pulls veil over face; then lifts it.

parts.say: I am Polly's antiquated aunt. She has cakes to sell.
Yes, do have one.
POTTS
. But what means this masquerading?
I must see Roger, Pinky, and could think of no way but this. I must tell him of the plot I overheard.
I thought you were to leave that to me. Lost your faith in your old friend?

. Don't think that for a moment. I could not remain at home. I did not dare tell Ruth, and I must tell my thoughts to some one; they were driving me frantic. Do find Roger for me—that's a dear fellow.
That is easier said than done. He must keep out of the colonel's way, and that is his tent.
You have wits enough to manage that. Don't tell him who is here, leave that to me; I mean to give him a surprise.
Let a woman alone for keeping a secret. You will undeceive him in five minutes. I know enough of the fair sex for that.
If you were not Roger's best friend, I should say something that you would not like.
I fly to do your bidding. Don't empty your vial of pent-up wrath over my defenceless shoulders. I should not dare to look a pretty girl in the face for a week.
What a vacation the pretty girls would have! Come, do hurry, or the colonel will return and spoil everything.

parts.direction: Salutes and exit past sentinel, who salutes.

parts.say:
My heart is fluttering like an imprisoned butterfly. Hark! Polly, some one else is coming.
POLLY
. Pity sakes alive! It's Bijah Bright; seat yourself on this log and don't speak.

parts.direction: DOR. _covers face; seats herself on log_; POLLY _draws hood together_.

parts.say: Wal, I agree with the major. This is getting monotonous; my blood boils for excitement; even the sight of a pretty face wouldn't go bad. That reminds me.
If I can't do that, there is no law to prevent me from looking at a pretty girl's picture; and “by gorry,” she is worth looking at.
Well, I never! Now, I should just like to know—

girl, has he? I'll pay him well for that; deceiving me with his soft speeches.
BIJAH

. Bless my soul! if here isn't a sweet lass now. What! ho! my pretty maid; where are you going?
POLLY
. If you please, sir, I have cakes to sell.
Here's luck. Just what I've been looking for. I'll take half a dozen.
My! what cakes! “Is this heaven, Uncle Tom?”

These bring to me visions of Polly's kitchen and her pies.
Where'er I roam, where'er I be, No cakes can equal Polly P's.
This is richness.
Why do you hide your face? Let me look at you.
Indeed I can't.
You can't. Wal, I can.
Come now, give me a kiss.

parts.direction: POLLY _suddenly raises head, throws back hood and discloses herself to_ BIJAH'S _astonished gaze_.

parts.say:
Polly—Polly Primrose!
POLLY
. Yes, Polly—Polly Primrose. Aren't you ashamed of yourself? You're a nice kind of a man, you are, pretending to be fond of me.
Oh, come, Polly, I didn't mean any harm.
Oh no, no harm, of course not. Kissing every girl you meet. Don't speak to me—I'll never trust you or any other man again.
What is this? An indignation meeting? Bijah quarrelling with a pretty woman? No, yes, it is—Polly Primrose; but who is this?
That's my aunt, she came with me.
Poor old lady; she seems tired.
That she is; but she's never too tired to tell fortunes; wouldn't you like to hear yours?
Anything to kill time.
Come, let's hear it. My time is short.
No danger of the colonel's appearance, is there, Potts?
No, Roger, he is busily engaged. I've looked out for that.
Good! Now, what is the wheel of fortune to bring me? Oh!
I remember, no golden treasure disclosed, unless the key be silver.

. Young man, you have had serious trouble; some cloud hangs over you. You are suspected of some crime.
ROGER
. What witchcraft is here?
But you are innocent. If you have patience, your name will soon be cleared.
I hope so with all my heart.
You have a good heart, and, let me see—yes—that line is crossed—you have given it to some one.
. Your time is coming, sir. “He laughs best who laughs last.”
Ha, ha! Potts, some time that heart of yours won't stand the fire. Then I will charter a Gatling gun to return all your volleys.
. But what is this? Some danger lurks near a friend; perhaps a brother.
I have no brother.
No; not a real brother, but—
The colonel?
. Yes, yes. You must save him. He shall owe his life to you. Some one calling himself friend is his foe.

parts.direction: Rising; forgets, and assumes natural voice.

parts.say: He has done you a grievous wrong, but you will forgive that?
That voice!
Dorothy?
Cleverly done, little maid. You actually waited eight minutes.
Major! Dorothy, what does this mean?
A well-laid scheme, Roger, to hold a stolen interview with you. Miss Dorothy, you can talk with Roger just five minutes, no longer. The colonel will return by that time.

lines.source: (_Exit_ MAJOR. ROGER _sits on log_; DOR. _kneels at his side_.)

parts.say: Forgive me for coming, Roger, but I was so anxious.
Anxious, little one? Why, what is the trouble? Is it a quarrel with “my dearest friend Mollie”?
Don't speak like that. No one ever gives me credit for any depth of feeling, just because I laugh and take the good of life as it comes along.
Which I hope you will always do, Dorothy dear. Come, forgive me, and tell me your trouble.

Before the colonel left home after his illness, Mr. Newcomb called one day. I entered the drawing-room, and overheard a conversation which he was having with some man,—a soldier in the colonel's regiment.
Did you hear the man's name?
Yes; Mr. Newcomb called him Gibbs. Oh, I was so frightened, for I heard them plan to kill the colonel.
Kill the colonel? How? When?
This man was, some night, to be placed as the colonel's sentinel. That was to be the time and place. “After Taps” they said.
Have you told any one of this?
Only the major. It would never do to tell Ruth. She worries enough without that.
And you have kept it all to yourself? No wonder you were anxious. Dorothy, you are a treasure.
But tell me, how can you save Gordon?
He says and thinks hard things of me, Dorothy.
But you know at heart he does not mean it. It is all through that horrid Newcomb.
Yes; that horrid Newcomb.
Promise me that you will do your best to save him.
No need to promise that. He is your brother; for that, if for no other reason, I must forget and forgive.
Roger, you have made me so happy.
Then, for all I have suffered, I ask no better reward.
Time's up.
Where is Polly?
Here I am, sir.
Bijah, escort them both. Give the countersign, that they may cross the lines safely.
We do not need his assistance. He had better wait for another girl.

Come, Miss Dorothy.
ROGER
. Good-by, sweetheart. No more anxious moments, remember.
Never. Good-by, Pinky.

Poor Bijah looks unhappy, because the maid of his heart won't smile upon him. He has a good heart, and is “true as steel.”
ROGER

. Indeed he is. No one knows it better than I. He stood my friend in my darkest hours. Ah, Potts! I have a hard battle yet to fight. Newcomb must not win the day. My plan is a bold one. Stand by me, old man; your friendship will be tried.
But those honest eyes of yours never failed me yet. This firm pressure of your hand, and the knowledge of Dorothy's faith and love, give me strength and courage to do my duty.

lines.source:
SCENE II.—_Same as Scene I. Evening._ KILROY _has been relieved;
  lights across the river; table removed from the stage_, C.

parts.say:
Faith, and if it ain't the shmall heathen we saved from the other soide. Luk at the shtyle of him,—parading about wid the colonel's shtripes and buttons. Whist, honey, phat are yees doing wid that coat?
PETE
. I's habin' heaps of fun, I is. Massa Colonel gib me dis yer coat, an' I's playin' wid my 'magination, an' tinks I'se de colonel.
Playin' wid phat is it? The nixt thing you know, it may be powder phat's playin' wid you.
Does yer 'member, sah, when I comed across de line?

Will, indade I does. A foine specimen yees were. Shure, for a minit, I thought it was the divil himself, coming to give me a surprise party.
PETE
. Den yer don't trabel wid him all de time, massa?
Oh, yer shpalpeen!

parts.direction: Strikes at_ PETE, _who dodges, turns a somersault, and exit past sentinel_.

parts.say: A shmart one, by the powers! Travel with the divil is it? Faith, and he goes it so fast, niver a bit cud I kape up wid him. If that shmall imp don't show more respict to his betthers, a shmall chance he'll get to travel with any one.

lines.source: (_Exit_ KIL., R.; GUARD _approaches with change of sentinel_.)

parts.say: Halt! Who comes there?
Friend.
Advance, friend, and give the countersign.

lines.source:
(GUARD _gives it_; GIBBS _stands as sentinel; relieved_ SENTINEL
_marches off behind_ GUARD.)

parts.say: I wonder if Newcomb is on the watch. Yes; here he comes. Too clever to miss the game.

lines.source:
(_Enter_ COL. _and_ NEW.; GIBBS _salutes_ COL.; NEW. _looks at_ GIBBS,
_and starts_.)

parts.say: What's the matter, Newcomb? Not nervous, are you?
It's nothing. Thought I saw a shadow. Do you have any of those black devils hanging about here?

Yes, occasionally one; but they never give us any trouble. One little fellow crossed the line to-day, and he was so bright and clever,—wanted to stay here with me; so I have set him to work, and I expect he will take excellent care of me. I admire the devotion of that race; treat them kindly, and you are always sure of plenty of friends.
I prefer a higher type of humanity for associates.
What a pity, Newcomb, that two such warm friends as we should not have heart for the same cause! However, some day you will be of my opinion, I hope.

lines.source: (COL. _sits at table inside tent_; NEW. _on stool at opening_.)

parts.say: Hardly that, yet. Whatever the end may be, I trust we shall still be good comrades.
That sentiment I echo with my whole heart. But tell me, Newcomb, do you ever hear anything of Roger Carruth?
Never. He won't show himself in this part of the country again.
You are sure that you have evidence of his guilt? I would not misjudge the boy for all the world; I am too fond of him for that.

Why should I, his friend and yours, seek to turn you against him?
GIBBS
. Why, indeed!
I cannot understand it—so true and honorable, always. Some fearful temptation must have stood in his way.
Evil will show itself. If the seed is there, time will surely make it grow.
No, no, Newcomb; don't say that. Why, man, would you have me think for a moment that it was more than a sudden pitfall?
The evidence grows stronger and stronger against him.
Oh, Newcomb, this is so hard to bear!

parts.direction: Covers face with hands_; GIBBS _returns to place and resumes march_.

parts.say: . Never mind, old fellow.
You have some friends left who have not played the knave.
. True, Newcomb; I have much to thank you for. This kindly interest in my welfare, I trust the time will come when I can repay it.
Don't worry about that.
It is almost time for taps.
Won't you stay and smoke with me?
Not to-night. Early hours are prescribed for you. Good-night.
Good-night.

lines.source:
(NEW. _goes up stage_; COL. _enters tent; enter_ PETE, R.; _sees_ NEW.
_talking with_ GIBBS.)

parts.say: I wonder if he lubs de colonel. 'Specs I jes listen to der comversation.
Well, are you ready for your work?
Yes, sir.
No chicken-hearted business about this. Is your aim a true one?
Yes; true as steel.
I can depend upon you?
You can, sir. I feel a special interest in the work to-night.
At what time?
After taps.
It will soon be here.
That is the call. Ten minutes more; before the lights are out.
All right. Make your shot tell.
I will do my best, sir.
Good-night.
PETE
. Golly, my hair just frozen stiff; bof my knees powerful confectionate. Dey's plotting mischief, dey is. An' if Pete don't keep bof eyes wide open, dere will be trouble in de camp.
Newcomb is about the camp. I fear mischief is brewing.

I'd jest like to see the sport. I wonder who he is working this time.
MAJOR
. All right for the night, colonel?
. Yes, major; good-night.
Good-night.
BIJAH

parts.direction: looking through trees in flat_, L.

parts.say:
. Major, look there! I'll bet you a fiver, that's Newcomb.
POTTS
. You're right. Let us hide and watch him.

parts.direction: Both hide in trees_, L.; _drum-call for lights out; stage darkens_; COL. _puts out candle and stands in doorway_.

parts.say:
I wonder where that snowball of mine is? Pete! Pete!
PETE
. Here I is
, massa!
What are you doing at this time of night?
I's watchin' somefin, massa. I heard a crackling in der bushes; 'specs it possum. Yer don't mind if I looks, massa?
No; only don't stray away too far.
'Deed I won't, Massa Colonel.
You bet he scents the game.

parts.direction: crosses stage, goes up back; stands looking at river.

parts.say: I wonder why it is my thoughts are all of Roger to-night. Poor Ruth! how heavy her heart is; and I spoke words which did not lighten the burden. Down deep in my heart I cannot think him guilty. Yet Newcomb is so sure,—and Newcomb knows.

Everything all right?
GIBBS
. All right, sir.

lines.source:
(COL. _turns to enter tent_; NEW. _appears at extreme_ L., _and
  watches_ GIBBS; GIBBS _sees_ NEW., _stops a moment, then follows_
  COL., _aims at him, turns quickly, and fires at_ NEW. PETE, _who has
  followed_ GIBBS, _springs upon his back, and grasps him soon as shot
  is fired_. NEW. _is wounded in wrist_. GIBBS _swings_ PETE _around
  and knocks him senseless with butt of gun_. POTTS _and_ BIJAH _seize_

parts.say: COL.
; SOLDIERS
; KIL.
PETE
. The traitor! I'll pay him well for this.
What does this mean? Treason in the camp?
It means, colonel, that this man attempted your life. I overheard his plotting and came to warn you. He missed fire, and my wrist caught the shot.
Where is the sentinel?
. Faith, and there he is.
So, sir, placed here on honor to guard your colonel's life, you turn traitor. Speak, man, why have you done this?
. Poor little fellow! You have killed him.
If yees plaze, colonel, his sinses are only knocked out of him.
. Man, why are you silent?
He is too great a coward to defend himself. He dare not speak.
Dare not? Be careful, Newcomb; the game is not yet yours. You call me traitor: coward. Yet beneath the stars in heaven there is not one who wears, beneath his coat, a blacker heart than yours.

What do you mean? Who are you that dares to accuse me?
GIBBS

. One who has suffered much at your hands; who has borne with patience your taunts and slurs; who, knowing of the colonel's danger, tried to save his life. One whom you thought “as good as dead” stands before you. A victim of your treachery.
Roger Carruth.

lines.source: (TABLEAU.—KIL., C., _kneeling and holding_ PETE'S _head on knees_;

parts.direction: staggers back and leans against soldiers, who support him

parts.say: ; POTTS
BIJAH
ROGER'S
; ROGER
NEW.,

lines.source:
SCENE.—_Same as Act I.: three months later. Time—evening._ PETE, _as_
  BUTTONS, _discovered lighting the lamps_; POLLY _arranging papers on
  table, and putting room in order, generally_.

parts.say: Now, Pete, make everything bright and cheerful. Mr. Roger is expected home to-night; we must do our share towards a warm welcome. The poor colonel is so unhappy. Between the treachery of his friend, and Mr. Roger's brave deed, he is torn with conflicting emotions.
I's powerful sorry for dear Massa Colonel. Wish I could do somefin for him.
You do your work well, that will satisfy him.
But I tell you what, Pete, you can do something for me. Play a dance tune on this banjo. I haven't heard one since I left Oldtown. I can tell you what, Pete, I knew how to dance once.
Yer don't need to tell me dat, Polly; I kin see de dancin' peeking out ob yer shoes. What yer gwine ter have?
Give me a Virginia Reel. My gracious! I just adored that dance.
All right, Polly. You do der dancin', an' I play de tune.

lines.source:
(POLLY _keeps time with head and hands; growing interested, enters
  into the dance; advances with right hand extended, pretends to swing
  partner; then left hand; then both hands; marches, slapping hands;
  grows more interested; finally swings_ PETE _and banjo; then sinks
  into chair, laughing_; KIL., _in livery, appears at door_, C.)

parts.say: Pete, that was just glorious! I'm ever so much obliged to you for playing.
I's right proud ob you, I is. If dis yer heart ob mine didn't belong to a nigger, 'specs I should frow it at yer feet.

Faith, and it's an Irish heart she can have, anyway.
POLLY
. Pity sakes alive! What are you doing here?
It's a missage I have for the colonel.
Lor, Polly. Dis yer is de soger what didn't shoot when dis yer nigger crossed de line.
I's heaps glad to see you, sah. Does yer disremember me?
Faith, an' it's Pete, the colonel's guard.
What a foine by yees grown to. Shure it's a betther fitting coat yees have on, anyway.
Yas, indeed. I's Buttons, now, I is. Don't yer tink dis yer coat obercomes me?
Faith, it's a foine picture yees look in it.
I remember; you are the soldier that was so kind to Pete.

Oh, yees make me blush,—the sight of those bright eyes, and the swate words yees be afther saying. Shure, a foiner jig I never saw in the ould country. Will yees be afther telling the colonel I am here?
Yes, Pete will do that. Ask if the messenger shall be sent to his room.
All right, Polly. Who is de message from, sah?
Mr. Randolph Newcomb, if yees plaze.
Should think that Mr. Newcomb had done mischief enough. You can't be very proud of your master.
Faith, and it's little I care about him. I applied for the situation to plaze Mr. Roger. Shure, it's a policeman I am in foine livery.
Oh, I see, something more mysterious.
Massa Colonel will receib de message, sah. Yer is to follow me.
An' phat if that foine man, the divil, be afther kaping me company?
Den I goes first, massa, ebery time. I wouldn't for de world disturb de confections dat exist between you two.
Faith, an' if yees have a foiner coat, you're a
shtill.

lines.source: (_Exeunt_ KIL. _and_ PETE; _the latter making fun of_ KIL.)

parts.say: Pete's bright enough for him. I've taken quite a shine to my black diamond.
How devoted he is to the colonel! Heigho! wish some one was devoted to me. Nonsense; I don't care. I am so happy, now that horrid war is over. I am ready to embrace anybody and everybody.

parts.direction: Extends arms_; BIJAH _steps quickly, and_ POLLY _embraces him_.

parts.say: And I am just the man to appreciate it, Polly.
Bijah Bright! Bless my soul, how you frighten me! Back from the war, are you?

Yes, Polly. When I left you, patriotism filled my breast. I carried the flag, torn and tattered as it was, and, contrary to your expectations, was not suspended in mid-air. I lived for glory by day, and at night dreamed sweet dreams. They were all of you, Polly.
Dreaming of me! Stuff and nonsense. Do you take me for a brainless Down-Easter, that you come with your sweet words and “palaverin” smiles.

Away! “I'll have none of you.”
BIJAH
. Won't you ever forgive me, Polly, for that day in camp?

Never!
Think of me, dream of me, Whatever you will, That hour, that moment, It rankles me still.
Besides, what should I have to say to you? A man who carries in his pocket other girls' pictures, and spends all his time kissing them.
BIJAH
. Oho! I see where the shoe pinches.

Why shouldn't I? That's what I'd like to know. One moment you smile upon me, and my blood frantically and joyfully perambulates through my veins; and the next time my eager orbs behold you, an animated iceberg would be a more cheerful companion. You needn't flatter yourself that because you don't want me, no one else does. You can bet your sweet life, Bijah Bright doesn't mean to get left. No, ma'am.

Not when he has such a sweet face as this to look at.
POLLY
. Don't flatter yourself that you can make me jealous. Precious little thought I give to you or your picture.
You are just dying to see who it is.
Indeed, I'm not. Some baby-faced simpleton.
Come, Polly, it is too bad for you to treat me so when I returned, hoping to share with you a secret.
Secret! Oh, tell it to me, do.
Oh, no, Miss Primrose; I only make a confidant of my friends.
Well, I'll be friends for just ten minutes.
Will you though? Not by a large majority. No friendship for me on the instalment plan.
I'll be friends.
Now, tell me quick.
Ha, ha, ho, ho! I thought that would fetch it. A woman's curiosity is not fireproof against a volley of gossip.

If you talk like that, I shall leave the room.
BIJAH

parts.direction: taking her arm; brings her down front

parts.say: . No, you won't, you are just dying to stay here.

parts.direction: Holds picture and forces_ POLLY _to look at it_; POLLY _looks at picture, then at_ BIJAH.

parts.say: Oh, Bijah!

parts.direction: Hides her face on his shoulder.

parts.say: BIJAH

. You had better hide your face, Polly. Jealous of your own picture. That settles it: no more “Nays” for me. We'll give the folks in Oldtown a surprise, Polly, and the wedding shall be in the old church.
Oh, Bijah! But don't be in a hurry. Be serious and tell me about Mr. Roger.
You know how he did old Newcomb up that day in camp?
Yes, that was the time when Pete was injured and was sent home by the colonel.

Wal, Newcomb ain't done for yet. You see, when Mr. Roger was in the bank, I was there too. Of course, I wasn't president or director, Polly; only had to sorter keep my eye on everybody, and I jest did. I saw something that when it's known will be worse than dynamite, you jest bet.
It seems to me that you are a rolling-stone, Bijah. The last time I heard of you before the war, you were poultry farming in Oldtown.

I could not make that work. I had read about the money in raising poultry. Fortunes made in no time; and my fancy pictured this enormous poultry farm. The name of Bijah Bright immortalized. Oh, yes, there's money in it, Polly; for I left all mine there, and had only experience to put in my pocket.
But what is the wonderful news you have to tell?
Just wait. You want to be proud of me. It will be a scorcher.
Don't be so mysterious, Bijah; you don't know everything in this world.

No, and I don't want to. Let me be sure that the heart of Miss Polly Primrose beats for me alone, and that will satisfy my cravings for knowledge. Come, let us depart to the charms of the culinary department. Methinks I see visions of your pies, Polly. There in each other's genial society we will partake of pie, and talk over that coming wedding in Oldtown.

parts.direction: Exeunt_ POLLY _and_ BIJAH, R.; _enter_ COLONEL _and_ KILROY, L.

parts.say: Tell your master, Mr. Newcomb, that I will see him this evening.
Indade, sir, he shall have your orders.
Faith, it's a foine pie they be afther baking for Newcomb. By me powers, I wouldn't loike to be here at the cutting of it.
. It is hard to believe in Newcomb's treachery; he has always seemed so warm a friend.
RUTH
. Gordon, what did that messenger want? Who sent him?
Randolph Newcomb.
I thought as much; what was the message?
Asking permission to see me!
You did not consent?
Yes, Ruth, I am to see him this evening.
He shall not see you.

Ruth!
RUTH

. Gordon, why will you let him poison your heart against Roger? He is wily and cunning; you have proof of his treachery, yet your heart, once loyal to your friend, cannot without a struggle believe in his dishonor. Think no more of this man, but tell me of Roger, and that night in camp.
Poor fellow, his experience has been a bitter one. Shall I tell you the whole story, little one?
Yes, Gordon, every word.

. When the call for volunteers was heard throughout the country, Roger's heart responded to the call. Entering the service as a private, he tried to forget his wrongs in earnest work. Knowing the attempt upon my life, he sought the man who fired the shot. Dowling was confined as prisoner, awaiting sentence. Roger promised to help him, if he would confess the name of the instigator of the crime. Dowling at last did so, and you know who the guilty one proved to be. Oh, Ruth, to think a tried and old friend could be so base.
Never mind, Gordon; perhaps better now to learn his falseness than later; go on.

Roger, knowing that Newcomb would not stop at one attempt, determined to place himself in his way and act the knave. Assuming a disguise, he so completely lost his identity that Newcomb was well deceived, and before many meetings employed Roger to finish the work which had proved a blunder in the beginning. It was, as you know, planned for the night that Roger would act as my sentinel: the time after taps. Newcomb, always solicitous for my welfare, was a daily visitor in camp, and that night was on the watch to be sure that there was no blundering in the work.
Gordon, it chills my blood to think of it.

To deceive him, Roger aimed at me, but fired at him, and would have killed him on the spot, but Pete, having been warned that my life was in danger, was on the watch, and sprang upon Roger's back and caught his arm; the shot grazed Newcomb's wrist.
Brave Pete and noble Roger.
And to think, Ruth, that this was all for revenge. Thank Heaven, he did not succeed in winning the heart that, full of love and noble devotion, has been my inspiration in my darkest hours.
Yet you will see Newcomb again.
He wishes to compromise.
Ruth, how pale you look. When are the roses coming back to your cheeks?
When all is well with Roger, and you are happy again.
My heart will not be lighter until I ask Roger's forgiveness for doubting him. I wonder why he does not return?
He is seeking more evidence to clear his name.
I am going to my study, Ruth. My head feels heavy; perhaps a short sleep will refresh me. Ruth, you too have much to forgive. I have doubted your brother.
But not in your heart, Gordon. I have always been sure of that.
Thank Heaven that my harsh words have not crushed out all your faith.

parts.direction: Exeunt_ COLONEL _and_ RUTH, L.; _enter_ POTTS _and_ DOROTHY, R.

parts.say: Go on, Pinky, I am just dying to hear.

You see, we knew it all the time, but just how and when Roger was to square it with Newcomb was beyond our knowledge. You ought to have been there—just a jolly row. When Roger threw off his disguise, you should have seen Newcomb's face. Old Nick himself could not have looked more insane.
Then the plot I overheard was no news to Roger?
No, for under the disguise of Gibbs he held that interview with Newcomb.
Right in this room, and I didn't know it. Well, I never! But isn't it just glorious, Pinky. How did Roger escape arrest?

Hard as it was for the colonel to believe Newcomb guilty, he, of course, took Roger's side. Newcomb tried a game of bluff, but it didn't work. He is at large, but we are only waiting for some new development. It will come, and with it the downfall of Newcomb.

He richly deserves it. Think of the wrong he has done Roger.
POTTS
. Your faith and devotion to Roger have just made me hungry. I want some one to have faith in me, too. Now, don't breathe it, but I've just “gone and done” it myself.
Pinky, what do you mean? You are in love with a girl?
Why, of course. You would not have me fall in love with a spinster of many summers, would you? Guess who it is.
. I cannot for the very life of me imagine who it can be.
Let me whisper it.
. No, really? Mollie? My dearest friend. There, I knew she had some secret. Pinky, I could just hug you, but I won't. I will reserve that demonstration for Mollie.
Do you remember what I told you about the fascinating little woman? Now Roger will have an opportunity to return some of your happy remarks.
Polly, my hat and wrap.
Yes, miss.
Why, where are you going?
To see Mollie, of course, and talk it all over. I will tell her what a sweet lamb I think you are.
POTTS
. Good enough, Potts: your ears will burn steadily for just one hour. No, I will follow and save my reputation.
The colonel will see me in his private room?
Yes, sah; dis way, sah.

parts.direction: Goes towards door_, L.; RUTH _enters, closes door, and stands before it_.

parts.say: What would you have, Mr. Newcomb?
I would speak with the colonel, madam.
Not in this house. You have done mischief enough with your treachery. My house shall see no more of it.
Harsh words from you, an old friend, Mrs. Graham.

Don't call us friends, Mr. Newcomb. The time is past for that. From the first, your presence has been distasteful to me. I tried to be courteous, for you posed as my husband's friend. Now that we know you in your true colors, I can speak freely. I loathe and despise you; leave this house.
Excuse me, Mrs. Graham, but your husband has given me his word that he will see me.
And you have mine—you shall not see him.

You are a clever woman, Mrs. Graham, and though you once scorned my love, I cannot but admire your courage.
RUTH

. Your love! That is an emotion which has never entered your being. Your heart is too cold and treacherous; it cannot harbor that which is loyal and true. I am only too thankful that I escaped such pretensions.
Have a care, madam; I am too dangerous to trifle with. Let me pass! No woman shall stand in my way!

parts.direction: Tries to take her from door by force_; ROGER _enters, takes_ NEWCOMB _by shoulder and turns him round_.

parts.say: What are you trying to do, sir?
Roger Carruth! You here?
Yes, I am here.
He wishes to hold a private interview with the colonel, and I object.
Pete, tell your master I would like to see him here.
Yas, massa.
Golly, tribulations am a-comin'. Massa Newcomb wish he were a deader.
Mr. Carruth, this interview is for the colonel alone.
Sorry, Newcomb, but as I take an active interest in your welfare, you must submit to my presence.
. Roger and Newcomb together?
Yes, colonel. Newcomb wishes to see you on a matter of business; I surely think I have the right to hear.
No one has a better. Speak, Newcomb, before us all.
Very well; I have no hesitancy. I thought possibly Mrs. Graham—
If you have anything worth saying, speak, and don't waste words.

parts.direction: cool but angry; turns to_ ROGER

parts.say: . Your scheme was a bold one, young man, and perhaps you think that we are quits; but you have not yet been acquitted of the crime of forgery. I alone hold the key to that mystery
, and it will be well for you to listen to what I have to say. You accuse me as instigator of the crime of attempting the life of the colonel. Branded as a forger, who will take your word for that?
Newcomb, leave this house!
Wait, colonel. Let me deal with him. What compromise do you wish to make?
Let all suspicion fall from me, and I will give you my word that your name shall be cleared.
You would buy my silence, sir, as you thought you did that of your accomplice. You, deeply scarred as you are by depravity and guilt, dare to make me such an offer? No; a thousand times, no.
will meet your deserts. For myself, time will prove my innocence.

Will it, indeed? You overrate your ability. I hold you in my power.
BIJAH
. And I hold you in mine.
Bijah!
Bright, the bank's private detective!

Exactly so. Mr. Newcomb, I am afraid your nice little scheme will be “smashed to smithereens,” for it's my turn to play my hand. You forget that, as private detective, it was my duty to shadow every one
,—even your Royal Highness; and you can jest bet your life, I did my duty.
What is it? Have you any proofs?
Proofs? Yes; that Roger Carruth is innocent of forgery, and that Mr. Randolph Newcomb has that honor.
Newcomb!
Man, it is false.
Don't blacken your soul with another lie.
I hold the trump card.
Two gentlemen are at the door.
Yes; friends of Mr. Newcomb. Colonel, shall we not bid him good-evening?
Newcomb, leave my house; and may you never enter it again.
No fear of that. He has two accounts to settle.

parts.direction: NEW. _glares at_ BIJAH; _bows to_ RUTH, _and exit_.

parts.say: ROGER
. Bijah, how much I have to thank you for!

Mr. Bright, you have done your work well. I have seen your bravery on the battlefield, your honor and loyalty here. Your country may well be proud of you.
BIJAH
. Thank you, colonel. If I could only hear Polly say that.
Indeed I will, if you will give me the chance.
That's well said, Polly.
We'll all be bright and gay When Polly names the day.

lines.source: (_Both laugh and walk up stage to window._)

parts.say: Gordon, are you satisfied?

Roger, can you ever forgive me?
ROGER
. With my whole heart, sir. We have much to be grateful for, that fate led me into Newcomb's way. But where is Dorothy?
Here she comes, laughing as usual. If she were wrecked in mid ocean, that silvery laugh of hers would wake echoes on the waves.

lines.source:
(_Enter_ DOR. _and_ POTTS; DOR. _does not see_ ROGER, _who stands in
window_.)

parts.direction: putting arms about_ RUTH, _who is seated by table

parts.say: . Another ripple on the matrimonial sea. Somebody's engaged. Guess who it is.
Engaged? I give it up.
Allow me to present Major Pinkerton Potts as the culprit, and his victim is

parts.direction: turns around; sees_ ROGER, _and rushes into his arms

parts.say: —Roger!
That is news to me, major.
Back again, old man. I am glad to see you.
Well, you needn't make fun of me. It's my dearest friend Mollie.
Major, I indeed congratulate you.
Thought you would follow my example, eh, old man?
Yes; yours was such a lucky prize, thought I would try my hand.
Mollie is well worth winning, major.
Thank you, Mrs. Graham.
Dorothy, what is the best news you could wish for?
Your name cleared, and all happy once more.
Then it is yours. I am an accused man no longer.
Honor bright? How did you find it out?
Through that good friend of ours, Bijah Bright.
. Mr. Bright, I come to thank you once more. Polly, you can trust this man. He has proved loyal every time.
Thank you, Miss Dorothy. It's pleased I am to hear you say so.
She has promised to marry me, and we invite you to Oldtown for the wedding.
I accept upon the spot. Be good to him, Polly; he deserves it.
That she will. I can trust her for that.
O Massa Colonel, such a time; it's jest orful. Massa Newcomb he jests rants and tears like a house afire. Down in de hall am two gennlemen a-talking to him right smart. Shall I ax 'em up?
No, Pete. They will settle it amongst themselves. Do you remember what I promised you? That when the war was over I would help you find your mammy.
'Deed, Massa Colonel, I 'members, but 'specs der ain't no great hurry for dat. Yer's been so good to me, an' de missis, too. I should jes lub to stay wid you. Please massa, don't send me away.
No; no fear of that. As long as you are a good boy, you shall stay with me. I shall not forget what you did for me.
Please, massa, I done de bes I knows.
We all know that, and when your mammy does find you, she will be proud of her boy. And now, Pete, for the sake of the good old times in camp, give us one of your songs.

lines.source: (PETE _brings banjo; takes stage_, C., _and sings something pathetic_.)

parts.say: Those songs brought the tears to our eyes when we thought of you all at home.
But no more tears now. No more trouble: only sunshine. Just think of it, Roger. Pinky is to be married, you his best man, and I maid of honor.
I like that. Why not reverse things?
Oh, no; my last chance for that dignity. Wouldn't miss it for worlds. Besides, I promised for us both; didn't I, Pinky?
Indeed you did. No backsliding, old man.
As this little maid has signed the compact, I will help her keep it.
Is your heart lighter, Gordon?

Yes, Ruth; and already the color is coming to your cheeks. That, with Roger's forgiveness, makes me happy again. Ah! we all have suffered much, and have gained the happiness which I trust the future will bring.
Ruth, the household enemy is routed at last. There are bright days before us, but ever and anon will cross our paths memories of these dark days: the treachery of a friend; the bravery of our brother
, who could forget and forgive, and, at the risk of his own life, come to your husband's rescue “After Taps.”

lines.source: Enter Barnardo and Francisco two Centinels.

parts.say: Who's there?
Nay answer me: Stand & vnfold your selfe
Long liue the King
Barnardo?
He
You come most carefully vpon your houre
'Tis now strook twelue, get thee to bed Francisco
For this releefe much thankes: 'Tis bitter cold, And I am sicke at heart
Haue you had quiet Guard?
Not a Mouse stirring
Well, goodnight. If you do meet Horatio and Marcellus, the Riuals of my Watch, bid them make hast.
I thinke I heare them. Stand: who's there?
Friends to this ground
And Leige-men to the Dane
Giue you good night
O farwel honest Soldier, who hath relieu'd you? Fra. Barnardo ha's my place: giue you goodnight.
Holla Barnardo
Say, what is Horatio there?
A peece of him
Welcome Horatio, welcome good Marcellus
What, ha's this thing appear'd againe to night
I haue seene nothing

Horatio saies, 'tis but our Fantasie, And will not let beleefe take hold of him Touching this dreaded sight, twice seene of vs, Therefore I haue intreated him along With vs, to watch the minutes of this Night, That if againe this Apparition come, He may approue our eyes, and speake to it
Tush, tush, 'twill not appeare
Sit downe a-while, And let vs once againe assaile your eares, That are so fortified against our Story, What we two Nights haue seene
Well, sit we downe, And let vs heare Barnardo speake of this
Last night of all, When yond same Starre that's Westward from the Pole Had made his course t' illume that part of Heauen Where now it burnes, Marcellus and my selfe, The Bell then beating one
Peace, breake thee of:
In the same figure, like the King that's dead
Thou art a Scholler; speake to it Horatio
Lookes it not like the King? Marke it Horatio
Most like: It harrowes me with fear & wonder
It would be spoke too
Question it Horatio
What art thou that vsurp'st this time of night, Together with that Faire and Warlike forme In which the Maiesty of buried Denmarke Did sometimes march: By Heauen I charge thee speake
It is offended
See, it stalkes away
Stay: speake; speake: I Charge thee, speake.
'Tis gone, and will not answer
How now Horatio? You tremble & look pale: Is not this something more then Fantasie? What thinke you on't?
Before my God, I might not this beleeue Without the sensible and true auouch Of mine owne eyes
Is it not like the King?
As thou art to thy selfe, Such was the very Armour he had on, When th' Ambitious Norwey combatted: So frown'd he once, when in an angry parle He smot the sledded Pollax on the Ice. 'Tis strange
Thus twice before, and iust at this dead houre, With Martiall stalke, hath he gone by our Watch
In what particular thought to work, I know not: But in the grosse and scope of my Opinion, This boades some strange erruption to our State

Good now sit downe, & tell me he that knowes Why this same strict and most obseruant Watch, So nightly toyles the subiect of the Land, And why such dayly Cast of Brazon Cannon And Forraigne Mart for Implements of warre: Why such impresse of Ship-wrights, whose sore Taske Do's not diuide the Sunday from the weeke, What might be toward, that this sweaty hast Doth make the Night ioynt-Labourer with the day: Who is't that can informe me?
That can I, At least the whisper goes so: Our last King, Whose Image euen but now appear'd to vs, Was
by Fortinbras of Norway,

parts.direction: Thereto prick'd on by a most emulate Pride

parts.say: Dar'd to the Combate. In which, our Valiant Hamlet,

parts.direction: For so this side of our knowne world esteem'd him

parts.say: Did slay this Fortinbras: who by a Seal'd Compact, Well ratified by Law, and Heraldrie, Did forfeite

all those his Lands Which he stood seiz'd on, to the Conqueror: Against the which, a Moity competent Was gaged by our King: which had return'd To the Inheritance of Fortinbras, Had he bin Vanquisher, as by the same Cou'nant And carriage of the Article designe, His fell to Hamlet. Now sir, young Fortinbras, Of vnimproued Mettle, hot and full, Hath in the skirts of Norway, heere and there, Shark'd vp a List of Landlesse Resolutes, For Foode and Diet, to some Enterprize That hath a stomacke in't: which is no other

parts.direction: And it doth well appeare vnto our State

parts.say: But to recouer of vs by strong hand And termes Compulsatiue, those foresaid Lands So by his Father lost: and this
Is the maine Motiue of our Preparations, The Sourse of this our Watch, and the cheefe head Of this post-hast, and Romage in the Land.
Shall I strike at it with my Partizan?
Do, if it will not stand
'Tis heere
'Tis heere
'Tis gone.
It was about to speake, when the Cocke crew

And then it started, like a guilty thing Vpon a fearfull Summons. I haue heard, The Cocke that is the Trumpet to the day, Doth with his lofty and shrill-sounding Throate Awake the God of Day: and at his warning, Whether in Sea, or Fire, in Earth, or Ayre, Th' extrauagant, and erring Spirit, hyes To his Confine. And of the truth heerein, This present Obiect made probation
It faded on the crowing of the Cocke. Some sayes, that euer 'gainst that Season comes Wherein our Sauiours Birch is celebrated, The Bird of Dawning singeth all night long: And then
no Spirit can walke abroad, The nights are wholsome, then no Planets strike, No Faiery talkes, nor Witch hath power to Charme: So hallow'd, and so gracious is the time

So haue I heard, and do in part beleeue it. But looke, the Morne in Russet mantle clad, Walkes o're the dew of yon high Easterne Hill, Breake we our Watch vp, and by my aduice Let vs impart what we haue seene to night Vnto yong Hamlet. For vpon my life, This Spirit dumbe to vs, will speake to him: Do you consent we shall acquaint him with it, As needfull in our Loues, fitting our Duty?
Let do't I pray, and I this morning know Where we shall finde him most conueniently.

lines.source:
Enter Claudius King of Denmarke, Gertrude the Queene, Hamlet,
Polonius,
Laertes, and his Sister Ophelia, Lords Attendant.

parts.say: Though yet of Hamlet our deere Brothers death The memory be greene: and that it vs befitted To beare our hearts in greefe, and our whole Kingdome To be contracted in one brow of woe: Yet so farre hath Discretion fought with Nature, That we with wisest sorrow thinke on him, Together with remembrance of our selues. Therefore our sometimes Sister, now our Queene, Th' imperiall Ioyntresse of this warlike State, Haue we, as 'twere, with a defeated ioy, With one Auspicious, and one Dropping eye, With mirth in Funerall, and with Dirge in Marriage, In equall Scale weighing Delight and Dole Taken to Wife; nor haue we heerein barr'd Your better Wisedomes, which haue freely gone With this affaire along, for all our Thankes. Now followes, that you know young Fortinbras, Holding a weake supposall of our worth; Or thinking by our late deere Brothers death, Our State to be disioynt, and out of Frame, Colleagued with the dreame of his Aduantage; He hath not fayl'd to pester vs with Message, Importing the surrender of those Lands Lost by his Father: with all Bonds of Law To our most valiant Brother. So much for him.
We doubt it nothing, heartily farewell.

Dread my Lord, Your leaue and fauour to returne to France, From whence, though willingly I came to Denmarke To shew my duty in your Coronation, Yet now I must confesse, that duty done, My thoughts and wishes bend againe towards France, And bow them to your gracious leaue and pardon
Haue you your Fathers leaue? What sayes Pollonius?
He hath my Lord: I do beseech you giue him leaue to go
Take thy faire houre Laertes, time be thine, And thy best graces spend it at thy will: But now my Cosin Hamlet, and my Sonne?
A little more then kin, and lesse then kinde
How is it that the Clouds still hang on you?
Not so my Lord, I am too much i'th' Sun

Good Hamlet cast thy nightly colour off, And let thine eye looke like a Friend on Denmarke. Do not for euer with thy veyled lids Seeke for thy Noble Father in the dust; Thou know'st 'tis common, all that liues must dye, Passing through Nature, to Eternity
I Madam, it is common
If it be; Why seemes it so particular with thee
Seemes Madam? Nay, it is: I know not Seemes: 'Tis not alone my Inky Cloake

Nor Customary suites of solemne Blacke, Nor windy suspiration of forc'd breath, No, nor the fruitfull Riuer in the Eye, Nor the deiected hauiour of the Visage, Together with all Formes, Moods, shewes of Griefe, That can denote me truly. These indeed Seeme, For they are actions that a man might play: But I haue that Within, which passeth show; These, but the Trappings, and the Suites of woe

'Tis sweet and commendable In your Nature Hamlet, To giue these mourning duties to your Father: But you must know, your Father lost a Father, That Father lost, lost his, and the Suruiuer bound In filiall Obligation, for some terme To do obsequious Sorrow. But to perseuer In obstinate Condolement, is a course Of impious stubbornnesse. 'Tis vnmanly greefe, It shewes a will most incorrect to Heauen, A Heart vnfortified, a Minde impatient, An Vnderstanding simple, and vnschool'd: For, what we know must be, and is as common As any the most vulgar thing to sence, Why should we in our peeuish Opposition Take it to heart? Fye, 'tis a fault to Heauen, A fault against the Dead, a fault to Nature, To Reason most absurd, whose common Theame Is death of Fathers, and who still hath cried, From the first Coarse, till he that dyed to day, This must be so. We pray you throw to earth This vnpreuayling woe, and thinke of vs As of a Father; For let the world take note, You are the most immediate to our Throne, And with no lesse Nobility of Loue, Then that which deerest Father beares his Sonne, Do I impart towards you. For your intent In going backe to Schoole in Wittenberg, It is most retrograde to our desire: And we beseech you, bend you to remaine Heere in the cheere and comfort of our eye, Our cheefest Courtier Cosin, and our Sonne
Let not thy Mother lose her Prayers Hamlet: I prythee stay with vs, go not to Wittenberg
I shall in all my best Obey you Madam

Why 'tis a louing, and a faire Reply, Be as our selfe in Denmarke. Madam come, This gentle and vnforc'd accord of Hamlet Sits smiling to my heart; in grace whereof, No iocond health that Denmarke drinkes to day, But the great Cannon to the Clowds shall tell, And the Kings Rouce, the Heauens shall bruite againe, Respeaking earthly Thunder. Come away.

Oh that this too too solid Flesh, would melt, Thaw, and resolue it selfe into a Dew: Or that the Euerlasting had not fixt His Cannon 'gainst Selfe-slaughter. O God, O God! How weary, stale, flat, and vnprofitable Seemes to me all the vses of this world? Fie on't? Oh fie, fie, 'tis an vnweeded Garden That growes to Seed: Things rank, and grosse in Nature Possesse it meerely. That it should come to this: But two months dead: Nay, not so much; not two, So excellent a King, that was to this Hiperion to a Satyre: so louing to my Mother, That he might not beteene the windes of heauen Visit her face too roughly. Heauen and Earth Must I remember: why she would hang on him, As if encrease of Appetite had growne By what is fed on; and yet within a month? Let me not thinke on't: Frailty, thy name is woman. A little Month, or ere those shooes were old, With which she followed my poore Fathers body Like Niobe, all teares. Why she, euen she.

parts.direction: O Heauen! A beast that wants discourse of Reason Would haue mourn'd longer

parts.say: married with mine Vnkle, My Fathers Brother: but no more like my Father, Then I to Hercules. Within a Moneth? Ere yet the salt of most vnrighteous Teares Had left the flushing of her gauled eyes, She married. O most wicked speed, to post With such dexterity to Incestuous sheets: It is not, nor it cannot come to good. But breake my heart, for I must hold my tongue.
Haile to your Lordship
I am glad to see you well: Horatio, or I do forget my selfe
The same my Lord, And your poore Seruant euer
Sir my good friend, Ile change that name with you: And what make you from Wittenberg Horatio? Marcellus
My good Lord
I am very glad to see you: good euen Sir. But what in faith make you from Wittemberge?
A truant disposition, good my Lord

I would not haue your Enemy say so; Nor shall you doe mine eare that violence, To make it truster of your owne report Against your selfe. I know you are no Truant: But what is your affaire in Elsenour? Wee'l teach you to drinke deepe, ere you depart
My Lord, I came to see your Fathers Funerall
I pray thee doe not mock me
I thinke it was to see my Mothers Wedding
Indeed my Lord, it followed hard vpon

Thrift thrift Horatio: the Funerall Bakt-meats Did coldly furnish forth the Marriage Tables; Would I had met my dearest foe in heauen, Ere I had euer seene that day Horatio. My father, me thinkes I see my father
Oh where my Lord?
In my minds eye
I saw him once; he was a goodly King
He was a man, take him for all in all: I shall not look vpon his like againe
My Lord, I thinke I saw him yesternight
Saw? Who?
My Lord, the King your Father
The King my Father?
Season your admiration for a while With an attent eare; till I may deliuer Vpon the witnesse of these Gentlemen, This maruell to you
For Heauens loue let me heare
Two nights together, had these Gentlemen

on their Watch In the dead wast and middle of the night Beene thus encountred. A figure like your Father, Arm'd at all points exactly, Cap a Pe, Appeares before them, and with sollemne march Goes slow and stately: By them thrice he walkt, By their opprest and feare-surprized eyes, Within his Truncheons length; whilst they bestil'd Almost to Ielly with the Act of feare, Stand dumbe and speake not to him. This to me In dreadfull secrecie impart they did, And I with them the third Night kept the Watch, Whereas they had deliuer'd both in time, Forme of the thing; each word made true and good, The Apparition comes. I knew your Father: These hands are not more like
But where was this?
My Lord vpon the platforme where we watcht
Did you not speake to it?

My Lord, I did; But answere made it none: yet once me thought It lifted vp it head, and did addresse It selfe to motion, like as it would speake: But euen then, the Morning Cocke crew lowd; And at the sound it shrunke in hast away, And vanisht from our sight
Tis very strange
As I doe liue my honourd Lord 'tis true; And we did thinke it writ downe in our duty To let you know of it
Indeed, indeed Sirs; but this troubles me. Hold you the watch to Night?
We doe my Lord
Arm'd, say you?
Arm'd, my Lord
From top to toe?
My Lord, from head to foote
Then saw you not his face?
O yes, my Lord, he wore his Beauer vp
What, lookt he frowningly?
A countenance more in sorrow then in anger
Pale, or red?
Nay very pale
And fixt his eyes vpon you?
Most constantly
I would I had beene there
It would haue much amaz'd you
Very like, very like: staid it long?
While one with moderate hast might tell a hundred
Longer, longer
Not when I saw't
His Beard was grisly? no
It was, as I haue seene it in his life, A Sable Siluer'd
Ile watch to Night; perchance 'twill wake againe
I warrant you it will

If it assume my noble Fathers person, Ile speake to it, though Hell it selfe should gape And bid me hold my peace. I pray you all, If you haue hitherto conceald this sight; Let it bee treble in your silence still: And whatsoeuer els shall hap to night, Giue it an vnderstanding but no tongue; I will requite your loues; so fare ye well: Vpon the Platforme twixt eleuen and twelue, Ile visit you
Our duty to your Honour.

Your loue, as mine to you: farewell. My Fathers Spirit in Armes? All is not well: I doubt some foule play: would the Night were come; Till then sit still my soule; foule deeds will rise, Though all the earth orewhelm them to mens eies.
My necessaries are imbark't; Farewell: And Sister, as the Winds giue Benefit, And Conuoy is assistant; doe not sleepe, But let me heare from you
Doe you doubt that?

For Hamlet, and the trifling of his fauours, Hold it a fashion and a toy in Bloude; A Violet in the youth of Primy Nature; Froward, not permanent; sweet not lasting The suppliance of a minute? No more
No more but so

Thinke it no more: For nature cressant does not grow alone, In thewes and Bulke: but as his Temple waxes, The inward seruice of the Minde and Soule Growes wide withall. Perhaps he loues you now, And now no soyle nor cautell doth besmerch The vertue of his feare: but you must feare His greatnesse weigh'd, his will is not his owne; For hee himselfe is subiect to his Birth: Hee may not, as vnuallued persons doe, Carue for himselfe; for, on his choyce depends The sanctity and health of the whole State. And therefore must his choyce be circumscrib'd Vnto the voyce and yeelding of that Body, Whereof he is the Head. Then if he sayes he loues you, It fits your wisedome so farre to beleeue it; As he in his peculiar Sect and force May giue his saying deed: which is no further, Then the maine voyce of Denmarke goes withall. Then weight what losse your Honour may sustaine, If with too credent eare you list his Songs; Or lose your Heart; or your chast Treasure open To his vnmastred importunity. Feare it Ophelia, feare it my deare Sister, And keepe within the reare of your Affection; Out of the shot and danger of Desire.
