SCENE 1: _The stage of the Fulton Theatre, during the morning hours
just preceding the afternoon dress rehearsal of “April Follies.”_

AT RISE: _The curtain rises on a disorderly stage where a song and
comedy “number” is being rehearsed. We are looking at the stage from
the back—that is, we see directly into the footlights and into an empty
auditorium._

_Stage hands are working, shifting scenery back and forth; electricians
are placing lamps and experimenting with lighting effects. As the
curtain rises we hear the banging of a piano. We see a chorus in

_In the back, at the footlights, Lee, the producer, sits in a tilted
chair, a manuscript in his hand. Grouped between_ LEE _and the chorus,
on either side of_ CARTER, _are_ GENE, MISS GLYNN, MARY DALE, JIMMY
_and another actor. Seated in the shadowy foreground, playing cards
with a stage-hand, is_ JACK ROBIN.

_Most of the action in this scene is paced very swiftly. It gives the
effect of the hurried disorder which is characteristic of the eleventh
hour of a theatrical production. The action is almost frantic—one
speech piles on top of another so that you can scarcely follow it. It
is not necessary that you follow it. The picture is enough. It is only
at certain moments—moments when the story of the play enters with its
deeper note—that the action is slow, that characters begin to come into
focus—such moments as when_ JACK _and_ MARY _are alone, when_ JACK _is
alone with_ LEE, _etc._

parts.say: That’s all right! Is everybody concerned in the Dixie scene here?
Everybody concerned in the Dixie scene stand by.

parts.direction: A tall, stout man, meticulously dressed. He has a black mustache—probably dyed—and scant, grayish hair on an impressive bald head. Adversity sent him to the theatre, where he made money. Money sent him to Europe, where he achieved good clothes and an air of distinction. He never allows his air of distinction to interfere with efficiency, however; and, on the other hand, no matter how intense the excitement and confusion of the rehearsal, he never takes his coat off. He rises

parts.say: . Now, remember—this is the finale of the first act and I want lots of pep. Speak out so that everybody can hear you. This is the last time we do this scene before the Dress Rehearsal, so get it right. All ready? Let’s go.

parts.direction: He is gray-haired. He has large, wistful, cynical eyes. He has a droll, rolling, weary mouth. Once he was a great comedian. Today, while still well-known, he is relying on formula—and is speeding, without realizing it, into oblivion. Reads from part

parts.say: . “Mr. Carruthers, I’m from headquarters and I tell you that Gus, your colored porter, is none other than Dixie Dan, the Bootlegger.”
“Is that right?”
“That’s right, chief.”
“And what’s more, he has been very disrespectful to your daughter, Gwendolyn.”

parts.direction: He is the stage manager and one of the actors. He is a big, fat man in shirt sleeves, with the stub of a cigar in his mouth

parts.say: . “Gwendolyn, come here!”

parts.direction: She is bob-haired, slim and lovely. Five years ago she was a flapper. Four years ago she was a debutante. Three years ago she ran away and entered the chorus of the Metropolitan. Two years ago she had a minor rôle in musical comedy. Now she has the feminine lead. She is democratic, ironical, fastidious, informal, subtle and hearty

parts.say: . “Yes, father.”
“Did you know that Gus is a bootlegger?”
“Father, don’t believe a word he says. It’s too bad Mr. Gus isn’t here to defend himself.”
“Where is Gus the porter? Has any one seen him? Where can he be?”
“Look! Here he comes now.”

lines.source:
[_In typical musical comedy fashion every one stagily steps one foot
to the right and points with outstretched arm to the right. There is
the typical musical comedy hush which announces the entrance of a
principal._]

parts.say: “Ah”!
Where is Jack?... Robin! That’s your cue. Come on!

lines.source:
[_There is a moment of confused silence and then_ JACK, _coming out
of his absorption in the card game, rises hastily, apologetically. He
turns for a second to the stage-hand._]

parts.say: Spade—spade—spade! You lose! [_Now he hastens to the center of the

lines.source: scene. With an apologetic word to_ MR. LEE _he turns to his

parts.say: script._] Now, where are we?
“Gus, where’ve you been?”
“I’ve been down to my father’s farm where we have a black hen that lays a white egg.”
“What’s so wonderful about that?”
“You go home and try it!”
That’s the cue for my Poppy number, isn’t it, Mr. Lee?
No, Carter, I’ve changed my mind about that. I’ve decided to let Jack do that Poppy number in the second act.
Now, Mr. Lee, that’s the best number I got. That’s where I do my specialty.
Yes, Mr. Lee, I think you should let Carter keep that number. I’ve got enough to do now.

. That’s all right, Jack. I know that. Why do you think I postponed the opening? In order to give you more to do. You can carry this number, too. Now continue the scene and go right into the Dixie Number.

I’m sorry, Eddie.... Where were we? Oh, yes, sir. “I’m going down South again to the land of cotton and jasmine, where the watermelons grow, where I can be with my mammy. If you’ll all sit down, I’ll sing you a song all about it.”

lines.source:
[_The girls all sink down in a wide semi-circle. The other principals
back away. The piano beats out the “vamp.”_ JACK, _his back to us,
facing his own footlights, his shoulders shaking, his hat carelessly
on the back of his head, goes into his jazz song. He does not do it
earnestly, except for an occasional note on which he lingers with the
easy assurance of the man who knows that when the time comes he will do
it well. He sings._]
[LEE _blows his whistle and stops the singing._]

parts.say: I’ve got an idea. We won’t use this stage again until the dress rehearsal. Gene, send the girls up on the roof.

parts.mic: In less time than it takes to tell, the chorus girls have been shooed off the stage._ CARTER _and the rest move back to an obscure part of the stage._ LEE _brings_ JACK _down where we can hear clearly what they say._ MARY _comes with them. During the following conversation a drop comes down. It is the back of a country scene—you gather from the lights which play around its translucent surfaces that it represents a wisteria-hung house front.

parts.say: Now, Jack, there’s a big kick in the Mammy number. I want you to do it alone with no one on the stage. Just you and the spot light. Cut out the running around and put your heart into it. Give it all you’ve got. If you do it that way, you’ll be a knockout.
That’ll be wonderful, Jack.
. Do you think so?
. Harry, they just brought my last act costume and it’s nothing like the sketch.
Let me see it, Mary.
All right.

parts.direction: He has been lingering, ill at ease and resentful, in the back

parts.say: . Mr. Lee, I want to see you.
Well, Carter, what’s on your mind? Make it snappy.

All right, I’ll make it snappy. What’s the big idea cutting my numbers down? Half the house tonight is going to be my personal friends. What do you think they’re going to say about your show tomorrow on Broadway?

parts.direction: Comes between_ LEE _and_ CARTER. _He is disturbed. Something is troubling him. It must be something more serious than his words reveal

parts.say: . Mr. Lee, I think you ought to let Carter keep that Poppy number. He’s an old song-and-dance man and that’s more in his line.
What’s the matter, Jack, losing your nerve?
It isn’t my nerve, Mr. Lee. It’s just the success of your show I’m thinking about.
Let me worry about the success of my show, Jack. Don’t you want the opportunity I’m giving you?
I think it’s great, Mr. Lee, but—
. All right, then.
Gene, tell O’Hara to send that little Glynn girl here at once.
Yes, sir.
O’Hara, send that Glynn girl here. Mr. Lee wants to see her at once.

lines.source:
[CARTER _and_ JACK _sit on trunk facing up stage._ GENE _returns, sits
at table._]

parts.say: . I haven’t had anything like this happen to me in over forty years. I’m going to quit.

parts.direction: Pity for the old man swiftly welling up in him, yet realizing that nothing can be done, casts about for a jest with which to salve the other’s pain

parts.say: . Look here, Eddie, you’re not going to quit on the night I’m making my debutt.
Debutt?
Well, if that ain’t right, you can sue me! Now listen, Eddie. You just wait until after the opening tonight and you’ll probably have all your numbers back and maybe some of mine.
Come here, Eddie. I wrote a new scene for us.

lines.source:
[CARTER, _pathetically grateful for the respect and affection this
implies, moves back, out of the scene, with_ JACK. MISS GLYNN _comes
in. She is blond, pretty. She is in the rompers which chorus girls use
as practice clothes. As she moves toward_ Mr. LEE _she is obviously
frightened._]

parts.say: Mr. Lee, did you want me?
Yes, Miss Glynn. I’ve been watching your work in the finale this morning, and it’s very bad. Didn’t you tell me you were an experienced Spanish dancer when I hired you?
. Yes, sir.
Well, you’re not. I don’t believe you ever had any stage experience in your life. You dance like a school girl. Now answer my question. Did you do any professional work before?
N—no—B—but I thought—
I don’t care what you thought. Did you or didn’t you tell me you were in the “Follies”?

parts.direction: He has been listening to them while chatting with_ CARTER, _and now moves down

parts.say: . Excuse me, Mr. Lee. Could I see you just a minute?... Don’t blame this kid. Anything she slipped over on you was my fault. She—well I saw her in the waiting room—and she looked kind of bashful, poor kid—so I told her to tell you she had been in the “Follies.” I know you and Ziegfeld aren’t talking, so you’d never find out!
Well, I’ll be damned!

parts.direction: A master of the tempo of kidding, he moves hastily toward the stricken_ MISS GLYNN _and whispers to her. Her face lights up as she runs off the stage happily. Crescendo,_ JACK _turns to_ LEE

parts.say: . That’s all right, Mr. Lee. She forgives you! She isn’t mad at you at all!

parts.direction: JACK _doubles up with a grimace of mock humility, and_ LEE _succumbs. He laughs.

parts.say: You better not let Miss Dale catch you doing favors for little girls.

lines.source:
[JACK _grins and strolls across the stage, watching the electrician who
is playing with lighting effects._]

parts.direction: Comes in and goes to_ LEE _by the table. She has a sheet of paper which she places before him

parts.say: . Harry, here’s the sketch—
. Mr. Lee, Mr. Randolph Dillings just phoned and told me to tell you he was coming here this afternoon.
Thank you, Jimmy.

parts.direction: JIMMY _goes_. LEE _rises, and the act settles into a slower pace; for the “atmosphere” is over._ LEE _speaks half to himself.

parts.say: That’s too bad.
Is Randy still bothering you about Jack?
Yes. The last time he was down he wanted me to let Jack go.
Why?
You.
I don’t understand.
He’s jealous.
But he hasn’t even met Jack. He didn’t say anything to me about it.
Of course he wouldn’t—to you.
That’s perfectly childish of him.

parts.direction: He has been half absorbed during this dialogue with papers on the table. He picks them up and mumbles

parts.say: . Yes, I suppose it is.

lines.source:
[JACK, _who has been standing back-stage chatting with some girls, is
now heard laughing and joking with them. They are called away and_ JACK
_comes down to_ MARY _who is sitting on a trunk._]

parts.say: Well, you seem to be happy, Jack. I was afraid you’d be nervous on your opening night.
Me happy? I feel like I’ve been elected mayor and can’t find the City Hall. Mary, if any one gave me an unkind look, I’d lie down on the floor and cry.
Is there anything wrong, Jack? Is something worrying you?
You’re worrying me.
I?

. I can’t get over the feeling that if I don’t make good tonight, you’re going to be the goat. You and Mr. Lee. You’ve done everything for me—the two of you. So far, I haven’t done a thing in return.... I ain’t even thinking about what it would mean to me deep down here—
—if I flop. But then, that’s my business and nobody else’s.... The way things are now, though.... Gee, if I don’t make good with you—and with Lee—I’ll feel like hell.
Is
all that’s worrying you? Why, Jack, how silly you are! You’re going to be a sensational success, don’t you realize that? And everybody’s going to be proud of you.
. Not everybody. I know somebody who won’t be proud of me.
. You mean—your people?... I’ve often wondered why you never mentioned your people to me.
Well, I—I quarreled with them.
Where are they?
They’re far away.
Oh, it’s no use to talk about it.
I’m sorry.
. The point is, my people had other plans for me.... They—they’d sooner I was a criminal than be on the stage....
Well, I guess a lot of stage people have the same sort of problem you have.
My father and mother are different. I’m the only son, and they ... had other ideas about me.... I ran away from home.... They don’t think I’ll ever be any good.
Oh, my dear, serious young man, there’s nothing terrible in that.
You don’t know my father and mother, Mary.

Jack, there’s nothing as selfish as the selfishness of parents. Do you think my people liked the idea of my being on the stage? Mother threatened to have a nervous collapse. Father was frantic. But I did what I wanted, and they both got over it. And now they brag about me to the rest of the family.
Well, my father ain’t ever going to brag about me, I can tell you that!

lines.source:
[_There is a deepening cloud on his face as he moves away from_ MARY.
_He has almost forgotten the excitement of the dress rehearsal._ LEE
_and_ FRANKLYN FORBES _enter briskly._ FORBES _is snappily dressed,
about 30. The two of them bring back the speed and exuberance of the
theatre._]

parts.say: Here they are! Jack, you know Franklyn Forbes, our publicity man?
How are you, Mr. Forbes?
Franklyn wants to do a story on you in a hurry.
First of all, I want to get the story of your life.

parts.direction: Turns upon them in a curious mood—sardonic and humble, flippant and bitter

parts.say: . Say I was born when I was very young. When I was a year old I sold newspapers. By the time I was two I owned the stand.
Come on, Jack. Franklyn’s in a hurry.
Stop your kidding, Mr. Robin. I can get some real stuff into the papers about the way you put over a jazz song.
What has the story of my life got to do with the way I put over a jazz song?
Everything, Jack. If it’s the right kind of a story.
You know how Jack puts over a song. That intensity of his. Something like the intensity of Billy Sunday. It’s a new note.
Yes, and if I can weave a colorful life story behind it—based just a little on fact—
All right. I’ll tell you. Say that every morning at eight o’clock I take a bath in certified milk.
Don’t waste any time kidding, Jack. Give Franklyn a general outline of your life—where you were born, your parents, and so on.

I—I’m sorry, Mr. Lee, but I’m kinda sensitive about my childhood. Not that I’ve been in jail or anything like that. But why doesn’t Mr. Forbes fake a story—I don’t care what he says—it’ll be O. K. with me.
Fine! I think I’ll have the usual East Side back-ground—hanging around with the gang—singing waiter in a Bowery dive—pious old father—
I—I don’t think that East Side stuff is so good.
I do. It always makes fine human interest material.
. Well, I don’t think so.
We can’t waste any more time on this. Write anything you want to, Franklyn.

Now, please.... I don’t want you to think I am swell-headed.... I appreciate the fact that you are all trying to help me. But look—isn’t there enough in that Chicago stuff without going back to my cradle days?
That’s not a bad idea. Franklyn, why don’t you use the story of how Miss Dale discovered Jack?
I’ll tell it to you, Franklyn. I was playing in Chicago—

parts.direction: Takes out pad and pencil, sits at table

parts.say: . You were playing in Chicago?
I had a half hour to kill one day, and I dropped into one of those West Madison Street movie houses, and there he was.
This won’t be any good either—
Why?

Because after the opening night I’ll probably go back to Chicago—by freight. And the old gang at the movie house will give me the laugh. They’ll say, “Here he is—the great Jack Robin from Broadway! Hurray! Catch a broom and sweep out the place!”
What movie house was it, Miss Dale?
I don’t know. What house was it, Jack?
Oh, a funny little place under an elevated station—called The Happy Hour.
What were you doing there?
I was looking at Mary.
Jack was standing in a spotlight—dressed in
clothes....
You ought to see the suit I had, Mr. Lee, for eighteen fifty, with nine pair of pants!

And he was singing, “Take Me Back to Tennessee.” I never heard jazz sung quite like that before. There was a tear in it. I came every day that week. Jack did all sorts of things, comic songs, Mammy songs, sold candy up and down the aisle, announced next week’s program—about fourteen times a day.
Yeh, and I checked baby carriages, too! I did everything in that joint except collect the money. They wouldn’t let me do that.
Well, you know the rest, Franklyn.
. Thanks very much, Mr. Robin. You gave me more stuff for a good story than you thought you did. So long, Miss Dale. See you in your office, Mr. Lee.
Come on, Jack. We’ve got a lot of work to do.
Mary, do you want to come along with us?
I’d love to, Jack, but I have to telephone Dad.
Give my regards to your father, Mary.
Thanks, I will.

Mr. Lee, I took the liberty of writing a new gag in. It’s a good hot weather gag I’m going to pull with Carter. I say to Carter, “Now that the days are getting longer, I’m going into the ice business, so that when it gets too hot to work I can sit down on my business, and—”....
. Mr. Robin, that tailor just brought your suit. He wants you to try it on.
That funny suit for the last act with the little hat?
Yes.
I want to see that.
Excuse me.

lines.source:
[_He goes._ LEE _is at the table sorting out some manuscripts when_
RANDOLPH DILLINGS _enters._ DILLINGS _is about 30, well tailored,
poised, healthy looking. He is clearly a person of wealth and
breeding—a man whose only weakness, perhaps, is that he does not know
what he wants and is not intently concerned with finding out._]

parts.say: Hello, Randy.
Hello, Harry.
Come to see the rehearsal?
No, I came to see you. Can we go to your office?
The office is full of people. We can talk here. What’s on your mind?
This jazz singer of yours, Jack Robin, and Mary’s interest in him.
I thought we settled that a month ago.
I’m afraid we didn’t. I’ve been thinking it over, and I’ve decided to take my money out of your show.
I don’t get you, Randy. You know it isn’t very businesslike of you to come here at the last moment like this and—

This wasn’t a business arrangement in the first place—and you know it. I think you know that Mary and I were once engaged to be married. You must realize that the only reason I put my money into this show was to protect her interests. She means a great deal to me....
Her interests are the same today as they were a month ago. The fact that she has discovered Jack and made me engage him does not alter anything.

. Well, I’ve learned differently. The thing I was afraid of has happened. It was bound to happen sooner or later, I suppose—an attachment of this sort.... Now, I’m no stage-door Johnny. I have my limit, and I’ve reached it. Today I wash my hands of all responsibility for Mary’s career. Be a good fellow and don’t let’s argue the matter any more. Simply mail me a check today.
You’re not taking him seriously, are you? Why, he’s just a harmless kid—eager to get along—
. You’re taking him seriously enough to prefer him to my money, aren’t you?
. Yes, I am.
And Mary is taking him seriously enough to risk the gossip of her friends, isn’t she?
Yes, but—
I haven’t a thing against the boy. I wouldn’t know him if I saw him. But it’s clear he’s not Mary’s sort. And if she’s traveling in that direction, she’s going to travel without me.

parts.direction: He has made a decision; calls suddenly

parts.say: . Gene!
. Yes, sir?
Get Miss Dale.
Here! I won’t have any of that. No scenes, please.
. We’re going to have it out right now. I’m going to prove to you that Jack Robin doesn’t mean anything in Mary Dale’s life.
I won’t have Mary Dale brought into this discussion.
If I can prove to you that this boy doesn’t mean anything to Mary, will you leave things as they are?
. Hello, Randolph.
. Hello, Mary. Just dropped in for a moment. I must be running along.

parts.direction: A direct man if not a subtle one

parts.say: . Just a moment, Mary. Randy here thinks you are seriously in love with Jack Robin, and because of that he’s taking his money out of this show.
You gentlemen take my breath away with your—shall I say, delicacy? It’s very sweet of you to discuss me so intimately.
. See here, Harry, this isn’t the sort of thing—
The point is this—I told Randy that Jack doesn’t mean anything to you—except, of course—
Except what?
Really, this is becoming intolerable. I’m going.

. Just a minute, Randy. I know you too well not to understand that you’re acting, as usual, on principle. And I know Harry too well to mind his blunt ways. Apparently what you both want me to say is that Jack Robin doesn’t mean anything at all to me and that I shan’t see him after this except as one sees a fellow performer.

parts.direction: With a hearty sigh of relief

parts.say: . Exactly!
Well, I can’t say it. I like Jack tremendously and expect to see more of him than ever.
I’m sorry this has happened.
Harry, does this mean that you’re going to be in a terrible fix for money?
I’m always in a terrible fix for money. But I’m going to put this show through with what I’ve got if it breaks me.
Harry—you’re a darling.
No—just a business man.
There’s Jack now. Do you want to meet him? Jack! Yoo-hoo!
No.
How do you like these clothes, Mr. Lee? Don’t you think I look just like a manager? How’s this “Between the Acts”?
Long acts.
Jack, I want you to meet Mr. Randolph Dillings. Randy, this is Mr. Jack Robin.
. How are you, Mr. Dillings?
. How do you do?
Beautiful day for the opening of the new show, isn’t it?

parts.direction: There is a dead silence. It is not that_ DILLINGS _wishes to snub_ JACK, _but that he is furious and confused at the situation he has been forced into, and he does not quite know what to say._ JACK _turns to_ MARY _and murmurs out of the corner of his mouth.

parts.say: What’s the matter with this guy?
I say, it’s a beautiful day.
. Yes, Jack, it is a beautiful day.
Thank God, THAT’S settled!

parts.direction: There is another silence, then_ JACK _turns, good-humoredly, to_ DILLINGS. _He is like a healthy puppy wishing to make friends.

parts.say: I feel that I have known you a long time, Mr. Dillings. Mary has spoken of you very often and any friend of Mary’s is a friend of mine....
. Well, I must be going. Goodbye, Mary.

lines.source:
[JACK _realizes clearly now that he has been snubbed. With a hurt
expression he backs out of the scene and sits on the trunk._]

parts.say: Will I see you again, Randy?
I’m sorry—I’m afraid I won’t have time to see you again, Harry.
. Very well.
Goodbye, Randy.... I know you don’t mean to be like this.

lines.source:
[DILLINGS _pauses a second, then he bows stiffly, turns, and, ignoring_
JACK, _goes. After he has passed,_ JACK _in solemn mockery tips his
hat._]

parts.say: . That’s that Randolph Dillings, isn’t it? I don’t think he likes me. Maybe he thinks I wear these clothes on the street.
He’s an old friend of mine. Fearfully rich and awfully nice, but old-fashioned.
Is he in the show business?
He was.
Smart enough to get out, huh?... He’s stuck on you, ain’t he?
We were engaged once.
Yeh.... Any time you see a guy act like that, you know he’s in love. Well, there’s one thing I’ll say about him, he’s got good taste.
Do you think so?

parts.direction: Moves closer to_ MARY. _She is still sitting on the trunk. All of the flippancy has left him. He is suddenly shy and very earnest

parts.say: . Yeh.... You know, if I make one-half the hit tonight that Lee expects me to make—if I go over half as big as everybody thinks I will—do you know what I’d like to do? I’d like to come over close to you, like this, and tell you ... that I love you.
Mr. Robin.
That guy picks the darndest time to come in!
There’s a man out there asking for a Jakie Robin. His name is—
—Yudelson, Dealer in Diamonds and Jewelry. Do you know who it is?
Yudelson? It can’t be.
Well, well, well, Yudelson! What are you doing here?... He’s all right, Jimmy.
Well, well, Jakele, what a big boy you are! I never would have known you. What a trouble I had with him! First I asked for Jakie Rabinowitz. I forgot your Mama told me to ask for Jakie Robin.
My Mama? What’s the matter with Mama?
She’s all right. She told me to ask you—she asked I should say to you—

parts.direction: He is obviously uncomfortable in the presence of_ MARY.

parts.say: I must see you in person.
. Oh, Mary ... I I want you to meet Mr. Yudelson. This is Miss Mary Dale.
How do you do?
How do you do.

parts.direction: Looks at_ JACK _as he shakes her hand.

parts.say: A pleasure!
Mr. Yudelson is an old friend of the family. He’s known me since I was so high.
He and my father are great friends.
Cantor Rabinowitz and me, we are like this.

parts.direction: There is a pause._ YUDELSON _has revealed significant detail._ MARY’s _involuntary expression of surprise shows this._ JACK, _for an instant, is confused. Then, with pride in his voice

parts.say: . Yeh, my Father is the finest Cantor on the East Side.
Did you never heard of Cantor Rabinowitz of the Orchard Street Synagogue? I’m surprised!

parts.direction: The warm, friendly smile on her face is her answer—her fraternal declaration—to_ YUDELSON _and to_ JACK

parts.say: . Well I’ll run along. See you later, Jack. Goodbye, Mr. Yudelson. It was a pleasure to have met you.
By me it’s all right, too!

parts.direction: His arm about_ YUDELSON’s _shoulder, they move over to the table._ YUDELSON _sits in the chair and_ JACK _lounges on the table leaning on his elbow

parts.say: . Well, Yudelson, I’m glad to see you. Sit down. What brings you up in this neighborhood?
Jakie, I came to tell you your papa is sick.
. What’s the matter with him? Has he got a good doctor?

The best doctor in New York. Dr. O’Shaughnessy from the Rockenfeller Institute.... Jakie, my boy, tonight starts the Day of Atonement—Yom Kippur—and this is the first time in your papa’s life what he wouldn’t be able to sing in the synagogue on Yom Kippur. So we had a meeting from the committee, who should sing in his place. Well, I was speaking to your mama, and she thought it would be a beautiful surprise for your papa if you would do it.
Me to sing? My God, Yudelson, he kicked me out of the house only a month ago.

Don’t be foolish, Jakie. How much times was you kicked out—one time? A son could be kicked out twenty times, and yet a son is a son. If your papa knew you was singing tonight, it would make him happy.
But, Yudelson, I can’t do it!

Nonsense. I was telling the committee—you know how it is a committee—they wanted Levy, the Shamus, should sing. But I’m the chairman, and they all owe me money, so when they voted it was the way your mama wanted. I told them, “Jakie, when he was a little boy and he sang in the choir, his papa learned him all the words of all the prayers. And what a little boy learns he never forgets....” And even if maybe a few words you should forget, you can look in the prayer book. Jakie, you can do it! I got confidence in you! And your mama—she’ll be the happiest—
But, Yudelson, this show opens tonight!
What’s the matter with you, Jakie? Ain’t I telling you your papa is sick and your mama is waiting I should give her an answer?

. Yudelson, the show business is different from anything else. The finest actors keep right on working, even if there’s a death in the family. The show must go on.... It’s like a religion.... It’s like soldiers in an army....
. Now remember, Jimmy, I don’t want any strangers on the stage during dress rehearsal.
Jack! I want to see you.

Excuse me, this is Mr. Lee—my boss. Mr. Lee—gee, I don’t know how I can explain this to you. Well—this is Mr. Yudelson, an old family friend. He just told me that my father, down on the East Side, is very sick—
East Side?

I held out on you, Mr. Lee, because my father and I had quarreled. I thought he never wanted to see me again. It hurt me so much that I wanted to start fresh, live a new life.... But now I find I didn’t quite understand. My father is the Cantor of the Orchard Street Synagogue. Tonight is the eve of the Day of Atonement. He and my mother sent Mr. Yudelson to ask me to sing in my father’s place tonight. I know all the prayers—
My dear boy, it’s out of the question.
Mr. Lee, isn’t there any possible chance?
Only tonight and tomorrow until it gets dark.

No, absolutely not. Why you’re the whole show. I’ve staked everything on you.... Jack, I’m going to tell you something. I was an actor myself once. My mother died one afternoon, but I went on that night....
. Say, chief—
What is it?
The fire underwriters are here.
I’m coming.

parts.direction: To_ JACK, _slowly, earnestly, in a lowered voice.

parts.say: Something happened a while ago that puts me in a position where I’m depending on you more than you know. Now, talk him out of it.
That’s your boss?
. Yes.... Yudelson, do you realize what an awful lot of money is tied up in this show? It costs thousands and thousands of dollars....

parts.direction: Impressed, the business man in him responding

parts.say: . Is
so!
The scenery ... the costumes ... and all the actors.... Mr. Lee is responsible for everything—and he’s counting on me. You heard him—he’s staking everything on me.
that so?
Yudelson, you’re a business man ... now I ask you, how can I leave this show ... on a big opening night ... just because my mama and papa all of a sudden ... don’t you see?
Well, Jakie, if you can’t sing tonight, I’ll have to sit and listen to that voice from Levy’s.
Levy—that’s the Sexton, isn’t it? I’ll bet he’s got a fine voice.
Yeh, like a nanny goat! Nu, what can I do? I’ll explain to your mama the best way I can.
Yes, try to explain to them, Yudelson.
You’re sure you can’t come?
. You wouldn’t have to ask me twice. You know I’d come if I could.
. All right, Jakie. Well, goodbye. Leshono Tovo Tikosamu.
Thank you. Happy New Year to you, too.
Look! He remembers!
. Dress rehearsal just starting. Everybody concerned in the opening on stage!

lines.source:
[_From off-stage come the bustling sounds of final preparations for
the dress rehearsal._ JACK _is standing motionless where_ YUDELSON
_left him. A brown velvet drop comes down._ JACK _is the figure of
a tragic Pierrot as he stands against this simple background in his
ludicrously wide comedy pants and his ludicrously short comedy coat....
He turns ... finds himself sitting on the trunk alone, heavy-hearted._
LEE _comes bustling in. He goes over to table, not seeing_ JACK. _He
is busy with a manuscript for a few seconds, then he feels_ JACK’s
_presence; looks up._]

parts.say: Well, Jack, that old boy from the East Side has gone, eh?
. Yes, he’s gone.
. Talked him out of it, did you?
. Yes, I talked him out of it.

I knew you could do it! You’re clever enough to get away with anything.... Just think of it, one more rehearsal and then the big opening. Aren’t you thrilled? Tomorrow everybody will be talking about you.

parts.direction: To himself, in barely audible tones

parts.say: . This is the first time in his life he won’t be able to sing in the synagogue....
What’s that, Jack?

parts.direction: He rises, with a visible effort to shake himself out of his mood. He turns to_ LEE _and begins walking off with the manager

parts.say: . Oh, yes, Mr. Lee. I’ll do the best I can tonight—I only hope I won’t disappoint you.

lines.source:
[_The words are scarcely out of_ JACK’s _mouth when music is heard
blaring off-stage, and the lights black out._]

Scene 2: JACK’s _dressing room a few minutes later._ JACK _enters
looking very unhappy. Automatically he glances at himself in the
mirror, takes off his tie, his coat, his trousers, revealing another
pair underneath. Then he sits down before the mirror. There is a knock
at the door._

parts.say: Come in.

lines.source:
[MARY _enters. She is in pink costume. As she opens the door, music
off-stage is heard. As the door closes the music is muted._]

parts.say: Hello.
Hello.
Well?
Well, what?
Haven’t you anything to say about my costume?
Oh ... it’s nice ... very nice....
What enthusiasm!

lines.source:
[_The dialogue that follows goes on while_ JACK _is preparing his
make-up. He moves about occasionally, going from his dressing table to
the wash-basin, to the clothes closet. This movement and this general
business of his hands give an air of casualness to the rendition of
lines which are anything but casual in their meaning to_ JACK _and to_
MARY.]

parts.say: Gee, Mary, I’ve got other things besides costumes on my mind.
What is worrying you? That man who was here just now?
What’s the matter with him?
Nothing the matter with him. He brought me some news about my father and mother.

Oh, it isn’t fair! It isn’t fair for him to disturb you when you are all keyed up before your opening tonight.... Oh, Jack—I just want to keep you away from everything—from everybody—until tonight is over.
You’ve got the right hunch all right. Mary, Yudelson told me things that are making me hate myself.
Tell me about it. Maybe I can help.
No, if I told you about it, you’d hate me, too.
I don’t think anything could make me hate you, Jack....

parts.direction: There is a pause. She leans back, pretends to be absorbed in the ruffles on her costume.

parts.say: Did you mean it ... when you said you loved me?
Sure, didn’t you know that? I’m crazy about you....
No, I didn’t know it.... Jack, since you told me about your father I’ve been thinking about you. I can’t get you out of my mind. A son of a Cantor....
Maybe it’s better that you
get me out of your mind. Maybe it would be better if I got you out of
mind.... Since Yudelson was here, I got a different slant on everything.... Yudelson and me, Dillings and you.... We’re far apart. We’re worlds apart.

parts.direction: He is now standing by the wash-basin filing a small bowl of water, and he moves slowly back to the dressing table carefully balancing the water.

parts.say: You don’t have to worry about Randolph. I’m not like him.
Well, you’re certainly not like
.... I know what you’re figuring. I’m a rough diamond—you’ll get me and polish me. Well, it’ll never happen. I’m going to be what I am all my life. And you’re going to be what you are.
. Then why did you say you loved me?
. Do you really want to know?
Because I couldn’t help it. Love means marriage to me, and marriage means a home and kids.... I—I’d like to have a kid like you ... a little boy—but like you.... Gee, I’m crazy about you!
. Say it again!
I ain’t going to say it no more ... because I’ve got no right to say it.... Yudelson came and told me—
You’ve simply got to forget.... Let’s just talk about you and me.

I can’t forget what Yudelson said. He said my father is sick. Tonight is the eve of the Day of Atonement—the most solemn Jewish holy day of the year, the big day of every Cantor’s year. You know what a Cantor is? He’s the mouthpiece of the congregation. He sings to God. My mother sent Yudelson to ask me to sing in my father’s place. You don’t know what it means to them. For five generations the Rabinowitzes have been Cantors. The name Rabinowitz is like a trade mark on Orchard Street. No substitutes will do....
What did you tell Mr. Yudelson?

What could I tell him?... The most important part of the services will be starting just about the time I have to go on the stage tonight.... I told him no, that I wouldn’t miss this opening, not even for my father and mother.
. I am glad you said that, Jack.
Glad?
Yes, my dear. You’ve got to think only of your work.

I’ve tried so hard to do that, but ... Mary, here’s something I never told anybody in my life.... Sometimes when I’m alone—and I’m alone a lot more than you think—the old songs from the synagogue start wailing in my ears ... and I—I cry.... In that hall bedroom in Chicago, I used to get down on my knees in the dark and talk to God in Hebrew. I—bawled him out ... because he made me only half a Cantor—half a Cantor, and half a bum.
If I was all bum, I wouldn’t care. What does a bum care? But if I was all Cantor, I would be happy.
Would you?
I think I would.
Then why didn’t you go with Yudelson?

. Why? You know why—people like you—like Lee. I’ve got Broadway in my blood. There’s something sweet about the sound of the English language in my ears.... I want to be part of America. I want to take it in my arms.... Gee, I wish I could express myself!...
. My dear, I think I realize what you’re going through.
No you don’t....
Mary, my father is sick because of me.
. Nonsense.
He said a month ago he never wanted to see me again. I can see him now, eating his heart out ever since.
. What can you do about it? Go down on the East Side and be a Cantor the rest of your life?
No.
Don’t you care about your career on the stage?
. It’s the only thing in the world for me.
The only thing?
Yes, the only thing.
. More than me, Jack?
More than you.
. That’s what I’ve been waiting to find out.

parts.sound: Music begins again off-stage.

parts.say: Oh, don’t you see, Jack—I don’t want you selfishly. I want to see you live your own life. If the thing you want most is to be a black-face minstrel, then don’t let
stand in your way—not your parents—me—anything....
. I guess you’ve got the right idea, Mary. You’re O. K.

parts.sound: There is a knock on the door.

parts.say: Come in.
. Time you’re ready for your first number, Mr. Robin.
I’m almost ready now, Gene.
All right, Mr. Robin.
Hear that music? That’s that new fox-trot.

parts.direction: Hums, crosses stage and washes hands.

parts.say: It’s a steal from something.... Mary, you know, if people only knew what it was to black up like this, I bet everybody would do it. What’s the name of that bird that puts his head in the ground and thinks he’s all covered up?
Ostrich?
Well, I feel like him with this black on. It covers your face and hides everything.... You know, Mary, this would be a good job if I didn’t have to buy so much soap.

parts.sound: Crosses to make-up shelf. Another knock on the door.

parts.say: Come in.

parts.sound: Enters, leaving door wide open. Music swells until door closes

parts.say: . That man, Mr. Robin, the one who was here a while ago—he’s back. He insists on seeing you at once.
. It’s Yudelson.... Tell him he’ll have to wait until after this number.
There’s somebody with him—a lady.
A lady?
I’ll go, Jack.
No, Mary. Stay here.

parts.sound: JACK _moves swiftly in front of her. He has almost got to the door when_ YUDELSON _enters, followed by_ SARA. _She has evidently come in great haste, for all she wears is a shawl over her house dress. She is almost exhausted from the trip, and numb with the emotions with which she is stricken.

parts.say: Mama!
Jakie, this ain’t you....
It’s a nigger!
. Yudelson, didn’t you tell my mama?
I told her everything, the same way you told me, Jakie, but she made me I should bring her here.
. Jakie, your papa is sick. He is laying in bed. His face is white....
Mama, sit down, please.

lines.source:
[_All this happens very quickly. And now_ JACK, _for an instant, has
forgotten everything except his mother’s presence. He places a chair
for her and automatically sinks back in his chair, arms on knees,
facing her._]

parts.direction: Continues numbly, hardly seeing the youth in blackface

parts.say: . All the time he is talking about you. His eyes is open like a baby’s eyes. His face is white like a
candle. He was saying, “Sara,” he said—his voice was so low, I could hardly hear him—“maybe Jakie will sing tonight in the synagogue....”
. He really said that, Mama?

He said it—the way I’m sitting here this minute, he said it.... For five generations God always heard a Rabinowitz sing every Day of Atonement, every holy day, every Sabbath. God is used to it now.... Maybe your papa is dying. God will ask him, Is Jakie singing in the synagogue tonight? How can he say, No, he is singing in a theatre!... Oh, my son, my heart is breaking in pieces.... You got two hours before the sun goes out of the sky and it gets dark. Come with me home, Jakie.

parts.direction: Despairingly, head sunk on his chest

parts.say: . Mama, I can’t. I can’t do it!

. How can you say this to me, your mama?... When you was a little boy, we were so poor.... I slaved my fingers to the bone that there should be money to buy you nice things. My fingers, they used to bleed. Look at my hands, Jakie. It is still there the marks.
. I know, Mama. I know.
Your specialty’ll be on in a minute, Mr. Robin.
All right, Gene.... Mama, I haven’t time to tell you—I’ve got to go on! Yudelson ... Mary ... tell my mother....
I’ll go out and see if I can’t hold them for a moment.

. Your papa said, “Ask Jakie he should forgive me. He is doing things from sin, but he don’t mean it. In his heart he is a Rabinowitz”.... Jakie, the way I’m sitting here, before God I swear it—that is what he said.
. I believe you, mama! I believe you!
. We’re waiting for you, Mr. Robin. We can’t hold it any longer.
. Yes, yes, I’m coming!... Mama, if you only knew how the manager is depending on me....

parts.mic: Off-stage can be heard the introductory chords to a jazz song.

parts.say: They’re going to make me a star, Mama....
. There’s your introduction, Mr. Robin!
Yes, yes!

parts.direction: He is now in full comedy costume and is kneeling before his mother.

parts.say: Mama, there’s my introduction—wait here fifteen minutes—I haven’t got time to tell you.... Yudelson! Please talk to my mama.
. Mr. Robin, they’ll blame me for this!
Yes, yes, I’m coming. Mama—Yudelson—wait! Please!

lines.source:
[_He goes. The door is open. We see the changing lights through the
door._ YUDELSON _gently forces_ SARA _into a chair by the door as we
hear_ JACK _off-stage shouting the comedy lines of the beginning of the
act.... “I’m going down South to the land of cotton and jasmine, where

parts.say: the watermelons grow, where I can be with my Mammy. If you’ll all sit down I’ll sing you a song all about it”...._

lines.source:
_Then the orchestra throbs into wailing, syncopating life, and_ JACK
_is heard, off-stage singing a verse and chorus of “Dixie Mammy.” His
rendition is excellent jazz—that is, it has an evangelical fervor,
a fanatical frenzy; it wallows in plaintiveness and has moments of
staggering dramatic intensity, despite the obvious shoddiness of the
words and the music. We are listening to a Cantor in blackface, to a
ritual supplication on the stage, to religion cheapened and intensified
by the trappings of Broadway. He finishes his first chorus._]

parts.sound: Crosses to the door, listens

parts.say: . That’s Jakie.

lines.source:
[JACK _is going into a complicated staccato “talking” dramatization of
the last half of the chorus—something like this:_

[SARA _rises, a broken creature, her frail body barely able to carry
her out. She moves out of the door,_ YUDELSON _following her, trying to
detain her._]

parts.say: That ain’t my Jakie! That ain’t my boy!... I’m going home!

lines.source:
[_The stage is empty. We see the grotesque, elongated shadows of_ SARA
_and_ YUDELSON _against the multi-colored lights back-stage as they
pass, evidently out of the theatre. We are hearing_ JACK’s _last line
of the song—_

_“I’ve had my fling,
    And it don’t mean a thing—”_

_His voice breaks. He repeats in intensely personal agony, “It don’t
mean a thing ... it don’t mean a thing—my God!—it don’t mean a....”_

_There is a sudden awkward silence—a silence of a fraction of a second;
and then we hear, offstage, a surge of congratulations. We hear_
CARTER’s _voice, the voices of women,_ GENE’s _voice. The next instant_
JACK _is in the door-way. He sees that the dressing room is empty. He
turns, helplessly looking about. He knows it is no use—that his mother
has gone. He stands for a second brushing the eyes of his blacked up
face with his white glove._

_And then_ CARTER, GENE, _half a dozen chorus girls, and_ FORBES _break
in upon him. They are enthusiastic, excited, congratulatory. Their
remarks tumble one on top of the other in a confusion of sound:_
_“I take off my hat to you,_ Jack_!”_
_“You certainly can put over a song!”_
_“You won’t need a press agent after tonight, old fellow!”_

parts.say: Jack, that was wonderful! Why, you actually cried! Say, do it that way tonight and you’ll be a knock-out.

parts.direction: LEE _bolts out, calling as he goes.

parts.say: All right, Gene! Ready for the next number!

lines.source:
[JACK _is alone on the stage. He sinks into a chair as the curtain
falls._]
TIME: _About an hour and a half after Act II._

AT RISE: _Stage is empty. Since it is about six o’clock on a September
day, the light is beginning to wane. Throughout this act, dark
gradually creeps into the room, while outside the window a bar of
sunset radiance deepens in contrast._

_There is a knock on the door, and_ LEVY, _the Shamus, or Sexton,
corner in. He looks about, opening one or two doors, and apparently
he finds no one. He shrugs his shoulders, muttering and humming to
himself, and is about to go out when_ MOEY _enters from the music room._

parts.say: Where is Mr. Yudelson?
He went with Mrs. Rabinowitz to take the Cantor to the hospital.
Is he coming back here?
Sure he’s coming back. He told me to wait here and he’d give me a dime.
Well, you tell him I got to see him personal—it’s very important. I’ll be back.

parts.sound: LEVY _goes._ MOEY _looks out of the window with the air of a conspirator, takes a cookie from his pocket, munches it, draws a lurid dime novel from another pocket and settles himself comfortably to read. The door opens and he hastily thrusts the dime novel under the table, jamming the rest of the cookie, evidently stolen from the kitchen, into his pocket.

parts.direction: Enters, followed by_ DR. O’SHAUGHNESSY _and_ YUDELSON. _Her face is deadly pale and lined with suffering. She is so weary that she can hardly move. She says over and over again

parts.say: . He didn’t want I should stay with him.... My Yosele didn’t want I should stay with him.

lines.source:
[_The doctor helps her over to the settee; then he takes bottles from
his medicine case and prepares a potion for her._]

parts.say: Did anybody come, Moey?
Yeh, a lot of people. Gee, Mrs. Schultz from upstairs, and Mrs. Lefkowitch ... and a lot of people.
Did you tell them—
Yeh, I told them you were taking the Cantor to a hospital.
Did they said anything about Jakie?
Yeh, they all asked about him, and if he’s coming to sing. And Mr. Levy was here three times. He said you should see him as soon as you came.
All right, Moey, you can go—you’re a good boy. Here is the nickel I promised you for minding the house.
. You promised me a dime.
. That’s right. I’ll give you later!
Here, drink some of this. You’ll feel much better.
He didn’t want I should stay with him. My Yosele didn’t want I should stay with him—
That’s very natural, Mrs. Rabinowitz—the Cantor is weak. He needs the quiet of a hospital.
Quiet he needs? You think he’s laying there in the hospital quiet? Why did I tell him Jakie ain’t coming? Why didn’t I tell him a lie?

Now, drink this. Then you must lie down for a half-hour. And then you simply must eat. You promised the Cantor you were going to attend the services, you know, and you must have some nourishment if you’re going to fast tonight and tomorrow.
Doctor, tell me the true. The Cantor, he’s dying?
. I think, if we keep him very quiet, he’ll come through. He has a powerful constitution. Come now, Mrs. Rabinowitz, take this.
Yes, drink, drink.
Now, let me help you into your room. Just lie down for a little while—

parts.sound: He takes her to door.

parts.say: Stay here as long as you can, Mr. Yudelson. And keep the neighbors out.
I did that already.

lines.source:
[_The doctor goes into_ SARA’s _room. A knock, and_ CLARENCE KAHN
_enters._]

parts.say: . Mr. Yudelson! I don’t know what to do with the choir!
What’s the matter now?
They don’t want to sing tonight.
They don’t want to sing?
They say Mr. Levy doesn’t know any of the Cantor’s tunes, that his voice is inadequate, and that he’d be better off singing alone than spoiling the services with a choir.

. They’re loafers, but they’re right.... What can I do? The members are paying a special assessment five dollars for the Day of Atonement singing.... If Levy sings, they’ll want we should give them the money back.
Have you tried my cousin, Avram Lipski? He came from Russia last week. He lives around the corner.
Why didn’t you speak from this before? Avram Lipski I know—at least a voice he’s got.

parts.sound: Knocks and enters

parts.say: . Aha! Mr. Yudelson! You’re just the man I was wanting to see!
. Nu, Mr. Levy—?
. I must get from you official the order I should sing tonight.
. Oh no, I couldn’t give you yet.
If you couldn’t give me, who could?
could give you, but I couldn’t give you yet.
What kind answer is this? It’s nearly dark, and you couldn’t give me official the appointment yet?
. Mr. Levy, several points of view must be taken into consideration. The choir must be considered, for instance.
I told you, I couldn’t give you yet. In half an hour I’ll know.
In a half an hour it will be too late. I got to practise a little bit in advance with the choir, ain’t I?
In half an hour it’ll be too late? For thirty years you waited the Cantor should get sick, you can wait another half hour!
. Brother Yudelson, you are the chairman from the Executive Committee, no?
Brother Levy, I am the chairman of the Executive Committee. Make yourself a
from it.
All right—
right.
you are the chairman from the Executive Committee. So I want to
you, who is the shamus of the Orchard Street Synagogue? Am I the shamus oder
I the shamus?

lines.source:
[_The argument has reached its vociferous height when suddenly the door
is opened and_ JACK _stands on the threshold. His appearance cuts the
noise of the three men in the room as if with a knife. They stare at
him open-mouthed. He is out of breath. He is a young man who has made a
grave decision, and that decision has already given him a new dignity.
In an instant, pale and quiet, he is by_ YUDELSON’s _side._]

parts.direction: The first of the three to recover

parts.say: . Jakie!
Yudelson, get me a praying shawl, and see if you can find a plush skull cap like the Cantor’s, only a little smaller.
. A praying shawl and a skull cap! Jakie is going to sing!
Jack is going to sing!

parts.direction: He rushes out with the news.

parts.say: Levy, get a praying shawl and a skull cap, quick!
Where could I find—
You’re the shamus, ain’t you? For a shamus it ain’t hard to find plenty praying shawls.

parts.sound: Moves to the door, protestingly

parts.say: . He’s going to sing? A young boy from Broadway! What does he know from Shool? The committee is making a big mistake—
. I’ll speak from this at the next committee meeting.

parts.direction: Moves over to_ JACK, _deep feeling in his voice.

parts.say: Jakie, I’m so glad you came.... I’m so glad.
Where you going?
To see my father.
He ain’t there.
We just took him to the hospital.
. Hospital?
Yes. Gouverneur Hospital.
Where’s Mama?
She’s inside. You stay here. I’ll call her.
Mrs. Rabinowitz! Mrs. Rabinowitz! Jakie is here! Jakie is here!

parts.direction: Can be heard, her voice throbbing

parts.say: . Jakie here?
I knew you was coming, Jakie. I knew you was coming!

parts.direction: She sinks on the settee and for the first time tears stream from her eyes.

parts.say: Oh, my Jakie ... my darling ... I knew you was coming....
Mama, Mama.... I couldn’t stand it.... I had to come.... Yudelson told me about Papa—
Hello, Dr. O’Shaughnessy.
How do you do, Jakie.
. Is my father ... worse?
Oh, Jakie, he’ll be better now—he’ll be better. The doctor will tell him. Doctor, please go right away and tell the Cantor Jakie is here.
I’ll go with you, if you don’t think it’ll do any harm.
Better not. It might excite him too much to see you. I’ll tell him. It’ll do him all the good in the world....
. Jakie—you’re going to sing, ain’t you?
Yes, Mama.
. Doctor, tell the Cantor Jakie is going to sing!... Couldn’t I please speak with him on the telephone?
No! That’s impossible, Mrs. Rabinowitz.

parts.sound: He is moving toward the door.

parts.say: Doctor, remember to tell him everything.
Yes.
Tell him Jakie came right away.
Yes, yes.
Tell him Jakie looks beautiful!
I’ll tell him.
Tell him Jakie is standing on pins and needles, so anxious he is to practise with the choir. Tell him Jakie ain’t even
from no theatre.
I’ll tell him, Mrs. Rabinowitz.
Don’t forget!
I won’t. And don’t
forget to eat and get a good night’s sleep. Goodbye.

parts.sound: He goes toward the door, stopping by_ YUDELSON.

parts.say: My telephone number’s on this card. I’ll be at the hospital. If you want me call me there.
The doctor said you must eat, Mama.
Sure I’ll eat. And you, too. I made ready such a lot to eat before fasting.
I don’t want anything, Mama.
Never mind, I’ll make you anyway a cup of tea.
You see, she’s a new person already.

. Yudelson ... don’t tell Mama ... but I left without even seeing the boss. Just as soon as the dress rehearsal was finished, I told the stage manager I wasn’t going to show up.... Well—you were there. You know what I told you about the show....
. It’s a lot of money, and you’re throwing it away for your papa!
It isn’t the money, Yudelson. Mr. Lee believed in me, and I left him flat.
Never mind. Never mind. Don’t worry from bosses. A papa is hard to find, but bosses there’s planty....
I’m finished.
Jakie, don’t worry. You can always have a job in my store.
. Why doesn’t Levy show up with that praying shawl? Why does everybody take so long?

parts.sound: Moves to the door

parts.sound: YUDELSON _hastens out._ JACK _sits in silence for a moment; then, head in his hands, he begins humming to himself the plaintive, majestic cadences of Kol Nidre. parts.say: Mr. Lee!

parts.direction: He crosses to_ JACK. _They both are standing, tense.

I’d rather cut off my right arm than do this to you.
Forget me—think of yourself. You’re a young fellow. Tonight is the chance of a lifetime for you.
I know it.

You may think in your heart you’ll succeed anyway. I know better.... If you don’t come through for me tonight, I could never bring myself to engage you again. Rumors will creep out on Broadway. . I know it, Mr. Lee. I don’t want any mercy.
. How sick
your father?... Is he too sick to be talked to?... I should think he’d be proud of you when you tell him what a great opportunity you’re getting....
He couldn’t understand any more than you can understand.
Why
you doing this?
I don’t know.... I’m doing it.... Isn’t that enough?
Well, I’ll
you why you’re doing it—
Don’t give me any more analysis. It gives me a headache.
It’s going to give you a much greater headache when the lawyers get after you.
Lawyers?

You know, my boy, you signed a pay-or-play contract. And you didn’t sign it with me as an individual. You signed it with a corporation of which I am the president. That corporation has stockholders. Those stockholders vote....

No.
Then
me without asking them....

. Now listen. This afternoon I broke with my biggest backer on your account. And now my own money—every dollar I have on earth—is at stake.... I hate to bring in the personal element, Jack, but you have it in your hands either to make or break me.

Why don’t you get another theatre?
At this time of the year?
You’ve got a lot of nerve, asking me that! Nobody ever did that much for me, and I’ll be damned if I’ll do it for you!
You’re hard.
You bet I’m hard. I’m in a hard business. It’s like being in an army. The soft man gets licked. You’re soft—and you’re getting licked.

. Soft, because I’m giving up the biggest night of my life to keep my mother’s heart from breaking? You think it’s going to be easy for me to stand there singing stuff that doesn’t mean anything to me anymore and give up playing to a big Broadway opening night?... Soft because I’m giving up the only girl I ever loved—

. You’re kidding yourself. You really want to sing in a Synagogue tonight. You’re getting a kick out of feeling like a martyr. I’ve seen this sort of thing before. First-rate people don’t pull it. . Jakie, I got ready for you a cup of tea.
Not now, Mama.

Thank you.
Circle 13876....

Your papa and mama wouldn’t attend to
business if

You’re just as big a baby as he is! Jack is crazy to make good for you. You ought to know that.
You didn’t talk to him. I did.

For good?

. Sometimes, Harry, when I hear you big successful men in critical moments, I wonder how you ever got where you are. You know so little about why people do things. You ought to know, Harry, that Jack will be back in three days, ready to sing his heart out for you.
. You just take one look at that boy and you’ll change your mind.

. You can’t do anything with him.... Maybe you can with his mother.... That’s why I stayed behind. I want to talk to her just once more.... I want to convince her that he belongs to us, and not down here.

Yes.
She’s real.... That’s why it took me so long to make up my mind. And then I realized that if I could show her the truth—
. How do you do, Mrs. Rabinowitz?
Hello, lady. Your name I don’t know, so excited I was in the theatre. You came maybe you should hear Jakie sing tonight?

Right now you couldn’t see him. He’s in the synagogue. He’s practising with the choir. Open the window, and you could hear him just like you was sitting there.

I love Jack, too, Mrs. Rabinowitz—and that’s why I want him to go to the theatre tonight.... It’s his one great opportunity.
You know, I found him.
You found him?
I recognized his ability—I helped him to realize his own powers.
Oh, please, can’t you understand? I’m trying to do the one thing a woman can do for a man.

parts.direction: He has come to a decision and now breaks in

parts.say: . Mrs. Rabinowitz, let me ask you a question.... When was the last time that Jack attended a synagogue?
When he was confirmed. He was thirteen years old. He sang a solo in the choir. It was beautiful.
Mary, did he ever attend a synagogue during the time you have known him?
No.
Mrs. Rabinowitz, he ran away from all this,
didn’t he?
. Why are you asking me like this questions?

. Because I want that boy to be true to himself. Do you suppose the Cantor would want Jack to sing unless he sings with the heart of a Jew? I know that boy. He’s saying to himself, “My career is gone. The girl I love is losing faith in me. I don’t want to sing this stuff that I don’t understand—to a God whose meaning I don’t get.” He’s saying to himself, “My mother will be heartbroken if I don’t do it. My father will die. That’s why I’ll do it.”
. No, no. You are telling me lies!
. Harry—let’s go—can’t you see you are hurting—
. Supposing the Cantor could see into Jack’s heart? Do you know what he would see there? Jazz music,
—if you want to call it that. Do you think that would make him happy?

lines.source:
[_The door opens and_ JACK _enters. The evening light has deepened._
JACK’s _face is white, his eyes burning black. There is a new quality
in him; he has become fanatic_].

parts.say: Mama, you better get ready.

parts.direction: He sees no one, apparently, except his mother.

parts.say: The services will begin soon.

parts.direction: Now he sees_ MARY. _Carefully laying down the praying shawl and skull cap he brought with him, he turns to her. He speaks quietly.

parts.say: You came!
Yes, Jack.
. I’m glad.
Jakie.
Yes.
I want to ask you something....
Yes, Mama.
I want you should tell me the truth.
Yes, Mama.

Jakie, I want you to do only what is in your heart. Answer me: Are you singing tonight because you love me and your Papa and your God—because you want to be in the Synagogue on the Day of Atonement—or is your heart far away in theatres with jazz music?
. What are you people doing here—what are you trying to do to me?
We’re here for your sake, Jack.
Did
put this into my mother’s head?
I did, Jack.

So did I.... Oh, Jack—don’t you understand? I love you. I love you enough to be cruel to you for your sake. Oh, my dear, tell me that you are true to yourself, and I’ll go. I’ll go and I’ll come back to you. Tell me that you lied this afternoon when you said that the only real thing in your life was your career—tell me that you lied every time you got up on the stage in that Madison Street movie house—

parts.direction: Turns on her with an effort

parts.say: . Mama, get ready. We’ll be late.
. All we want is the truth, Jack. When I came in here—when I talked to you, didn’t you want to come back with me?

parts.mic: In your heart didn’t you want to come back?

parts.say: Jack—this afternoon, when you were talking to me, you told me—you said—
Jakie—did you
to come?

parts.direction: Sinks into chair. He is defeated

parts.say: . No.
. And yet you came ... you came home ... and you was singing with the choir....
Yes, I came home....

parts.direction: Her voice sings a hymn of sacrifice

parts.say: . It’s enough. I didn’t know until today how different your life is from your papa’s, from mine. I didn’t understand that by you being a ragtime singer is like by your papa being a Cantor.... Jakie—do what is in your heart.... Always you can come back to me. I’m your mama.... But if you sing tonight and God ain’t in your heart, your Papa he’ll know.... All his life your papa loved God and the truth. Maybe if I tell your papa, he will understand....

parts.direction: On the point of collapse. His voice is bitter, sardonic in defeat

parts.say: . Me a Cantor.... Funny—that’s what it is—funny.... I was just rehearsing with the choir, and they were like strangers to me—the same little boys that I used to play with—and they were strangers to me!... Sure! I’m from uptown—Broadway.... Seemed like every one of them was pointing his finger at me and saying, “Jakie Rabinowitz, jazz singer! Jakie Rabinowitz, jazz singer!”...
. We have exactly a half-hour to get to the theatre.
. It’s all right, Jakie.... You can go....

parts.sound: The telephone rings—she crosses to it.

parts.say: Hello—what?... Who?... I can’t hear you.... What?... It’s a buzzing in my ears—I can’t—
. Shall I?
. Thank you.
Hello.... I’ll talk for Mrs. Rabinowitz.... Yes, she’s right here. I’ll take the message.... What is it?... Doctor O’Shaughnessy? Yes....

Yes—he’s resting.
Thank you.
. Mama, you’d better get ready. We’ll be late.

parts.say: Is he ... worse?
. He just ... died.

parts.say: The Day of Atonement!—I’ll say it’s the Day of Atonement.

parts.direction: SARA _enters with lighted candles._ JACK _suddenly turns to her.

parts.say: Mama! I’m going with you! I’m going to the synagogue!
. Jakie!

parts.direction: He is strong in the power of his decision.

parts.say: . Jakie!

. Your papa will be so happy! He will be so happy....

Of course. Why not?
GRACE

. Never mind why. Now tell me, is this your first love affair?

parts.direction: amazed at the simplicity of the question

. Yes.

Julia Craven?

parts.direction: She shakes her head mysteriously, and he turns away from her moodily and adds

parts.say: CHARTERIS

parts.direction: yielding mechanically to the pull, and allowing her hand to rest on his arm, but sitting squarely without the least attempt to return the caress

parts.say: . Do I feel harder to the touch than I did five minutes ago?

parts.direction: Brooding, with his chin on his right hand and his elbow on his knee.

I have sat alone with her just as I am sitting with you--
GRACE

. Just!
CHARTERIS

parts.direction: sitting upright and facing her steadily

parts.say: . Just exactly. She has put her hands in mine, and laid her cheek against mine, and listened to me saying all sorts of silly things.

GRACE

. When did you break it off?
CHARTERIS

GRACE

CHARTERIS

parts.direction: mischievously, making it plainer and plainer that it has not been broken off

Oh, yes:
broke it off,

CHARTERIS
. As a favour to me, dearest, change the subject. Come away from the piano: I want you to sit here with me.
No. I also have grown hard to the touch--much harder than hickory for the present. Did she break it off?

She did what a woman like Julia always does. When I explained personally, she said it was not not my better self that was speaking, and that she knew I still really loved her. When I wrote it to her with brutal explicitness, she read the letter carefully and then sent it back to me with a note to say that she had not had the courage to open it, and that I ought to be ashamed of having written it.

parts.direction: Comes beside Grace, and puts his left hand caressingly round her neck.

parts.say: You see, dearie, she won't look the situation in the face.

parts.direction: shaking off his hand and turning a little away on the stool

parts.say: . I am afraid, from the light way in which you speak of it, you did not
My dear, when you are doing what a woman calls breaking her heart, you may sound the very prettiest chords you can find on the piano; but to her ears it is just like this--

parts.say: GRACE

. What are you going to try now?
CHARTERIS

parts.direction: on the hearthrug, turning to face her

GRACE
. Then, if you please, I decline to be made use of for any such purpose. I will not steal you from another woman.

parts.direction: She begins to walk up and down the room with ominous disquiet.

parts.say: Steal me!
Grace: I have a question to put to you as an advanced woman. Mind! as an advanced woman. Does Julia belong to me? Am I her owner--her master?

Quite right. Ibsen for ever! That's exactly my opinion. Now tell me, do I belong to Julia; or have I a right to belong to myself?
GRACE

. Of course you have; but--
CHARTERIS
. Then how can you steal me from Julia if I don't belong to her?

parts.direction: Catching her by the shoulders and holding her out at arm's length in front of him.

parts.say: Eh, little philosopher? No, my dear: if Ibsen sauce is good for the goose, it's good for the gander as well. Besides

GRACE
. So much the worse! I hate your philanderings: they make me ashamed of you and of myself.

parts.say: Grace: you utterly misunderstand the origin of my philanderings.

GRACE

parts.direction: turning to him as if astonished at his conceit

parts.say:
. No!
CHARTERIS
. You admit it. Am I a well dressed man?
Not particularly.

Not in the least.

Certainly not. No one can accuse me of it. Then whose fault is it that half the women I speak to fall in love with me? Not mine: I hate it: it bores me to distraction. CHARTERIS
. With you, dearest, the coyness was sheer coquetry. I loved you from the first, and fled only that you might pursue. But come! let us talk about something really interesting.
Do you love me better than anyone else in the world?

That depends on who the person is. You
cannot love me too much: you cannot love me half enough. I reproach you every day for your coldness--your--

parts.say:

CHARTERIS
. Julia! The devil!

. Oh, Julia, Julia! This is too bad.

Let her do it then. Let her ring the bell if she dares. Let us see how this pure virtuous creature will face the scandal of what I will declare about her. Let us see how you will face it. I have nothing to lose. Everybody knows how you have treated me: you have boasted of your conquests, you poor pitiful, vain creature--I am the common talk of your acquaintances and hers. Oh, I have calculated my advantage
: I am a most unhappy and injured woman; but I am not the fool you take me to be. I am going to stay--see!

parts.direction: She flings the mantle on the round table; puts her bonnet on it, and sits down.

parts.say: Now, Mrs. Tranfield: there is the bell:

parts.direction: pointing to the button beside the fireplace

parts.say: why don't you ring?

parts.direction: Grace, looking attentively at Charteris, does not move.

parts.say:
Ha! ha! I thought so.
CHARTERIS

parts.direction: quietly, without relaxing his watch on Julia

parts.say: . Mrs. Tranfield: I think you had better go into another room.

parts.direction: Grace makes a movement towards the door, but stops and looks inquiringly at Charteris as Julia springs up. He advances a step so as to prevent her from getting to the door.

parts.say: She shall not. She shall stay here. She shall know what you are, and how you have been in love with me--how it is not two days since you kissed me and told me that the future would be as happy as the past.

You did: deny it if you dare.
CHARTERIS

parts.direction: to Grace in a low voice

parts.say:
. Go!
GRACE
. Get her away as soon as you can, Leonard.

lines.source:
(Julia, with a stifled cry of rage, rushes at Grace, who is crossing
behind the sofa towards door. Charteris seizes her and prevents her
from getting past the sofa. Grace goes out. Charteris, holding Julia
fast, looks around to the door to see whether Grace is safely out of
the room.)

parts.say:
Only an intense desire to get you safely out of this.
JULIA

. I am not going to stir.
CHARTERIS
. Well, well.

parts.direction: Heaves a long sigh. They sit silent for awhile, Julia struggling, not to regain her self control, but to maintain her rage at boiling point.

parts.say: JULIA

. I am going to speak to that woman.
CHARTERIS
. No, no. Hang it, Julia, don't let's have another wrestling match. I have the strength, but not the wind: you're too young for me. Sit down or else let me take you home. Suppose her father comes in.
I don't care. It rests with you. I am ready to go if she will give you up: until then I stay. Those are my terms: you owe me that,

parts.direction: She sits down determinedly. Charteris looks at her for a moment; then, making up his mind, goes resolutely to the couch, sits down near the right hand end of it, she being at the left; and says with biting emphasis

parts.say:
I owe you just exactly nothing.
JULIA
. Nothing! You can look me in the face and say that? Oh, Leonard!
Let me remind you, Julia, that when first we became acquainted, the position you took up was that of a woman of advanced views.

That should have made you respect me the more.
CHARTERIS

. So it did, my dear. But that is not the point. As a woman of advanced views, you were determined to be free. You regarded marriage as a degrading bargain, by which a woman sold herself to a man for the social status of a wife and the right to be supported and pensioned in old age out of his income. That's the advanced view--our view. Besides, if you had married me, I might have turned out a drunkard, a criminal, an imbecile, a horror to you; and you couldn't have released yourself. Too big a risk, you see. That's the rational view--our view. Accordingly, you reserved the right to leave me at any time if you found our companionship incompatible with--what was the expression you used?--with your full development as a human being: I think that was how you put the Ibsenist view--our view. So I had to be content with a charming philander, which taught me a great deal, and brought me some hours of exquisite happiness.

Leonard: you confess then that you owe me something?
CHARTERIS

. No: what I received, I paid. Did you learn nothing from me?--was there no delight for you in our friendship?
JULIA

parts.direction: vehemently and movingly; for she is now sincere

parts.say: . No. You made me pay dearly for every moment of happiness. You revenged yourself on me for the humiliation of being the slave of your passion for me. I was never sure of you for a moment. I trembled whenever a letter came from you, lest it should contain some stab for me. I dreaded your visits almost as much as I longed for them. I was your plaything, not your companion.
Oh, there was such suffering in my happiness that I hardly knew joy from pain.

parts.direction: She sinks on the piano stool, and adds, as she buries her face in her hands and turns away from him

parts.say:
Better for me if I had never met you!
CHARTERIS

. You ungenerous wretch! Is this your gratitude for the way I have just been flattering you? What have I not endured from you--endured with angelic patience? Did I not find out, before our friendship was a fortnight old, that all your advanced views were merely a fashion picked up and followed like any other fashion, without understanding or meaning a word of them? Did you not, in spite of your care for your own liberty, set up claims on me compared to which the claims of the most jealous wife would have been trifles. Have I a single woman friend whom you have not abused as old, ugly, vicious--
JULIA
. So they are.

Well, then, I'll come to grievances that even you can understand. I accuse you of habitual and intolerable jealousy and ill temper; of insulting me on imaginary provocation: of positively beating me; of stealing letters of mine--
JULIA
. Yes, nice letters.

--of breaking your solemn promises not to do it again; of spending hours--aye, days! piecing together the contents of my waste paper basket in your search for more letters; and then representing yourself as an ill used saint and martyr wantonly betrayed and deserted by a selfish monster of a man.
I was justified in reading your letters. Our perfect confidence in one another gave me the right to do it.
Thank you. Then I hasten to break off a confidence which gives such rights.
JULIA

parts.direction: with her right hand on the back of the sofa, bending over him threateningly

parts.say: . You have no right to break it off.
I have. You refused to marry me because--

I did not. You never asked me. If we were married, you would never dare treat me as you are doing now.
CHARTERIS

parts.direction: laboriously going back to his argument

parts.say: . It was understood between us as people of advanced views that we were not to marry because, as the law stands, I might have become a drunkard, a--
--a criminal, an imbecile or a horror. You said that before.

parts.direction: Sits down beside him with a fling.

parts.say: CHARTERIS
. I beg your pardon, my dear. I know I have a habit of repeating myself. The point is that you reserved your freedom to give me up when you pleased.
Well, what of that? I do not please to give you up; and I will not. You have not become a drunkard or a criminal.

You don't see the point yet, Julia. You seem to forget that in reserving your freedom to leave me in case I should turn out badly, you also reserved my freedom to leave you in case you should turn out badly.
Very ingenious. And pray, have

become a drunkard, or a criminal, or an imbecile?
CHARTERIS

. You have become what is infinitely worse than all three together--a jealous termagant.
JULIA
. Yes, abuse me--call me names.

I now assert the right I reserved--the right of breaking with you when I please. Advanced views, Julia, involve advanced duties: you cannot be an advanced woman when you want to bring a man to your feet, and a conventional woman when you want to hold him there against his will. Advanced people form charming friendships: conventional people marry. Marriage suits a good deal of people; and its first duty is fidelity. Friendship suits some people; and its first duty is unhesitating, uncomplaining acceptance of a notice of a change of feeling from either side. You chose friendship instead of marriage. Now do your duty, and accept your notice.

Never! We are engaged in the eye of--the eye of--
CHARTERIS

. Yes, Julia. Can't you get it out? In the eye of something that advanced women don't believe in, en?
JULIA

. O Leonard, don't be cruel. I am too miserable to argue--to think. I only know I love you. You reproach me with not wanting to marry you. I would have married you at any time after I came to love you, if you had asked me. I will marry you now if you will.
I won't, my dear. That's flat. We're intellectually incompatible.

But why? We could be so happy. You love me--I know you love me--I feel it. You say "My dear" to me: you have said it several times this evening. I know I have been wicked, odious, bad. I say nothing in defence of myself. But don't be hard on me. I was distracted by the thought of losing you. I can't face life without you Leonard. I was happy when I met you: I had never loved anyone; and if you had only let me alone I could have gone on contentedly by myself. But I can't now. I must have you with me. Don't cast me off without a thought of all I have at stake. I could be a friend to you if you would only let me--if you would only tell me your plans--give me a share in your work---treat me as something more than the amusement of an idle hour. Oh Leonard, Leonard, you've never given me a chance: indeed you haven't. I'll take pains; I'll read; I'll try to think; I'll conquer my jealousy; I'll--

parts.direction: She breaks down, rocking her head desperately on his knee and writhing.

parts.say:
Oh, I'm mad: I'm mad: you'll kill me if you desert me.
CHARTERIS

. My dear love, don't cry--don't go on in this way. You know I can't help it.
JULIA

parts.direction: sobbing as he rises and coaxingly lifts her with him

parts.say:
. Oh, you can, you can. One word from you will make us happy for ever.
CHARTERIS
. Come, my dear: we really must go. We can't stay until Cuthbertson comes.

parts.direction: Releases her gently and takes her mantle from the table.

parts.say:
Here is your mantle: put it on and be good. You have given me a terrible evening: you must have some consideration for me.
JULIA

. Then I am to be cast off.
CHARTERIS
. You are to put on your bonnet, dearest.

parts.direction: He puts the mantle on her shoulders.

parts.say: JULIA

parts.direction: with a bitter half laugh, half sob

parts.say: . Well, I suppose I must do what I am told.

parts.direction: She goes to the table, and looks for her bonnet. She sees the yellow-backed French novel.

parts.say: Ah, look at that!
Look--look at what the creature reads--filthy, vile French stuff that no decent woman would touch. And you--you have been reading it with her.
You recommended that book to me yourself.
Faugh!
CHARTERIS
. Don't damage property,

parts.direction: He picks it up and dusts it.

parts.say: Making scenes is an affair of sentiment: damaging property is serious.

And now do pray come along.
JULIA
. You can go: there is nothing to prevent you. I will not stir.

parts.direction: She sits down stubbornly on the sofa.

parts.say: CHARTERIS
. Oh come! I am not going to begin all this over again. There are limits even to my forbearance. Come on.
I will not, I tell you.
Then good night.

parts.direction: He makes resolutely for the door. With a rush, she gets there before him, and bars his way.

parts.say:
I thought you wanted me to go.
JULIA
. You shall not leave me here alone.
Then come with me.
Not until you have sworn to me to give up that woman.

My dear, I will swear anything if you will only come away and put an end to this.
JULIA
. You will swear?

Solemnly. Propose the oath. I have been on the point of swearing for the last half hour.
JULIA
. You are only making fun of me. I want no oaths. I want your promise--your sacred word of honour.

Certainly--anything you demand, on condition that you come away immediately. On my sacred word of honour as a gentleman--as an Englishman--as anything you like--I will never see her again, never speak to her, never think of her. Now come.

But are you in earnest? Will you keep your word?
CHARTERIS
