parts.direction: Charteris sinks on a chair with a prolonged groan.

parts.say: Come: don't be silly: you'll not overtake the Colonel if you delay any longer.
Why was I ever born, child of misfortune that I am!
Well, if you must come, you must.

parts.direction: He offers his arm, which she takes.

parts.say: By the way, what happened after I left you?

I gave her a lecture on her behavior which she will remember to the last day of her life.
CHARTERIS
. That was right, darling.

parts.direction: He slips his arm round her waist.

parts.say:
Just one kiss--to soothe me.
GRACE
. Foolish boy!
Now come along.
No, thank you. I don't like sweet things.

parts.direction: She sets down the cup untasted.

parts.say: Anything wrong with the tea?
No, it's very nice.

I'm afraid I'm a very bad entertainer. The fact is, I'm too professional. I only shine in consultation. I almost wish you had something the matter with you; so that you might call out my knowledge and sympathy. As it is, I can only admire you, and feel how pleasant it is to have you here.
JULIA

. And pet me, and say pretty things to me! I wonder you don't offer me a saucer of milk at once?
PARAMORE
. Why?

Because you seem to regard me very much as if I were a Persian cat.
PARAMORE

. Miss Cra--
JULIA
. Oh, you needn't protest. I'm used to it: It's the only sort of attachment I seem always to inspire.
You can't think how flattering it is!

My dear Miss Craven, what a cynical thing to say! You! who are loved at first sight by the people in the street as you pass. Why, in the club I can tell by the faces of the men whether you have been lately in the room or not.
JULIA
. Oh, I hate that look in their faces. Do you know that I have never had one human being care for me since I was born?

That's not true, Miss Craven. Even if it were true of your father, and of Charteris, who loves you madly in spite of your dislike for him, it is not true of me.
JULIA
. Who told you that about Charteris?

Why, he himself.
JULIA
. He cares for only one person in the world; and that is himself. There is not in his whole nature one unselfish spot. He would not spend one hour of his real life with--

parts.direction: a sob chokes her: she rises passionately, crying

parts.say: You are all alike, every one of you. Even my father only makes a pet of me.

parts.direction: She goes away to the fireplace and stands with her back to him.

parts.say: PARAMORE

. I don't deserve this from you: indeed I do not.
JULIA
. Then why do you talk about me with Charteris, behind my back?
We said nothing disparaging of you. Nobody shall ever do that in my presence. We spoke of the subject nearest our hearts.
His heart! Oh, God, his heart!

parts.direction: She sits down on the couch and hides her face.

parts.say: PARAMORE

. I am afraid you love him, for all that, Miss Craven.
JULIA

. If he says that, he lies. If ever you hear it said that I cared for him, contradict it: it is false.
PARAMORE

. Miss Craven: is the way clear for me then?
JULIA

parts.direction: pettishly--losing interest in the conversation and looking crossly into the fire

parts.say:
. What do you mean?
PARAMORE
. You must see what I mean. Contradict the rumour of your attachment to Charteris, not by words--it has gone too far for that--but by becoming my wife.
Believe me: it is not merely your beauty that attracts me:

parts.direction: Julia, interested, looks up at him quickly

parts.say: I know other beautiful women. It is your heart, your sincerity, your sterling reality,

parts.direction: Julia rises and gazes at him, breathless with a new hope

parts.say:
your great gifts of character that are only half developed because you have never been understood by those about you.
JULIA

parts.direction: looking intently at him, and yet beginning to be derisively sceptical in spite of herself

parts.say: . Have you really seen all that in me?

I have felt it. I have been alone in the world; and I need you, Julia. That is how I have divined that you, also, are alone in the world.
JULIA

. You are right there. I am indeed alone in the world.
PARAMORE
. With you I should not be alone. And you?--with me?
You!

parts.direction: She gets quickly out of his reach, taking refuge at the tea-table.

parts.say: No, no. I can't bring myself--

parts.direction: She breaks off, perplexed, and looks uneasily about her.

parts.say: Oh, I don't know what to do. You will expect too much from me.

I have more faith in you than you have in yourself. Your nature is richer than you think.
JULIA
. Do you really believe that I am not the shallow, jealous, devilish tempered creature they all pretend I am?
I am ready to place my happiness in your hands. Does that prove what I think of you?
Yes: I believe you really care for me.

parts.direction: He approaches her eagerly: she has a violent revulsion, and rises with her hand raised as if to beat him off, crying

parts.say: No, no, no, no. I cannot. It's impossible.
PARAMORE

. Is it Charteris?
JULIA
. Ah, you think that!
Listen to me. If I say yes, will you promise not to touch me--to give me time to accustom myself to the idea of our new relations?
I promise most faithfully. I would not press you for the world.
Then--then--yes: I promise.

parts.direction: He is about to utter his rapture; she will not have it.

parts.say: Now, not another word of it. Let us forget it.

parts.direction: She resumes her seat at the table.

parts.say: Give me some more tea.

parts.direction: He hastens to his former seat. As he passes, she puts her left hand on his arm and says

parts.say:
Be good to me, Percy, I need it sorely.
PARAMORE
. You have called me Percy! Hurrah!

parts.direction: Charteris and Craven come in. Paramore hastens to meet them, beaming.

parts.say: Delighted to see you here with me, Colonel Craven. And you, too, Charteris. Sit down.

parts.direction: The Colonel sits down on the end of the couch.

parts.say: Where are the others?

Sylvia has dragged Cuthbertson off into the Burlington Arcade to buy some caramels. He likes to encourage her in eating caramels: he thinks it's a womanly taste. Besides, he likes them himself. They'll be here presently.

parts.direction: He strolls across to the cabinet and pretends to study the Rembrandt photograph, so as to be as far out of Julia's reach as possible.

parts.say: Yes; and Charteris has been trying to persuade me that there's a short cut between Cork Street and Savile Row somewhere in Conduit Street. Now did you ever hear such nonsense? Then he said my coat was getting shabby, and wanted me to go into Poole's and order a new one.
is my coat shabby?
Not that I can see.

I should think not. Then he wanted to draw me into a dispute about the Egyptian war. We should have been here quarter of an hour ago only for his nonsense.
CHARTERIS

. I did my best to keep him from disturbing you, Paramore.
PARAMORE

. You have come in the nick of time. Colonel Craven: I have something very particular to say to you.
CRAVEN

. In private, Paramore: now really it must be in private.
PARAMORE
. Of course. I was about to suggest my consulting room: there's nobody there. Miss Craven: will you excuse me: Charteris will entertain you until I return.

parts.direction: He leads the way to the green baize door.

parts.say: CHARTERIS

. Oh, I say, hadn't you better wait until the others come?
PARAMORE
. No need for further delay now, my best friend.
Will you come, Colonel?
At your service, Paramore: at your service.

parts.direction: Craven and Paramore go into the consulting room. Julia turns her head and stares insolently at Charteris. His nerves play him false: he is completely out of countenance in a moment. She rises suddenly. He starts, and comes hastily forward between the table and the bookcase. She crosses to that side behind the table; and he immediately crosses to the opposite side in front of it, dodging her.

parts.say: CHARTERIS
. Don't, Julia. Now don't abuse your advantage. You've got me here at your mercy. Be good for once; and don't make a
No. Of course not.

parts.direction: She comes forward on her side of the table. He retreats on his side of it. She looks at him with utter scorn; sweeps across to the couch; and sits down imperially. With a great sigh of relief he drops into Paramore's chair.

parts.say: Come here. I have something to say to you.
Yes?

parts.direction: He rolls the chair a few inches towards her.

parts.say: Come here, I say. I am not going to shout across the room at you. Are you afraid of me?
Horribly.

parts.direction: He moves the chair slowly, with great misgiving, to the end of the couch.

parts.say: JULIA

. Has that woman told you that she has given you up to me without an attempt to defend her conquest?
CHARTERIS
. Shew that you are capable of the same sacrifice. Give me up, too.
Sacrifice! And so you think I'm dying to marry you, do you?
I am afraid your intentions have been honourable, Julia.

You cad!
CHARTERIS
. I confess I am something either more or less than a gentleman, Julia. You once gave me the benefit of the doubt.
Indeed!
never told you so. If you cannot behave like a gentleman, you had better go back to the society of the woman who has given you up--if such a cold-blooded, cowardly creature can be called a woman.

parts.direction: She rises majestically; he makes his chair fly back to the table.

parts.say:
I know you now, Leonard Charteris, through and through, in all your falseness, your petty spite, your cruelty and your vanity. The place you coveted has been won by a man more worthy of it.
CHARTERIS

parts.direction: springing up, and coming close to her, gasping with eagerness

parts.say: . What do you mean? Out with it. Have you accep--

I am engaged to Dr. Paramore.
CHARTERIS
. My own Julia!
JULIA

parts.direction: recoiling--he catching her hands and holding them

parts.say: . How dare you! Are you mad? Do you wish me to call Dr. Paramore?

Call everybody, my darling--everybody in London. Now I shall no longer have to be brutal--to defend myself--to go in fear of you. How I have looked forward to this day! You know now that I don't want you to marry me or to love me: Paramore can have all that. I only want to look on and rejoice disinterestedly in the happiness of
my dear Julia
, my beautiful

parts.direction: She tears her hands away and raises them as if to strike him, as she did the night before at Cuthbertson's.

parts.say: No use to threaten me now: I am not afraid of those hands--the loveliest hands in the world.
How have you the face to turn round like this after insulting and torturing me!

Never mind, dearest: you never did understand me; and you never will. Our vivisecting friend has made a successful experiment at last.
JULIA
. It is you who are the vivisector--a far crueller, more wanton vivisector than he.

Yes; but then I learn so much more from my experiments than he does! And the victims learn as much as I do. That's where my moral superiority comes in.
JULIA

parts.direction: sitting down again on the couch with rueful humour

parts.say:
. Well, you shall not experiment on me any more. Go to your Grace if you want a victim. She'll be a tough one.
CHARTERIS
. And you drove me to propose to her to escape from you! Suppose she had accepted me, where should I be now?
Where
am, I suppose, now that I have accepted Paramore.
But I should have made Grace unhappy.

. However, now I come to think of it, you'll make Paramore unhappy. And yet if you refused him he would be in despair. Poor devil!
JULIA

parts.direction: her temper flashing up for a moment again

parts.say:
. He is a better man than you.
CHARTERIS

. I grant you that, my dear.
JULIA

. Don't call me your dear. And what do you mean by saying that I shall make him unhappy? Am I not good enough for him?
CHARTERIS

. Well, that depends on what you mean by good enough.
JULIA

. You might have made me good if you had chosen to. You had a great power over me. I was like a child in your hands; and you knew it.
CHARTERIS

. Yes, my dear. That means that whenever you got jealous and flew into a violent rage, I could always depend on it's ending happily if I only waited long enough, and petted you very hard all the time. When you had had your fling, and called the object of your jealousy every name you could lay your tongue to, and abused me to your heart's content for a couple of hours, then the reaction would come; and you would at last subside into a soothing rapture of affection which gave you a sensation of being angelically good and forgiving. Oh, I know that sort of goodness! You may have thought on these occasions that I was bringing out your latent amiability; but I thought you were bringing out mine, and using up rather more than your fair share of it.
According to you, then, I have no good in me! I am an utterly vile, worthless woman. Is that it?

Yes, if you are to be judged as you judge others. From the conventional point of view, there's nothing to be said for you, Julia--nothing. That's why I have to find some other point of view to save my self-respect when I remember how I have loved you. Oh, what I have learnt from you!--from you, who could learn nothing from me! I made a fool of you; and you brought me wisdom: I broke your heart; and you brought me joy: I made you curse your womanhood; and you revealed my manhood to me. Blessings forever and ever on my Julia's name!

parts.direction: With genuine emotion, he takes her hand to kiss it again.

parts.say: JULIA

parts.direction: snatching her hand away in disgust

parts.say:
. Oh, stop talking that nasty sneering stuff.
CHARTERIS
. She calls it nasty sneering stuff! Well, well: I'll never talk like that to you again, dearest. It only means that you are a beautiful woman, and that we all love you.
Don't say that: I hate it. It sounds as if I were a mere animal.
Hm! A fine animal is a very wonderful thing. Don't let us disparage animals, Julia.
That is what you really think me.
Come, Julia: you don't expect me to admire you for your moral qualities, do you?

parts.direction: She turns and looks hard at him. He starts up apprehensively and backs away from her. She rises and follows him up slowly and intently.

parts.say: JULIA

. I have seen you very much infatuated with this depraved creature who has no moral qualities.
CHARTERIS

. Keep off, Julia. Remember your new obligations to Paramore.
JULIA

parts.direction: overtaking him in the middle of the room

parts.say: . Never mind Paramore: that is my business.

parts.direction: She grasps the lappels of his coat in her hands, and looks fixedly at him.

parts.say:
Oh, if the people you talk so cleverly to could only know you as I know you! Sometimes I wonder at myself for ever caring for you.
CHARTERIS
. Only sometimes?
You fraud! You humbug! You miserable little plaster saint!
Oh!

parts.mic: In a paroxysm half of rage, half of tenderness, she shakes him, growling over him like a tigress over her cub. Paramore and Craven at this moment return from the consulting room, and are thunderstruck at the spectacle.

parts.say: CRAVEN
. Julia!!

parts.direction: Julia releases Charteris, but stands her ground disdainfully as they come forward, Craven on her left, Paramore on her right.

parts.say: What's the matter?
Nothing, nothing. You'll soon get used to this, Paramore.

Now really, Julia, this is a very extraordinary way to behave. It's not fair to Paramore.
JULIA
. If Dr. Paramore objects he can break off our engagement.

Pray don't hesitate.
PARAMORE

parts.direction: looking doubtfully and anxiously at her

parts.say:
. Do you wish me to break it off?
CHARTERIS
. Nonsense! don't act so hastily. It was my fault. I annoyed Miss Craven--insulted her. Hang it all, don't go and spoil everything like this.

This is most infernally perplexing. I can't believe that you insulted Julia, Charteris. I've no doubt you annoyed her--you'd annoy anybody; upon my soul you would--but insult!--now what do you mean by that?
PARAMORE
. Miss Craven; delicacy and sincerity I ask you to be frank with me. What are the relations between you and Charteris?
Ask him.

parts.direction: She goes to the fireplace, her back on them.

parts.say:
Certainly: I'll confess. I'm in love with Miss Craven--always have been; and I've persecuted her with my addresses ever since I knew her. It's been no use: she utterly despises me. A moment ago the spectacle of a rival's happiness stung me to make a nasty, sneering speech; and she--well, she just shook me a little, as you saw.
PARAMORE
. I shall never forget that you helped me to win her, Charteris.

parts.direction: Julia quickly, a spasm of fury in her face.

parts.say: Sh! For Heaven's sake don't mention it.
This is a very different story to the one you told Cuthbertson and myself this morning. You'll excuse my saying that it sounds much more like the the truth. Come: you were humbugging us, weren't you?
Ask Julia.

parts.direction: Paramore and Craven turn to Julia. Charteris remains doggedly looking straight before him.

parts.say: It's quite true. He has been in love with me; he has persecuted me; and I utterly despise him.
Don't rub it in, Julia: it's not kind. No man is quite himself when he's crossed in love.
Now listen to me,

When I was a young fellow, Cuthbertson and I fell in love with the same woman. She preferred Cuthbertson. I was taken aback: I won't deny it. But I knew my duty; and I did it. I gave her up and wished Cuthbertson joy. He told me this morning, when we met after many years, that he has respected and liked me ever since for it. And I believe him and feel the better for it.

Now, Charteris, Paramore and you stand to-day where Cuthbertson and I stood on a certain July evening thirty-five years ago. How are you going to take it?
JULIA

. How is he going to take it, indeed! Really, papa, this is too much. If Mrs. Cuthbertson wouldn't have you, it may have been very noble of you to make a virtue of giving her up, just as you made a virtue of being a teetotaller when Percy cut off your wine. But he shan't be virtuous over me. I have refused him; and if he doesn't like it he can--he can--
I can lump it. Precisely. Craven: you can depend on me. I'll lump it.

parts.direction: He moves off nonchalantly, and leans against the bookcase with his hands in his pockets.

parts.say: CRAVEN

. Julia: you don't treat me respectfully. I don't wish to complain; but that was not a becoming speech.
JULIA

parts.direction: bursting into tears and throwing herself into the large chair

parts.say: . Is there anyone in the world who has any feeling for me--who does not think me utterly vile?

parts.direction: Craven and Paramore hurry to her in the greatest consternation.

parts.say: CRAVEN
. My pet: I didn't for a moment mean--
Must I stand to be bargained for by two men--passed from one to the other like a slave in the market, and not say a word in my own defence?
But, my love--
Oh, go away, all of you. Leave me. I--oh--

parts.direction: She gives way to a passion of tears.

parts.say: PARAMORE
. You've wounded her cruelly, Colonel Craven--cruelly.
But I didn't mean to: I said nothing. Charteris: was I harsh?
You forget the revolt of the daughters, Craven. And you certainly wouldn't have gone on like that to any grown up woman who was not your daughter.
Do you mean to say that I am expected to treat my daughter the same as I would any other girl?
I should say certainly, Colonel Craven.
Well, dash me if I will. There!
If you take that tone, I have nothing more to say.

parts.direction: He crosses the room with offended dignity and posts himself with his back to the bookcase beside Charteris.

parts.say: JULIA

. Daddy.
CRAVEN

. Yes, my love.
JULIA

parts.direction: looking up at him tearfully and kissing his hand

parts.say: . Don't mind them. You didn't mean it, Daddy, did you?

No, no, my precious. Come: don't cry.
PARAMORE

parts.direction: to Charteris, looking at Julia with delight

parts.say:
. How beautiful she is!
CHARTERIS
. Oh, Lord help you, Paramore!

parts.direction: He leaves the bookcase and sits at the end of the couch farthest from the fire. Meanwhile Sylvia arrives.

parts.say: SYLVIA
. Crying again! Well, you are a womanly one!
Don't worry your sister, Sylvia. You know she can't bear it.
I speak for her good, Dad. All the world can't be expected to know that she's the family baby.
You will get your ears boxed presently, Silly.

Now, now, now, my dear children, really now! Come, Julia: put up your handkerchief before Mrs. Tranfield sees you. She's coming along with Jo.
JULIA
. That woman again!
Another row! Go it, Julia!
Hold your tongue, Sylvia.
Now look here, Julia.
Hallo! A revolt of the fathers!
Silence, Charteris.

The test of a man or woman's breeding is how they behave in a quarrel. Anybody can behave well when things are going smoothly. Now you said to-day, at that iniquitous club, that you were not a womanly woman. Very well: I don't mind. But if you are not going to behave like a lady when Mrs. Tranfield comes into this room, you've got to behave like a gentleman; or fond as I am of you, I'll cut you dead exactly as I would if you were my son.
PARAMORE

. Colonel Craven--
CRAVEN

. Don't be a fool, Paramore.
JULIA
. I'm sure, Daddy--
Stop snivelling. I'm not speaking as your Daddy now: I'm speaking as your commanding officer.
Good old Victoria Cross!

parts.direction: Craven turns sharply on her; and she darts away behind Charteris, and presently seats herself on the couch, so that she and Charteris are shoulder to shoulder, facing opposite ways. Cuthbertson arrives with Grace, who remains near the door whilst her father joins the others.

parts.say: Ah, Jo, here you are. Now, Paramore, tell 'em the news.

Mrs. Tranfield--Cuthbertson--allow me to introduce you to my future wife.
CUTHBERTSON

parts.direction: coming forward to shake hands with Paramore

parts.say: . My heartiest congratulations!

parts.direction: Paramore goes to shake hands with Grace.

parts.say: Miss Craven: you will accept Grace's congratulations as well as mine, I hope.
She will, Jo.
Now, Julia.
Now, Grace.

parts.direction: He conducts her to Julia's right; then posts himself on the hearthrug, with his back to the fire, watching them. The Colonel keeps guard on the other side.

parts.say: GRACE

parts.direction: speaking in a low voice to Julia alone

parts.say: . So you have shewn him that you can do without him! Now I take back everything I said. Will you shake hands with me?

parts.direction: Julia gives her hand painfully, with her face averted.

parts.say: They think this a happy ending, Julia--these men--our lords and masters!

parts.direction: The two stand silent, hand in hand.

parts.say: SYLVIA

parts.direction: leaning back across the couch, aside to Charteris

parts.say: . Has she really chucked you?

parts.direction: He nods assent. She looks at him dubiously, and adds

parts.say: I expect you chucked her.

And now, Paramore, mind you don't stand any chaff from Charteris about this. He's in the same predicament himself. He's engaged to Grace.
JULIA

parts.direction: dropping Grace's hand, and speaking with breathless anguish, but not violently

parts.say:
. Again!
CHARTERIS

. Don't be alarmed. It's all off.
SYLVIA
. What! You've chucked Grace too! What a shame!

parts.direction: She goes to the other side of the room, fuming.

parts.say: CHARTERIS

parts.direction: following her and putting his hand soothingly on her shoulder

parts.say: . She won't have me, old chap--that is
unless Mrs. Tranfield has changed her mind again.

parts.say: Why the dickens didn’t you tell me last night, Angela?
I had no wish to disturb my night’s rest.
Upon my soul, I don’t know what you mean. It’s incomprehensible to me that you should have slept like a top. I couldn’t have closed my eyes the whole night.
I know. And you would have taken excellent care that I shouldn’t close mine either.
I should have thought I had enough to do without being pestered with a foolish woman’s matrimonial difficulties.
You really have a very detached way of looking at things, Frank. No one would imagine, to hear you speak, that the foolish woman in question was your daughter.
Really, Angela, I must beg you not to make this a subject of flippancy.
Well, what do you propose to do?
Do? What do you expect me to do? You tell me that Kate came home at twelve o’clock last night without a stitch of clothing....
My dear, if I told you that I was most unwarrantably distorting the truth.
In a ball dress, with an opera cloak on--without her luggage, without even a dressing-case--and informs you that she’s left her husband.... It’s absurd.
Quite absurd. And so unnecessarily dramatic.
And when’s she going home?
She assures me that she’s not going home.
She’s not going to stay here?
Those are her plans at the moment.
And George?
Well?
You don’t suppose her husband’s going to put up with this nonsense? Has he made no sign?
Ten minutes after she arrived he sent a messenger boy--with a toothbrush.
Why a toothbrush?
I don’t know. Presumably to brush her teeth.
Well, that shows he doesn’t look upon the matter as serious. Of course, it was a whim on Kate’s part. Luckily he’s coming here this morning....
Is he?

Yes, he promised to fetch me in his car. We’re going to drive down to the City together. I’ll bring him in, and meanwhile you can talk to Kate. I dare say she’s thought better of it already. It only wants a little tact, and we can settle the whole thing. George is clever enough to have given some plausible explanation to the servants.
Are you really under the impression things are going to pass off in that way?
Why not?
They say it’s a wise man who knows his own father, but it’s apparently a wiser man still who knows his own daughter.
Angela, for goodness’ sake don’t try to be bright and amusing.
Do you know so little of Kate as to imagine she would have taken a step of this kind without having quite made up her mind?
You don’t mean to say you think Kate will refuse to go back to her husband?
I do.
But what reasons does she give? Why did she say she left him?
She gave no reasons. She merely stated the fact and asked if I could put her up.
Well, she must go back to her husband.

parts.direction: As if it were the most innocent question.

parts.say: Why?

Because a woman’s place is by her husband’s side, Angela. You know just as well as I do that I can’t afford to quarrel with George Winter. I’m chairman of half a dozen of his companies. The position would be intolerable. I should be expected to take Kate’s side if she were right or wrong.
I suppose you owe him money?
No, not exactly.
Ah!

parts.direction: With a shrewd look at him and a smile.

parts.say: And how much is it that you--don’t exactly owe him?

We’re mixed up together in any number of business undertakings, and naturally we have a sort of running account. If we settled up I dare say I should have to find something like fifteen thousand pounds.
Good heavens, I thought you’d been making money.
Yes, I did, but the fact is, we’ve been very badly hit lately. Practically all our interests are in Central America, and we couldn’t foresee that there’d be a revolution there.
The possibility might have crossed your mind.
Oh, I knew you’d blame me. And I suppose you’ll blame me because a confounded earthquake smashed up one of our railways.
And how d’you propose to raise fifteen thousand pounds?
That’s just it. It would be devilish awkward. And George is in a confounded tight place too.
You’d better talk to Kate. I’ll send for her.

lines.source: [_She touches a bell, and gives her order down a speaking tube._

parts.say: Ask Mrs. Winter to be good enough to come to the drawing room.
You must talk to her seriously, Angela. You must tell her that her behaviour is outrageous.
No, my dear. You are going to talk to her.

parts.say: Good-morning, father.

parts.direction: With a fine assumption of paternal authority.

parts.say: I want to talk to you. Your mother and I have sent for you....
Now what does all this mean? It’s ridiculous nonsense. You’re surely old enough to have learnt a little self-control.
I’ve shown a good deal of self-control during the four years of my married life, father. I was afraid it was growing into a habit.
Am I to understand that what your mother tells me is true?
I lived with George as long as I could. I put up with more than any woman I know would have done. But there are some things no one should suffer who has any self-respect.
You’ve never complained before of George’s behaviour.
No.

Why have you never said a word to your mother about it? I can’t imagine why you shouldn’t get on with George. I don’t suppose you’ve ever expressed a whim that he hasn’t gratified. Your allowance is princely. Your pearls are the envy of every woman in London.
Oh, yes, he’s generous. My pearls have been a splendid advertisement.

parts.direction: Ignoring the second sentence and pouncing on the admission.

parts.say: Then what have you got to complain of?
I dare say my mother knows what half London is chattering about.
Well, Angela?
Oh, my dear, I hoped it was idle gossip. A man as much in the public eye as George Winter--the most prominent financier of the moment--is certain to be talked about.
I suppose he’s been flirting with two or three pretty women.
I understand things are supposed to have gone rather further than that.

That’s the kind of thing a tactful woman must close her eyes to. You’re a woman of the world, Kate. You know what men are. You must extend a certain degree of licence to a man of George Winter’s temperament.

You don’t understand, father. I bore my life till I couldn’t bear it any longer. I’m not the sort of woman to make scenes. I held my tongue, I closed my eyes, till something happened which I couldn’t endure. I’ve left him fully decided to divorce him. Nothing that you can say will move me.
But you can’t divorce him. You’ve accused him of nothing but infidelity. You can’t be so ignorant of the law....
I’m not at all ignorant of the law. I assure you that he has complied fully with all the conditions which are needful.
Kate.
Please don’t ask me. I feel that my whole soul is foul with....
Well, of course there are always two sides to every question.
Oh, father, you’re not going to tell me that that, too, is usual in polite society, for a man to.... Oh!

parts.say: Why have you chosen this particular moment to leave your husband?
There are limits to human endurance.

You’ve lived a good deal apart. Like civilized people you’ve made the best of a mutual want of sympathy. I should have thought George interfered with you very little. I have an idea that no woman would care to undergo the--inconvenience of proceedings for divorce without a very good reason. You’ve got a peculiarly fastidious taste, Katie. parts.say: Are you in love?
You have no right to ask me that, mother.
Your indignation is almost an answer in itself, isn’t it? I suppose you want to marry.

lines.source: [CATHERINE _does not answer. She takes a step or two impatiently._

parts.say: Well?
I’ve got nothing to be ashamed of.
In that case, I should have thought you had nothing to conceal.

I haven’t. When I thought that everything was over for me and that life was meaningless, I found it was only just beginning. And I thanked God for all I’d gone through because perhaps it made me less unfit for the great love that descended upon me.
It’s Robert Colby, isn’t it?
Yes.
And you’ve made your arrangements, I suppose, to be married as soon as the decree is made absolute?
We haven’t discussed the matter.
But still, I may take it that is the intention?
Yes.
Your father wishes me to tell you that if you quarrel with George it will ruin him. He could hardly keep the position that George has given him on his various boards.
You will be no worse off than before I married.
Except that it appears your father owes George fifteen thousand pounds.
Do you want to cheat me again out of the little happiness that seems in store for me?
I want you to do what is right in your own eyes.

parts.say: George!
My dear, look pleased to see me. It’s only decent.
It’s infamous that you should come here. If you had any decent feeling....
My dear child, I had a business engagement with your father. It’s unreasonable to expect me not to keep it because you have temporarily abandoned the conjugal roof.
You might have warned me.
My dear, I was hoping that after a talk with your mother you’d have....
What can I do to show you that I’ve made up my mind for good and all?
Even after one’s made up one’s mind, it’s not too late to listen to reason.
I think for all our sakes you should listen to anything that George has to say.
Do you understand what my mother means?
I dimly suspect.
My father owes you a lot of money. He’s chairman of half your companies. He thinks that if I divorce you he’ll have to pay that money....
I’m sure his sense of delicacy would prevent him from remaining in my debt.
And you’ll make him resign his directorships?

parts.direction: With his tongue in his cheek.

parts.say: I know him well enough to feel certain that he would never wish to retain them.
Oh, it’s vile.
Or is it common sense?

lines.source:
[_There is a moment’s pause, and when_ GEORGE WINTER _speaks it is
     with great seriousness_.

parts.say: Now look here, Kate; listen to me carefully. You know that all our interests are in Central America. The Lewishams had it all their own way out there till I came along. They owned the railways and the mines and the trams--everything that was worth having. Well, I knew I couldn’t oust them, but I thought I could make them take me in. I’ve been fighting them tooth and nail for ten years. They’ve done all they could to smash me by fair means and foul, but they haven’t succeeded. And now I’m in sight of my goal. I can force them to come to terms.
All this is nothing to me.

The Lewishams got on to a big thing--a mine called the Campo del Oro. But that earthquake the other day queered their pitch, and they offered bills when hard cash was the only thing to do the trick. I thought that what was good enough for the Lewishams was good enough for me. I knew that if I could get it they’d have to take me in. I had two hours to think it over. I found the cash and bought the mine last week.
It doesn’t interest me.
It will. I sent Macdonald out there.
Macdonald is George’s expert. He’s the soundest man in the profession.

And straight, straight as a die. I’m expecting his report every day. He may cable me at any moment. Then I shall get to work. I’m going to float the mine as a company with a capital of half a million. Your father will be chairman, and he ought to make close on fifty thousand out of it. For a reason I needn’t tell you, we can’t afford to wait. We must have ready money, and that means floating the company at once. My only chance is in Middlepool, where three parts of my backing have come from before. We shall soon be in the middle of a General Election. And you know how uncertain my seat in Middlepool is. I keep it only by my personal popularity. I’m at the mercy of the Nonconformists, and if there’s talk of a divorce it’s all U.P. with me. They’ll make me retire before the election, and if that happens the new company won’t stand a dog’s chance.
Why?
Because with the general public nervous, I shall have to depend on Middlepool, and there I can only float it on my personal character.
I’m afraid you’ll think it very selfish, but I haven’t any more power of self-sacrifice in me.

If the Campo del Oro is a failure, it’ll knock down all the other companies I’m connected with. The Lewishams will seize the opportunity to make a raid on me. I’m standing on the edge of a precipice, and anyone who cares to give me a shove will send me over.... It’ll mean your father’s ruin and mine--I dare say you don’t mind that--but it’ll also mean the ruin of thousands of poor investors all over the country. Three-quarters of the population of Middlepool will lose their savings.
You’ve lied to me so often, George.
I can show you by plain figures that every word I say is true.
I haven’t much sympathy with the gamblers who want to make money without working for it. If they lose, it’s their own look out.

lines.source:
[_There is a pause._ GEORGE WINTER _looks at her and nods to
     himself_.

parts.say: I think you’d better go now. The rest of our conversation doesn’t need any listeners.
I have nothing more to say to you.
Don’t be a damned fool. It’s a matter of life and death to me, and d’you think I’m going to ...
Please, Lady Francis.
Of course we’ll leave you. Come, Frank.

parts.direction: With a twinkle in his eye.

parts.say: I don’t think your elopement receives the unqualified approval of your parents.
D’you want to repeat that odious scene of last night? Surely we said all that we had to say to one another.
You know, I wouldn’t have played the fool with other women if you hadn’t shown me very clearly that you didn’t want to have anything to do with me.
I would rather not discuss that.
After all, it isn’t as if I cared a tinker’s cuss for the whole lot of them.

And you think that makes it any better? I think I could have forgiven you if you’d had any love for those wretched women. But it wasn’t even that. You exposed me to all that humiliation merely to gratify your vanity. When I’ve seen how you’ve treated those women I, even I, have been sorry for them.
If you like I’ll give you my solemn word of honour that you shall have no cause to complain in future.
It’s too late. You’ve given me my chance of freedom and I mean to take it.
You’re not keeping your part of the bargain.
What d’you mean?
You didn’t marry me because you were in love with me....
That’s not true.
Think.
A year ago I would have said again that it wasn’t true. I didn’t know what love was.
You married me because I was rich.
No, no.

I’d just won a seat that they’d given me because they thought I hadn’t a chance. I won it off my own bat, because I imposed myself on Middlepool and forced them to vote for me. I was in the public eye. I was a power already. The world seemed at my feet.
All that’s very harmless. You flattered me. The life you offered me seemed so large, so full, and I was very young. I was dazzled by your brilliancy and your success. I mistook it for love.
And I married you because I wanted a wife. You happened to have an uncle who’s a duke, and aristocratic connexions are devilish useful in England to a Radical politician.
Oh, yes, I found out soon enough why you married me.
It was a business arrangement on both sides, and you’ve had your full share of the profits.
Oh, how can you?

You’d always lived in a pokey way and I gave you magnificence. I’ve kept even the spirit of my part of the bargain. Your father wasn’t mentioned in the settlements. But every stick of furniture in this house has been bought with my money. The very clothes on your mother’s back are paid for by me.
That’s not true.

You don’t think your father is worth the money I give him. He’s as incompetent as all the rest of these damned fools who come from the West-End and think they can make money in the City. The nincompoop thinks himself a financial authority. The charwoman of a bucket-shop could give him points.
He has his name and his position.
Nowadays even a country curate will fight shy of a title on a prospectus. The salaries he gets are merely payments for you.

Oh, you’ve said all this so often. For years you’ve bullied me with your money. I was such a fool, because you said it was dishonest of me to go, rather than that even you should have the smallest cause to blame me, I bore everything. I clenched my hands and suffered.
In a diamond tiara and a Paquin dress.

I thought I should have the strength to suffer to the end. But I haven’t. If you bought an article and it hasn’t turned out worth the money you gave for it, that’s your look out. You see, you’ve taught me something after all.

lines.source:
[_A very short pause._ GEORGE WINTER _makes up his mind to try
     compromise_.

parts.say: Now, look here; I’m willing to meet you half-way. I don’t ask you to come back to me. You can live as you like and where you like. I’ll give you five thousand a year. Your father can keep his directorships. The only thing I ask is that you shouldn’t apply for a divorce and that you should appear with me at certain public functions.

I want to be free. I’ve lived in an atmosphere of lies and hypocrisy till I can hardly breathe. Your good nature is merely a pose. Your generosity is merely an advertisement. You care for nothing but your own self-advancement. And I want to be rid of the horrible feeling that all sorts of shady things are going on around me that I don’t know.
What d’you mean?
I know that you’re not honest.

lines.source:
[_With a cry of rage_ GEORGE WINTER _seizes her by the shoulders
     violently. His passion for the moment is uncontrollable._

parts.say: What d’you mean? What d’you mean? What d’you mean?
You’re hurting me.

parts.mic: In his rage hardly able to articulate.

parts.say: Damn you, how dare you say that to me?
Let me go.
Why don’t you answer? What d’you mean?
I’ll tell you what I mean. I know that if the occasion arose you wouldn’t hesitate to steal.
Is that all?

For years I’ve been tortured by the horror of it. Each pearl you’ve given me--and you’ve thrust them upon me--I’ve asked myself if it was honestly come by. And that’s why I want to escape from you--not only because you’ve been odiously cruel to me, even now when you’re trying to persuade me to return to you, and because you’ve flaunted before me one vulgar intrigue after another--but because I feel that all this wealth rests on lying, and swindling, and roguery.
Well, you must confess that so far I’ve been eminently successful in not getting found out.

parts.direction: Taking no notice of his remark.

parts.say: And now surely you have nothing more to say to me.
My dear, knowing how important it is to me that you should return to the conjugal roof, you don’t imagine I have come without some means to persuade you.
I assure you you’re wasting your time. You’ve always told me it was valuable.
You seem to be under the delusion it rests with you to make conditions.
I make no conditions. I merely announce my decision.

parts.direction: Taking a letter from his pocket and quietly smoothing it out on a table.

parts.say: I’ve never suffered from that form of snobbishness which makes many self-made men hurl their origin in the face of a British public only too anxious to pretend it thinks them the scions of a noble house. But I have never concealed from you that mine was humble.
What is that paper?

That is one of the pills you had to swallow when I married you and your excellent but impoverished family. I started life with neither friend nor money, but with exceptionally fine parts. I soon discovered that the simplest way to succeed is by blackmail. It is astonishing how many men keep a large-sized skeleton in their cupboards. If you only get a sight of those discreditable bones, you can often make a whole family your bosom friends. I’m not boring you, am I?
You’re torturing me.

This is a copy of a letter which you may remember. The original was so crumpled that I can’t help thinking you were romantic enough to sleep with it under your pillow. It begins: My very dear friend....
How did you get that?
I can never understand why people are such fools as to write love-letters. I never do. I only send telegrams.
You didn’t go to my dressing-case?
I did indeed.

parts.direction: Looking at the Bramah-key on her bracelet.

parts.say: You broke it open?
When I made you a present of your dressing-case, I kept the duplicate key in case you lost yours.
It’s infamous. It’s--it’s just like you.
Why on earth were you so incautious as to leave it behind?
I thought I could trust you. It never struck me that you’d pry into my private papers.
Nonsense. You were so taken with the dramatic gesture of leaving the house in a pink satin opera cloak that you forgot all about it.
There’s nothing in any of my letters that I’m ashamed of.
Would you like to look at this one?
I know that there can be absolutely no harm in it.

I wonder what a clever counsel would make of it. I can imagine it read in such a manner that those vague words should gather form and substance. A little irony, a grotesque emphasis here and there, and I can see the junior bar rolling with laughter. I don’t imagine a parliamentary light like your friend Robert Colby would take ridicule very well. It’s only by his entire lack of humour that he’s risen to the exalted position he now adorns.
What d’you mean, George?
My dear, I’m going to bring a counter petition, that’s all. You want to wash your dirty linen in public, let’s have an entire spring cleaning.
Oh, my dear George, if you only knew how indifferent I am to such a threat! We haven’t done anything with which we can reproach ourselves.

You astonish me, my dear Kate. Surely it can’t have slipped your memory that Robert Colby, snatching a brief and well-earned holiday from affairs of state, made a tour of North Italy last Easter, and you accompanied him.
That’s not true. You know it’s not true. I went with Barbara Herbert....

parts.direction: Interrupting, with a twinkle in his eye.

parts.say: And a maid. It’s always a little unsafe to trust maids, especially Scotch maids with strongly religious principles.
What have you been doing?

parts.direction: Taking a paper out of his pocket.

parts.say: Here is another interesting little document that I’ve been at some pains to acquire. Being, alas! aware that the wife of my bosom might--turn troublesome one day or another, I thought it safe to have a weapon in my hand for future use. It is a list of the hotels at which you stayed. Shall I read it to you?
If you choose.
At Milan you stayed at the
, and Robert Colby at the
Damning, isn’t it?
But perhaps finding the
noisy, and trusting in Mr. Robert Colby’s better judgment, at Venice you both stayed at the

parts.say: Where else should one stay?
I find in my Baedeker that there are twenty-seven hotels in Venice, but I daresay it was very natural that you should both hit upon the
. And you took the precaution of arriving twenty hours after him. But at Ravenna, flinging prudence to the winds, you arrived on the same day, by the same train, and you put up at the same hotel.

You had rooms seventeen and eighteen, and Barbara Herbert had room five.
There was only one vacant room on the first floor, and of course I insisted that Barbara should take it.
Unselfish in the extreme, and just like you, my dear; but don’t you think it was a little indiscreet?
We had nothing to be ashamed of, and therefore we had nothing to fear.
I’ve often thought that was the greatest drawback of innocence. It makes one so devilish imprudent.

I went to Italy with your express consent. I wrote and told you that I’d met Robert Colby. Chance threw us together in Venice; we found we were making practically the same tour, and we joined forces. I saw no harm in it. I see no harm in it now. You can make what use of the admissions you like.
And do you think you will be able to persuade a British jury that you and Robert Colby travelled through Italy together merely to look at churches and pictures?
George, I know now that I never cared for you, but I promise you on my word of honour that I’ve never been unfaithful to you.
My dear, it’s not a question of convincing me--I am the most trusting, the most credulous of mortals--but of convincing the twelve good men and true who form a British jury.

You’re not a fool, George. You know people, and you know what I’m capable of and what I’m not. In your heart you’re certain that I’ve done nothing that can give you any cause for complaint. I’ve suffered a great deal during these four years--I wouldn’t wish my worst enemy to go through what I have--I implore you not to drag me through this horror.
My dear, your simple-mindedness positively takes me aback.
How can you be so ignoble?

parts.direction: Dropping his bantering tone, quickly and sternly.

parts.say: You must know me very little, Kate. My whole life is at stake, and you think I’m going to be moved by entreaties or abuse? I’m at the most critical point of my career. Part of my strength is that I never deceive myself. I’m only an adventurer. My millions are paper millions, and I want to be in such a position that if I’m in need of half a million I can go to the big men and get it, and if one of them asks me for half a million I can afford to put it down. And now, if only I hold on, I shall get everything I want. And you come and whine before me and play the fool. What d’you think I care for your twopenny-halfpenny love-affairs? Do what you like. I don’t care, so long as you’re not flagrant.
Oh!
That anyone can be such a fool as to let love interfere with his life! It’s so unimportant.
To me it means the whole world.
Well, I give you your choice. If you bring an action against me I bring a counter-petition.
My choice is made long ago. I’m strong in my innocence.
You’ll ruin me and ruin your father, but you’ll ruin Robert Colby as well.
What do you mean?

You don’t mean to say you’re so simple-minded as to imagine he can do anything but resign his seat if he were made co-respondent in a divorce case? They say, if we get in again, he’s to be given the Ministry of War. Humpty-Dumpty. It’s the end of his political career.
We have nothing to reproach ourselves with. Nothing.
You sent a note to him last night. What did you say?
I asked him to come here at twelve o’clock.
It’s nearly twelve now. I’ll wait. And you shall talk to him.

lines.source:
[_Enter_ ANNE ETCHINGHAM _and_ TEDDIE O’DONNELL. ANNE _is like her
     sister_ CATHERINE, _but smaller and slighter; she is brighter as
     well and more vivacious, with pretty caressing ways_. EDWARD
     O’DONNELL _is an insignificant, amiable, good-looking young man of
     three-and-twenty_.

parts.say: Good morning, good people.
Ah, Nan.
Well, how is my great brother-in-law?
He’s in his usual rude health, thank you.
I’ve brought Teddie to introduce him to you.
How d’you do?

This is the Napoleon of Finance. He owns seventeen companies, five gold mines, two railways, a house in Portman Square, two places in the country, a yacht, five motor-cars, the family of Etchingham....
Take a long breath and say ninety-nine.
Don’t be ridiculous.
Now, what is it you want?
I?
You’re an old dear, George.
I thought so. Well, what is it?
I want you to give Mr. O’Donnell a job.
Anne!
I say, Nan, you needn’t put it so bluntly.
It’s no good beating about the bush with George, is it?
Not much.
Now, sit down and let me talk sensibly to you.
Anne, I’d rather you didn’t--just now. George and I are busy.
Have they interrupted you, darling? I thought you had nothing more you wanted to say.
Is anything the matter?
Nothing. Kate’s a little under the weather this morning.
Oh, my dear, I’m so sorry. What is it?
I warned you not to eat that
last night, my dear. It always disagrees with you.
Please don’t worry about me.
Why d’you want me to give Mr. O’Donnell a job?
Because he’s my young man.
Is he, by Jove!
I offered her my hand and heart....
And being a practical person I promptly inquired what were his worldly possessions.
They’re not only nil, they’re astonishingly nil. In point of fact, if you reckon debts they’re positively minus.
So I fell into his arms and said, let us put up the banns at once.
That’s where I come in.
Well, I thought he might manage one of your railways or be your chauffeur, or if you didn’t think he was good enough for that you might make him director of one of your companies.
Nan, you don’t know what you’re talking about.
Good heavens, if papa can direct companies surely Teddie can.
No, I didn’t mean that. But there are circumstances that you don’t understand. Mr. O’Donnell can’t ask George to do anything for him. Mr. O’Donnell....
Really, Kate, you might let me answer for myself.
George always said he’d help me when I wanted to marry.
I presume your idea is to go into the City?
Yes, more or less.
Educated at a public school, I suppose?
Yes, I was at Harrow.

parts.direction: With a twinkle in his eye.

parts.say: Then I may take it that you tried to get into the Army and failed?
Yes, I suppose I did.
And you hadn’t got enough money to go into the diplomatic?
How on earth d’you know, George?

When a young man of family and education tells me he wants to go into the City, I know it’s because he’s too incompetent to do anything else. Fifty years ago the fool of good family went into the Church, now he goes into the City.
You’re not very flattering.
I dare say you’ll suit me all right.
Oh, George, you are a brick.
Give me a kiss and I’ll find him a job.
I’ll give you two.
I shan’t find him two jobs.
I can’t imagine why everybody’s so afraid of you, George. You’re an old dear.
A heart of gold, that’s what I always tell Kate.
Come and see me to-morrow morning, and we’ll have a talk about things.
It’s awfully good of you.
You know, you’ll have to do as you’re told if you come to me.
I dare say I shan’t mind that.
It’s not always pleasant being at the beck and call of a damned bounder.
How d’you mean?

Of course you look upon me as a damned bounder. I know that. I wasn’t educated at Harrow. My father was a hatter at Middlepool, a Nonconformist, and an aitchless one at that. I went to sea when I was fourteen, and when I was your age I was earning twenty-five bob a week as clerk in a bucket shop. Of course I’m a damned bounder.
Now, George, don’t be disagreeable.
Well, run along, children.... Have you spoken to your father about this?
No, we’re going to leave you to do that.
Are you?
Well, you see, father’s sure to kick up a bit of a row because Teddie’s so absolutely stony, but if you say you’ve given him a job....
Father may object....
Oh, he wouldn’t dare if George said it was all right.

lines.source:
[CATHERINE _gives a slight gesture, partly of vexation and partly
     of dismay_.

parts.say: Are you really very keen on marrying?
Awfully.
Well, I’ll see what I can do. Good-bye.

lines.source:
[_He nods to_ O’DONNELL. O’DONNELL _and_ ANNE _go out. As soon as
     they have gone_, CATHERINE _starts up_.

parts.say: George, you’re not going to take Teddie O’Donnell in your service. You must understand it’s impossible.
Why?
We can accept nothing from you.
This disinterestedness is rather a new trait in your family, isn’t it?
You’re only wasting his time in making him come down to see you to-morrow.
I don’t suppose it’s as valuable as all that.
Anne will have to be told the facts, and she’ll see at once that it’s out of the question for Teddie to accept favours from you.
I wonder.
I have no doubt of it.
Do you think she’ll be pleased when she’s told that, owing to your unreasonableness, her marriage can’t take place? Are you sure she won’t say that she has no quarrel with me?
I should make her understand.
It seems rather selfish on your part, doesn’t it? If Anne’s heart is set upon marrying this rather foolish boy, have
the heart to prevent her?
I’ve sacrificed myself long enough. It’s Anne’s turn now.
You’ll find self-sacrifice one of the forms of self-indulgence in which people are never wildly anxious to take turn and turn about.
What can you do with Teddie O’Donnell? He’s no good to you.
I’m not sure. I like dealing with gentlemen. When they go into the City they take to dirty work with an alacrity which you often don’t find in the City man born and bred.
Even if there was nothing else, I would do all I could to prevent a decent boy from being exposed to your influence.

Well, you may try yours on Anne. Tell her that I’ll start her young man on four hundred a year, and I’ll allow her a couple of hundred more, so that they can marry next week if they want to. And add that you are divorcing me, and it would be monstrous if either of them accepted my offer.

Oh, I know well enough that you didn’t make him pretty speeches because you took any interest in doing a kindness. It was merely another coil of the chain you’ve twisted round me. Oh, it’s fiendish. Each way I turn I find that you bar my way.
In the agitation of the moment you seem to be mixing your metaphors, my dear.
Mr. Robert Colby has come, madam.
Is he waiting downstairs?
I’ve shown him in the morning-room. He said he would wait till you were disengaged, ma’am.
Ask him to come up.
I’ll leave you----
Very good, sir.
With my best wishes. I’ll go and discuss the weather and the crops with your excellent father, and you shall discuss the situation with Robert Colby.
For goodness’ sake leave me alone.
Suggest a counter-petition and see how he takes it. My own impression is that he’ll run like a rabbit.

lines.source:
[GEORGE WINTER _goes towards the door that leads into the library
     and stops_.

parts.say: And if he does, you know whose arms are open to receive you. Whose 60 Mercedes is panting to take you to whose sheltering roof.

lines.source:
[_With a guffaw he goes out._ CATHERINE _gives a sigh of exhaustion
     and then braces herself for the coming interview_.

[_Enter_ ROBERT COLBY. _He is a handsome man of forty, spare and
     active, with a refined face and good features. He is clean shaven.
     His hair is grey. He has charming manners and an air of slightly
     old-fashioned courtesy. His voice is soft and pleasant._

parts.say: Mr. Robert Colby.

lines.source:
[CATHERINE _goes to him with both hands out-stretched. Her manner
     becomes brighter and more joyous. She seems to throw off the load
     of wretchedness which had oppressed her. The_ BUTLER _goes out_.

parts.say: How good of you to come.
You look as if you were surprised to see me.
You must be frantically busy. I thought you might not be able to manage it.
You know very well wild labour leaders couldn’t have prevented me.

Of course I know you wouldn’t really let me interfere with anything serious, but it’s very pleasant to flatter myself that the whole country is waiting while you’re wasting your time with me. D’you know what I’ve done?
I suspected what your note meant, but I’m anxious to hear it from your own lips.
I’ve crossed the Rubicon. I’m seeing my solicitor to-day, and the petition will be filed as soon as ever it’s possible.
I’m so glad. You had no right to go on with that degrading life.
I want you to assure me again that I’m right. I’m so weak. I feel so utterly defenceless.
It won’t be very long now before....
No, not yet, Robert.
I want to tell you at once how passionately I love you.

D’you think it’s needful? I’m so glad to think you’ve never made love to me. There was all the love I wanted in the look of your eyes, and your voice, though you said quite commonplace things, told me that you cared for me.
I’ve never even kissed your hand, Kate.
I’m very grateful to you. Now more than ever I want to feel quite sure that we have nothing to reproach ourselves with.
It’s rather hard on me.

Do you think I find it any easier? Sometimes when I’ve been dreadfully lonely, dreadfully wretched, I’ve longed to be able to rest my head on your shoulder, and I’ve thought I might have loved my tears if you could have kissed them away.
Were you angry with me when I wrote to you? The one foolish letter?
How could I be?
I was dreadfully unhappy then. Everything I tried seemed to go wrong. I was utterly dispirited, and I couldn’t help writing.
I read the letter till I knew every word by heart. Sometimes I wonder how I could have borne my life at all except for the knowledge that you cared for me.
You’ve never once told me that you love me, Kate.
D’you want me to say it in so many words? Why else d’you think I’m exposing myself to all the humiliation, all the horrors that are before me? Yes, I love you with all my heart and soul.
And after it’s all over?
It shall be as you wish.

You’ve meant so much to me, Kate. All the success I’ve had I feel that I owe to you. Sometimes I’ve hated the intrigues and the littleness of politics. I’ve been tempted to give the whole thing up. But you put fresh courage into me. It’s because of you that I’ve been able to ignore the rest and just keep my eyes fixed always on the greatness of the aim.
It makes me so proud to hear you say that.
Did you read the speech I made yesterday?

No, I’m afraid I haven’t yet.
Colby.

lines.source:
[_Gaily._] Wretched woman! And every jack one of the papers has given a
leader on it.

parts.say: I’m so sorry. It’s horrid of me.
What nonsense! Of course you’ve had much more important things to think about.
Tell me all about it. I suppose it was the Army debate.

Yes, I burnt my ships behind me. I said I thought some form of compulsory service was essential. Perigal’s going to the country at once. I think we shall get in. And if we do ... I wish to goodness they’d give me the War Office. Of course, after six years in office we can only hope for a small majority, and every seat will count. I wonder what will happen at Middlepool.
George is very popular.
Yes, that’s just it. As long as he was there the seat was safe. I wonder if anyone else will be able to hold it.
Do you think it will be impossible for him to stand again?
Quite. And rightly. No man’s obliged to go into Parliament. If he does it’s his duty to keep clear of scandal.

lines.source:
[CATHERINE _gives a very slight start, and when she speaks her
     voice is not quite steady_.

parts.say: That might be very difficult. A man might be an object of scandal, and yet be perfectly innocent. Supposing--a malicious person brought an action for divorce against him. It might be merely an attempt at blackmail. It would be monstrous to punish him for something that wasn’t his fault.

D’you honestly think that’s a possible case? If a man is shot at--it’s true he may not be technically guilty--but he can hardly be blameless. If a case can be made out at all against him he must have done something very foolish.

lines.source: [CATHERINE _does not answer. She is terrified at what he says._

parts.say: George Winter only went into the House for his private ambition. He contested a seat in order to give himself a stronger financial position, and now he wants to use his money to force himself into some sort of job. We’ve got no use for people like that.

parts.direction: As if she were changing the conversation.

parts.say: I wonder what you’d do if you were beaten at the General Election?
I don’t think my constituents will throw me out as long as I behave myself.
And if they did?
It would just about break me up. Politics are my whole life. I can’t imagine existence without the House of Commons. And I have so much to do. If they’ll only give me a chance I want to....
But, good heavens, I’m just going to make a speech.
Oh, my dear, I’m so proud of you. I admire you so enormously.
Not yet. Hang it all, wait to admire me till I’m Minister of War.
You dear.... Now you must go. I’ve got ever so much to do, and I’m sure you ought to have.
Good-bye, then. God bless you.... Say something nice to me before I leave you.
I shall think of you all day long.
Thank you. Good-bye.

lines.source:
[_He goes out._ CATHERINE _sinks exhausted into a chair, but she
     hears_ GEORGE WINTER _approach and pulls herself together. He comes
     in with_ ETCHINGHAM.

parts.say: The great man has taken his hook?

lines.source:
[CATHERINE _acknowledges his remark with a look, but does not
     answer_.

parts.say: I heard his fairy footsteps on the stairs.
Well, Catherine, I hope you’ve thought better of things.
Well?

lines.source:
[_He looks at her with malicious amusement, and she, her head
     thrown back, stares at him with hatred and anger._

parts.say: You think every man is a rogue, don’t you?
Certainly not. I think nine men out of ten are rogues or fools. That’s why I make money.
And what’ll you do when you come across the tenth man, who’s neither rogue nor fool?
Put him under a glass case.
You may find him awkward to deal with. Take care.

I shall. But I’ve looked for him so long that I can’t help thinking he doesn’t move in my set.... Now and then I’ve thought I’d really got him. But while I was scratching my head and wondering how the deuce I was going to manage, I’ve seen an itching palm steal softly out, and I knew it wasn’t the tenth man after all.
Mr. Bennett would like to speak to you, sir.
Is he on the telephone?
No, sir. He’s here.
What the deuce can he want?
I’ll come down to him.
No, let him come up. Perhaps it’s something important, and he’ll want to see me too.
Perhaps. Tell him to come up.
Very good, sir.
Who is Mr. Bennett?
He’s the secretary of two or three of our companies. He manages the office and that sort of thing.
He does all the work for which your father gets fees.
I don’t know about that. I flatter myself I’m worth my salt.

lines.source:
[_The_ BUTLER _shows in_ FREDERICK BENNETT. _He is a little man,
     thin, middle-aged, clean shaven, with a sharp face, and an
     extremely respectable appearance. He wears gold spectacles. He is
     in a tail coat and carries a tall hat in his hand. The_ BUTLER
     _goes out after announcing him_.

parts.say: What’s the matter, Fred?
I went round to Portman Square, Governor, and they told me you were here; I thought I’d better come on at once.
Nothing has happened, Mr. Bennett?
No, my lord.
May I speak to you for a moment, Governor?
Yes. Etchingham, d’you mind ...?
Of course not.

lines.source:
[_He goes up to_ CATHERINE, _who is standing at the window, and
     begins talking to her. The conversation between_ GEORGE WINTER
     _and_ BENNETT _proceeds in a lower tone, sinking almost to a
     whisper as it goes on_.

parts.say: What the devil’s the matter, Fred? You’re looking like a dying duck in a thunderstorm.
There’s been a cable from Macdonald, Governor.
Good business. And when’s the report due? I suppose it’s following.
Yes.
Why the deuce didn’t you ring me up? I’d have come down to the office at once. Now we’ve got that we can fire away.
I wouldn’t risk it on the phone. You never know who’s listening.
Drivel. You’re an old woman, Fred. Have you got it on you?
It’s not what you expect, Governor.
What the hell d’you mean?
It’s rotten. It’s....
You filthy liar, what are you talking about?
Take care, they’ll hear you.
Where is it?
I’ve got it in my pocket.
If you’ve been playing the fool with me, Fred....
I’m in it as deep as you are.

lines.source:
[GEORGE WINTER _takes the cable, is just going to unfold it, when,
     sick with apprehension, he hesitates. He is too terrified to read
     it._

parts.say: What does it say, Fred?
Why, there’s nothing there. We’ve been done in the eye. The mine’s worthless.

lines.source:
[GEORGE WINTER _turns away from him, a look of fear and
     bewilderment on his face. For a moment he hesitates uncertain what
     to do, then quickly makes up his mind and clenches his teeth._

parts.say: Governor.
If that’s true, the hundred thousand we paid for it might as well have been thrown down a drain-pipe.
What are you going to do?
Do? Fight it out.
Nothing serious, I hope, George?
Nothing.
You know what it means if you fail?
The Old Bailey. But I shan’t fail.
Luncheon is ready, my lord.

lines.source:
_The scene is the same as in the preceding act, the drawing room
     of_ LORD FRANCIS ETCHINGHAM’S _house in Norfolk Street_.

_It is afternoon._ LADY FRANCIS _is seated, working at embroidery
     on a drum_. CATHERINE _stands at the window, looking out into the
     street_.

parts.say: Aren’t you tired, Kate?

parts.direction: Still looking out of the window.

parts.say: No, mother.
You were out all the morning.
I went to see my lawyers.
I can’t understand that with such a father and such a mother, you should be such a monster of determination.

parts.direction: After a quick look at her.

parts.say: Dr. O’Farrell says your father will be well enough to come downstairs to-morrow.
I’m glad of that.
This is the second attack of gout he’s had this year.
Poor old thing!
Aren’t you tired of staring at the house opposite? You’re not expecting anyone, are you?
No.
You’re dreadfully restless.
I’m growing quite exhausted.

lines.source: [CATHERINE _gives a little cry of astonishment and alarm_.

parts.say: What’s the matter?
George has just driven up.
I suppose he’s come to see your father.
They mustn’t let him up. I won’t see him. It’s monstrous that I should have to put up with this.
My dear, don’t worry. George hasn’t made any attempt to see you for a fortnight.

lines.source:
[GEORGE WINTER _comes in hurriedly, unannounced; he shuts the door
     behind him_.

parts.say: What d’you want? You’ve got no right to force yourself upon me.

lines.source:
[_She makes a movement to leave the room, but he intercepts her. He
     takes a paper out of his pocket._

parts.say: I’ve just been served with this.
What else did you expect?
Your father told me that nothing was going to be done for the moment.
I can’t help what father said. It’s my business. I can allow no one to interfere with me.
What is that, George?
Would you like to look at it? It’s an interesting document.
It’s the petition, mother.
I wish I had my glasses. I’ve never seen one before.
You’ve been lucky.
Or virtuous.
You’ve got to withdraw this.
Surely you must see that from now all communications between us must pass through our lawyers.
Rats!

lines.source:
[CATHERINE _crosses the room and rings the bell at the side of the
     fireplace_.

parts.say: What are you ringing for?
For Thompson to open the door for you.
That’s excessively thoughtful of you.
Mother, can’t you protect me from this?
My dear, your husband is six feet high, and broad in proportion. I’ll tell Thompson to kick him downstairs if you like....
But it’s not a job that any well-regulated butler would enjoy.

lines.source: [_The_ BUTLER _comes in, and waits for an order_.

parts.say: Oh, Thompson, I’m expecting three gentlemen here at five o’clock. You’ll show them into the library, and let me know the moment they come.
Very good, sir.
What do you mean by this?
That’s precisely what I came to tell you.... I suppose you’ve been talking. There’ve been references to a dispute between us in the Middlepool papers, and the
, the Conservative rag, has stated in the current issue that you are divorcing me.
The Middlepool papers are singularly well-informed.
That’s where you’re mistaken. The
is printing a special edition with a complete and authoritative denial of the whole story. I’ve issued a writ for libel against the
One lie more or less on your conscience can make no great difference to you.
I’ve explained your presence here by your susceptibility to fresh paint.
What do you mean?
The day after Kate left Portman Square I came to the conclusion that the house needed re-decorating. I’m having it papered and painted from cellar to attic. When it’s finished I shall start again.
Fortunately the British workman takes his time.

But that’s not enough. The Middlepool people are nervous about the whole thing. You know Swalecliffe--he’s the Nonconformist minister--one of those confounded busybodies who go poking their noses into everybody’s private life. He’s on my committee. He and Ford control the dissenting interest between them.... They’ve got it into their heads that they want the truth from you.
Me?
Who is Ford?

Oh, he’s the richest man in Middlepool. He’s one of my directors on the Middlepool Investment Trust. Hard as nails! Shrewd as they make ’em! But a Nonconformist to the tips of his fingers. He’s just built a Congregational church out of his own pocket. He’s a corker to deal with.
But I don’t understand. What do these men want Kate to do?
They’re coming here at five o’clock with Boyce, my agent, to ask Kate if there’s any truth in the rumours.
But it’s outrageous!
Of course it’s outrageous! But what d’you expect from a parcel of sneaking Middlepool dissenters?
And what do you expect Kate to say?
She’s going to say it’s the first she’s heard of it. Then they’re going to ask her if she’s divorcing me, and she’s going to--repudiate the suggestion with all the scorn at her command.
I refuse to see these people.
Do you?

Or do you want me to tell them before your face that every word they’ve heard is true? Yes, I’ll see them. I’ll settle the whole thing. And then I shall be rid of this persecution. But I shall tell them the exact truth.
It’s not five o’clock yet.

lines.source:
[_The_ BUTLER _comes in, followed by_ MR. PERIGAL. _This is the
     Prime Minister. He is a stoutish man of middle height,
     clean-shaven, with abundant grey hair worn long. His face is
     sensual, shrewd and bland; his manner is kindly and restrained._

parts.say: Mr. Perigal.
My dear Bob, this is kind of you.
How d’you do? Well, Kate?
You never come and see us now you’re Prime Minister.
It’s a delusion of the public that the Prime Minister has nothing to do but pay afternoon calls.
I’m very glad to see you here.
On the best possible terms with my mother-in-law.
Well, when are you going to dissolve Parliament?

parts.direction: Making himself comfortable in an arm-chair.

parts.say: I’ve been so busy, I haven’t had time to read the papers for some days. What do they say about it?
Don’t be irritating, Bob.
My dear, a wise Prime Minister looks upon it as a privilege to fulfil the intelligent anticipations of the press.
I hope it’s not true that you’re going to give Emily Lascelles the Home Office?
Good heavens, you talk as if your sex were already comfortably installed in the House.

You know perfectly what I mean. It doesn’t matter about the men, because all the work is done by the permanent officials. But their wives are quite another matter. I tell you frankly it will be a great mistake if Emily Lascelles goes to the Home Office.
Why?
She can’t entertain. She doesn’t know a word of French. She dresses abominably.
That settles it. Emily Lascelles shall not go to the Home Office.
That is how history is made.
Oh, George, Frank bought a print of Napoleon the other day that he wants to show you. Do come up, will you?
Of course.
George collects things about Napoleon, you know.
Ah, the Napoleon of Finance.... I’m sorry to hear that Frank is laid up.
Oh, he’s much better to-day. We shall only be five minutes.
How naturally your mother did that! It almost took me in.
Have you come to see me by arrangement?
I’m up to my eyes in work! I’m afraid I could hardly find time for a chat in the middle of the afternoon without a rather special object.
I suppose not.
But your husband’s presence leads me to suppose that your common sense has made my errand unnecessary.
Haven’t you heard of the life we led together?
I make a point of never believing the disagreeable things that are said about a man who subscribes so handsomely to the Party funds as your husband.
Then I have you against me too?
My dear child, I’ve known you all your life. Your mother is my first cousin. We all desire nothing more than your happiness.
George was served with the petition this morning.

Ah!... It appears that two prominent supporters of your husband are coming up from Middlepool this afternoon to get from your own lips a denial of the rumours that have been circulating in the constituency.
I can promise you that they’re not going to get it.
I wish I could persuade you to pause before you take such an irrevocable step.
But why should you care?
We’ve been in for six years. We’re dissolving Parliament at once. I don’t know if we shall get in again. It’ll be a very close shave. We can’t afford to risk a couple of seats....
A couple?
The Chief Whip tells me that your husband proposes to lodge a counter petition.
If it weren’t so odious, the idea would be laughable. I promise you that....
Yes, yes, of course. Neither you nor Robert Colby has anything to reproach himself with. That is obvious. But ... well, I gather that the evidence is such that a

case could be made out. It would be awkward just at this moment, for all of us--I myself could wish that my relationship to your dear mother weren’t quite so close. The British people for some reason always judge moral delinquencies on the Radical side with great severity. I have always thought it a hardship that the Tories should have a sort of prescriptive right to the more amusing forms of immorality.
Let us understand one another plainly. Do you mean that if my husband drags Robert Colby through the Divorce Court, you’ll throw Robert overboard, even if his innocence is proved through and through?

My dear, no one is so innocent that there’s not occasion for many people to shake their heads and say: One never knows. I don’t suppose any Prime Minister would invite a man to enter his cabinet who’d been co-respondent in a divorce suit.
It’s nothing short of blackmail. George makes no concealment of the fact.
He has a brutal frankness which is sometimes rather engaging.
Oh, you drive me mad. My whole happiness is at stake, and you can pause to smile at that odious cynicism.... You’ve known Robert and me all our lives. Won’t you believe in us? Won’t you stand by us?

My dear, in the position entrusted to me I can’t take risks.... I dare say you know that one of the items in our programme is a modified form of compulsory service. I don’t know that I altogether like it myself, but it’ll take the wind out of the Tory sails, and we’ve got to do something. Robert has enthusiasm and he believes in the measure. He’s just the man to pilot it through the House.
He’s set his heart on getting the War Office.
Well, you have it in your hands to give it him.
I? Does he know that George Winter has made certain threats?
I think not.
Oh, what a responsibility you put upon me.
That generally goes with power, and at the moment you have that too.

Robert and I have never hidden anything from one another. He wouldn’t wish me to decide on a matter that concerns us both so nearly without consulting him. Do you object to my putting the whole thing before him?

Not a bit! But I can tell you at once what his answer will be. He’ll say that he loves you, and if he must choose between you and everything that has seemed to make his life worth living, he chooses you without a moment’s hesitation.

lines.source: [CATHERINE _gives a little sigh of relief and delight_.

parts.say: But while he’s in the very act of renouncing the world for your sake, look into his eyes, and perhaps you’ll see in them--oh, only for a moment, and you’ll have to look sharply--the shadow, the merest shadow of regret.... And perhaps in ten years, when I bring an ill-spent life to a close, you’ll say to yourself: If I hadn’t sacrificed him, he might be standing now in the shoes of that poor old incompetent Perigal.

parts.direction: Hoarsely, more moved than she wishes to show.

parts.say: I don’t believe Robert is ambitious.
You have to be a shrewd observer always to know the difference between ambition and patriotism.
I could think the world well lost for love.
Yes, but you’re a woman. D’you think a man can?

lines.source:
[CATHERINE _does not answer. Her face expresses the agony of her
     spirit as_ PERIGAL’S _words sink in_.

parts.say: May I ring and ask if my carriage has come back?
Let me!
I asked Colby to fetch me in it so that we might run down to the House together.

lines.source: [_The_ BUTLER _enters to announce_ ROBERT COLBY, _and goes out_.

parts.say: Mr. Colby.
I thought I’d come up for one moment just to say how d’you do.
I should have been furious if you hadn’t.
Of course!... I’ll just go up and see your father.
He will be so pleased. I’ll take you up.
No, no, no, no! I couldn’t hear of it. I can easily find my way.
I’ll do my best to entertain you while Mr. Perigal is gone.

parts.direction: MR. PERIGAL _leaves them, and_ COLBY _goes up to her gaily_.

parts.say: I jumped for joy when he sent me a note asking me to call for him here.
You might have come of your own accord.
