I’m always afraid that I shall bore you if I come too often. I rack my brains for plausible excuses to present myself at your front door.... What’s the matter, Kate?
With me? Nothing.
I thought you seemed worried.
D’you know that you haven’t shown the least desire to kiss me?
I? My dear, I was obeying your strict commands.
If you really wanted to, you wouldn’t have cared two straws for my commands.
My darling!
Oh no, don’t. I don’t beg for....
If you didn’t think of it of your own accord, it’s too late.
What on earth’s the matter with you?
If you love me why don’t you say so sometimes?
Good heavens, it’s on the tip of my tongue every moment of the day! I have to hold myself in to prevent falling at your feet and telling you how much I care.
Oh, forgive me! If you knew how dreadfully sometimes I long for a word of love!
Darling!
Oh, it’s too hard to restrain myself always. Have I been peevish and horrible?
Of course not.
But I want to know you love me.
Kate!

lines.source: [_He turns her face to him and kisses her on the lips._

parts.direction: Hiding her face and beginning to cry on his shoulder.

parts.say: You’re all I have in the world. I don’t know what I should do if I lost you.
In a very little while now we shall belong to one another for good and all.

parts.direction: Looking up, withdrawing herself a little and looking into his eyes.

parts.say: I wonder how much you love me?
With all my heart, with all my soul!
D’you love me enough to....

lines.source: [_She breaks off and turns away from him._

parts.say: What?
Nothing. I’m being silly and sentimental.
Let’s be wise and as well behaved as we generally are.
I can’t understand you this afternoon, Kate. You’re so different.
I shall frighten you. You’ve never realized that I’m a creature of moods. Are you sure it’s wise to link your life to a woman who’s capable of making almost a scene without any provocation?
If you had a bad temper I think I should love it.
Oh!
Kate!

parts.sound: Quite cheerfully, as if she were bantering.

parts.say: I want to put a purely hypothetical case to you. Supposing you had to choose between me and your career--which would you choose?
You, of course.
How glibly you say it!
Fortunately I shall never be forced to make such a tremendous choice.
Of course not.
Then why the dickens do you suggest it?
Because I’m nervous and restless and rather bored. I wanted to hear you say that you wouldn’t hesitate to sacrifice the world for my sake.
You absurd, delightful creature!

lines.source:
[_She is all smiles and coquetry. Suddenly the tears force
     themselves into her eyes and her voice breaks._

parts.say: Bob!

lines.source:
[_She stretches out her hands and he takes her in his arms and
     kisses her passionately; she breaks away from him and stands
     panting._ MR. PERIGAL _comes in followed by_ FRANCIS ETCHINGHAM,
     _who wears on one foot a large felt slipper, and walks with a
     stick_.

parts.say: Your father insisted on coming downstairs.
I really can’t stand my room any longer. And I can walk quite well now.
I thought Dr. O’Farrell said you were to stay upstairs till to-morrow, father.
O’Farrell’s an idiot.
It certainly looks as if you were better when you start abusing your doctor.
I hope I haven’t kept you waiting?
Not a bit!
Lady Francis has been showing me an old photograph.

parts.direction: Settling himself heavily into an armchair.

parts.say: That little joke of Angela’s didn’t quite come off.

lines.source: [CATHERINE _gives him a footstool and puts his foot on it_.

parts.say: I looked at it blankly, and then she said: Don’t you remember? It’s so-and-so. It gave me quite a start. It was the photograph of a young lady I’d been so madly in love with that I asked her to bolt with me--married woman and all that sort of thing--and, would you believe it? thirty years have passed since then, and upon my soul I didn’t know her from Adam!
Or Eve!

lines.source:
[CATHERINE _looks at him gravely, seeing the application to herself
     of his story_.

parts.say: You must congratulate yourself.

Well, my friends, I do. I’m not a high-minded, quixotic fellow like you, and I don’t mind telling you that I find it very agreeable to be Secretary for Foreign Affairs and Prime Minister. And yet, at the time, if anyone had given me the choice between my present position and a trip across Europe with the object of my affections, I wouldn’t have hesitated.
A merciful providence evidently had you under its care.

lines.source:
[CATHERINE _gives a slight start and rises as she hears these
     words, and looks at him steadily_.

parts.say: Well, we must be off. We mustn’t let even this charming lady interfere too much with the working of the British Empire.
Good-bye.
You must get your mother to show you that photograph. Thirty years ago I thought the little hussy much more attractive than that.
Good-bye, Frank. I hope your foot’ll be all right in a day or two.
I remember that little woman quite well. Not much to look at. I wondered at the time what Perigal saw in her.
You don’t want me just now, father, do you?
No, dear. Are you going out?
I’m only going to my room. I want--I want to be alone for a little bit.
Oh!

lines.source:
[_Before she can give any explanation, the_ BUTLER _comes in to
     announce_ BENNETT, _and she takes advantage of this to make her
     escape_.

parts.say: Mr. Bennett.
Ah, Mr. Bennett, forgive me if I don’t get up.
I’m glad to see you’re better, my lord.
Is anything the matter?
I thought your lordship expected me. You telephoned?
I?
Perhaps the Governor....
Ah yes, of course. George didn’t mention it. I suppose he wants me to sign cheques. I can do it just as well here as at the office. I expect Mr. Winter is in. Would you mind ringing?
Certainly.

lines.source: [_Before he can ring_, GEORGE WINTER _comes in_.

parts.say: I’ve given orders that no one is to be let up until those people arrive from Middlepool.
By Jove, I’d forgotten all about them. I say, George, you made a mistake in letting them come.
And I’ve told Lady Francis that we shall want this room to ourselves, and no one’s to come in without knocking at the door.
By the way, was it you who sent for Bennett?
It was. Your gout has come in very handy. Sit down, Fred. We’d better make ourselves cosy. Quite comfortable, Etchingham?
Quite, thank you.
Foot all right?
I don’t feel it at the moment.

lines.source:
[_Throughout the next scene_ GEORGE WINTER _is as gay and jovial as
     possible. He is thoroughly amused by the torture he is inflicting.
     He plays with_ FRANCIS ETCHINGHAM _as a cat would with a mouse_.

parts.say: I thought you might like to know at once that Macdonald’s report on the mine has come.
Ah, that’s good news. Now we can get to work at once.
Have you got it with you, Fred?
Yes, sir.
I’m sure his lordship would like to have a look at it.
Yes, hand it over, Bennett. This is really a thrilling moment. I believe I’m going to make my fortune at last.
As you justly remark, it’s a thrilling moment.

lines.source:
[BENNETT _takes the report out of a despatch-case and hands it to_
     ETCHINGHAM.

parts.say: Impressive document, isn’t it?

lines.source:
[_He smoothes it out and begins to read._ GEORGE WINTER _watches
     him with a certain amusement_.

parts.say: Rather technical, isn’t it?
Upon my soul, I don’t know why Macdonald can’t put it into plain English?
I’m thankful he didn’t put it any plainer.
I must honestly confess that I don’t quite grasp what he means.
I thought you wouldn’t. The long and the short of it can be told in two words.

parts.direction: Putting down the report with a slight sigh of relief.

parts.say: Ah!
The mine was practically worked out when we bought it. There’s no gold there worth speaking of. We’ve been done in the eye, and we’re eighty thousand pounds to the bad.

lines.source:
[_There is a moment’s pause._ ETCHINGHAM _looks at_ GEORGE WINTER
     _blankly_. BENNETT _glances nervously from one to the other_.

parts.direction: Hardly able to speak, his tongue sticking to his throat.

parts.say: You’re--you’re joking!
Read the report.
Then....
Your fortune is beginning to look rather silly, isn’t it? So’s mine.
Is this true, Mr. Bennett?
I’m afraid it is, my lord.
My God! What’s to be done now?
What do you think ought to be done?
I?
You’re chairman of the Syndicate. Your opinion can’t fail to be valuable.
We must just pocket our loss.
H’m!
With things in their present state a loss like that is about as much as we can stand.
The slump must come to an end soon.
We’ve been saying that for the last two months.
Then what the deuce is to be done?
That’s what we’re asking you.
We’ve got the Lewishams to reckon with.
Now’s their time to make a raid on us.
It doesn’t mean that we smash up, George?
Boyce will be here in a quarter of an hour.
George, don’t play the fool now. I’ve put all my eggs in this basket. I thought I was going to be rich at last. I wanted to get out of the whole thing. I wanted to live quietly and comfortably.
What are you going to do, Governor?
Suppress the report.

lines.source: [BENNETT _gives a start, but does not speak_.

parts.say: Go ahead as if we believed in the mine. We’ve got the Government expert’s report on which we bought the thing. We’ll put that in the prospectus.
But isn’t that dishonest?
Very.
George!
It’s an axiom in mining circles that when you’ve got hold of a rotten thing the proper course is to pass it on to the British public.
The public will find out there’s no gold there when you pay no dividends.
Oh, we’ll pay dividends for a year or two. By then we shall have turned the corner, and we’ll find another carrot for the British public.
But you say yourself it’s dishonest.
There’s another point you seem to have forgotten.
What is that?

lines.source:
[GEORGE WINTER _pauses and looks at him for an instant
     reflectively_.

parts.say: We paid for the mine with money that didn’t belong to us.
What d’you mean?

We’re in exactly the same position as the shop-boy who sneaks five bob from his master’s till to put it on a horse. If the horse comes in he puts it back, and if it doesn’t, he gets a month’s hard labour.... We shall get seven years.
What are you talking about, George?
Has it escaped your memory that you and I are Directors of the Middlepool Investment Trust?
Well?
We had to plank down eighty thousand pounds within twenty-four hours or lose the mine.
It looked like a certainty.

At that moment it was impossible for us to raise anything like that sum. The bank held a hundred thousand pounds of bearer bonds for the Middlepool Investment Trust. They delivered them on an order signed by you, me, and Bennett. We borrowed on them and completed the purchase of a worthless mine.
But I’ve never signed anything.
Yes, you did, my lord. They wouldn’t have delivered the bonds without.
Then my signature’s been forged.
Don’t you remember one day, after an excellent luncheon at Pym’s, you were just off to a wedding, and I asked you to come up into the office and sign some papers?
But I never looked at them. I didn’t know....
Ah, that’s your affair.
I shall go to the police.

D’you think you’ve got a plausible story to tell them? It sounds devilish improbable that a business man, a chairman of half a dozen companies, should sign documents without looking at them. Bennett and I will swear that you carefully read everything that was put before you--as, indeed, was your duty, my dear friend--and fully understood the nature of your act.
Mr. Bennett, you’ll testify that I never realized for a moment what I was doing. You told me they were purely formal documents. I saw George sign them. I added my signature without hesitation.
I think Mr. Bennett would be more than human if he cleared you at his own expense.
If there were any trouble, my lord, I should have to tell the truth.
That’s just what I want you to do.

I should have to say that you agreed with us in the necessity of borrowing the bonds with the idea of putting them back as soon as we’d floated the company, and that you signed the order to the bank with full knowledge of the seriousness of your act.
What is truth, said jesting Pilate.
You’re just as deep in it as we are, my lord.
Oh, my God!
It’s no use losing one’s head because one’s in a tight place.
You’ve tricked me. You’re a common swindler. In a month we may all be in prison.
I hear they make you very comfortable there nowadays.
Well, I see my duty before me. I didn’t know, but now there can be no excuse for me. I must go to Scotland Yard at once. I shall make a clean breast of the whole thing.
D’you think that’ll help you? It may mean five years instead of seven.
Every one will know that I’m incapable of such an act.
Don’t be a silly fool. Listen to me. We’ve got you tight. If we go under, you go under too. Let there be no doubt in your mind about that.
I must do my duty.
Your duty is to keep your head and help us out of the mess as best you can.
But nothing can be done. The mine’s worthless. How are we to raise eighty thousand pounds?
We’ve got six weeks before we need replace the bonds. If we can do it by then no one will ever know they’ve left the cellars of the bank.
There’s no more chance of replacing them in six weeks than there is the day after to-morrow.

Yes, there is, if we can float the company. That’s where you come in. I’ve got to keep my seat. I want all my prestige. I can’t have a divorce. You must go to Kate at once, and tell her that the only way she can save you from prison is by telling these men who are coming from Middlepool that she has no cause for complaint against me.
Good God! I’d forgotten Kate.
It’s only by going on now that we can save ourselves and the money that’s invested in our companies.
You wouldn’t have got into such a mess with Kate if you hadn’t made such a damned fool of yourself. Why couldn’t you leave these women alone?
My dear fellow, you speak as if I were to blame. They simply flung themselves into my arms. It would have been very rude if I hadn’t occasionally pressed them to my bosom.
It’s not much the Governor asks you, my lord.
To go and tell my daughter that I’m a thief and a swindler, and throw myself on her mercy!
That’s it.
I’ll see you damned first!
The alternative is prison.... It’s not very nice, penal servitude--is it, Fred? You know all about it. You can tell him.
Governor!
What does he mean?
Fred’s a solicitor who was struck off the rolls. He was sentenced to three years for misappropriating a client’s money.
Good God! Is that true, Mr. Bennett?
Yes, my lord.
I never knew.
Of course you didn’t. It’s not the kind of thing you’d expect him to brag about, is it? But it’ll go worse with him if we’re found out, because he’s been at it before. Tell him what it’s like, Fred.
Oh, Governor, don’t!

I knew him before he went in. His name was Feltman then. And when they let him out I took him because I felt sure he had everything to gain by sticking to me, and everything to lose by giving me away.
My God!

He can tell you what you’re in for. What the broad arrow’s like to wear, and what the food’s like to eat. And the work--it’s a healthy life, regular hours--you’re strong for your age. I don’t see why you shouldn’t break stones in the quarries with the rest of us. Hour after hour with your back feeling as if it were going to break, and your arms aching, aching, but not so badly as your heart.

lines.source:
[BENNETT _breaks down and sobs, difficultly trying to restrain
     himself_.

parts.say: And you count the days, three hundred and sixty-five in a year, and you wonder if they’ll ever come to an end. And your mind keeps on working. It wouldn’t be so bad if you were a brainless hulk like the man who’s sweating away beside you; but you think, and you can’t help thinking. And you curse yourself. And you think of the people outside who are free to do as they like, and you think of the spring-time and the flowers, and you think of the pleasant streets of London. And then there’s the regret which wrings your heart day after day, and you wish--you wish a thousand times you were dead. You sleep, you’re too tired not to, even though you’ve got hunger gnawing at your vitals, for you’re hungry, always hungry--and in your sleep you dream that you’re back again in your home, happy and comfortable; and when you wake up and feel your hard prison bed, you cry like a child.
Oh, my God! My God!

And then when you come out, it’s not over. You slink along the streets, feeling that it’s written on your forehead for every one to see, and your heart beats when you catch sight of a policeman. And at night it all comes back to you. You see it again, the warders, the convict gang, the prison food, and your back aches with the labour. And you wake shrieking with terror, shrieking, shrieking!

lines.source:
[_There is a pause._ ETCHINGHAM _looks straight in front of him
     with chill, stony eyes_. BENNETT _cowers brokenly, trembling in
     every limb. There is a knock at the door. Tap, tap, tap. Even_
     GEORGE WINTER _starts and a shiver runs through him. The knocking
     is repeated._

parts.say: Who the devil’s that? Come in!
What is it? I told you we weren’t to be disturbed.
The gentlemen have come, sir.

lines.source:
[GEORGE WINTER _reflects for an instant, and gives_ ETCHINGHAM _a
     rapid glance_.

parts.say: I’ll ring when you can show them up.
Very good, sir.
Now go to Kate, tell her what I’ve told you, and say the only way she can save you is by giving in.
I’ll see you damned first.
What!
I tell you I won’t. And you can go to Hell!
My lord, you don’t know what you’re doing.

parts.direction: Hardly able to believe his ears.

parts.say: D’you mean to say you refuse to speak to Kate?
If I speak to her it’ll only be to tell her that you’re a rotten scoundrel, and it’s worth her while to put up with anything to be rid of you.
It means seven years, you know that, don’t you?
For you and that dirty convict there.
You think you can get off by turning on us, but you can’t. We’ve got you tight.
You miserable fellow, d’you think I shall try to escape my penalty?
It’s tomfoolery. We haven’t got time for highfalutin now. Those fellows can’t be kept waiting all night. Kate’s the only person who can save us, and you....
I tell you I won’t. You’ve made a catspaw of me. And you thought you’d only got to say the word and I’d come to heel.
You’ve done it often enough before.
Don’t expect any mercy from him, my lord. He’ll do you in as sure as eggs is eggs.
I don’t want any mercy. You think you’ve got me tight. Don’t you know that I’ve got a way of escape whenever I choose to take it.
What are you going to do?
That’s my business.

lines.source: [GEORGE WINTER _understands; he drains a long breath_.

parts.say: What does he mean, Governor?
D’you think you’d have the courage?
Ah!... I tried it once, but I couldn’t do it. My hand shook. I let them take me.
I hadn’t thought of that. You can shoot yourself.
I’m obliged to you for the permission.
We drove him too far, Fred. We’ve made a mess of it.
You have, a confounded mess.

lines.source:
[_He gets up and hobbles across the room towards the door._ GEORGE
     WINTER _intercepts him_.

parts.say: Where are you going?
Get out of my way, you damned bounder.

lines.source: [GEORGE WINTER _looks at him for a moment and steps aside_.

parts.say: It is plain that you don’t think there’s anything more to be got out of me.

parts.direction: With a wave of the hand.

parts.say: I wish you a pleasant time at Portland, gentlemen.
Ring the bell, Fred.

lines.source: [ETCHINGHAM _stops as he hears the order and turns round_.

parts.say: That’ll bring those men up. Don’t you remember you told....
Ring the bell, damn you!

lines.source:
[BENNETT, _without a word, presses the button_. ETCHINGHAM _comes
     back into the middle of the room_.

parts.say: What are you going to do?
Hulloa, I thought you were routing out your pistols by now.
You’re not going to see those fellows?
They’ll insist on seeing Mrs. Winter.
Then I shall send for her.
Oh, you needn’t think she’ll back you up in your confounded lies.
Anyhow, I dare say you’d like to wait and see.
Have you got something up your sleeve?
My dear fellow, our sex would be at an impossible disadvantage in its dealings with the other, if it were not for the most obstinate of all their passions.... Self-sacrifice.
You’re counting on that?
You’ve given Kate such a training in it that I can’t help thinking it has become a habit.
I won’t say a word to move her.

lines.source:
[_He flings himself heavily into a chair. Already half his heroic
     resolutions have evaporated._ GEORGE WINTER _watches him with
     cynical amusement_.

parts.say: Like all great men I leave as little as possible to chance.
Perigal?
That’s it.
D’you think there’s a chance, Governor?
We must risk it. It’s the last fling.

lines.source:
[_The_ BUTLER _ushers in_ MR. SWALECLIFFE, JAMES FORD _and_ COLONEL
     BOYCE. MR. SWALECLIFFE _is a Nonconformist Minister, clean shaven,
     with a sallow grave face_. JAMES FORD _is a wealthy man, a pillar
     of the Nonconformist church in Middlepool and a local politician of
     importance; he is a large man, stout, oldish, badly dressed, with a
     slight North Country accent; he gives the impression of shrewdness,
     but also of complete honesty and straightforwardness_. COLONEL
     BOYCE, _who is_ GEORGE WINTER’S _agent, is spare and tall, bronzed,
     with grey hair and a grey waxed moustache; alert, neatly dressed
     and dapper. He is the kind of retired military man who may be seen
     by the score in Bath, Tunbridge Wells or Cheltenham._

parts.say: Mr. Swalecliffe, Mr. James Ford, Colonel Boyce.
How d’you do? I’m delighted to see you! I hope I haven’t kept you waiting?
Not a bit! It’s of no consequence.
Let me introduce you to my father-in-law. Mr. Swalecliffe--Lord Francis Etchingham.

lines.source:
[MR. SWALECLIFFE _bows stiffly. He is not going to open his mouth
     if he can help it._

parts.say: Mr. James Ford.
Pleased to meet you, Lord Francis.
It’s very kind of you to say so.

When I suggested to Lord Francis that it would be more convenient for you to come here, he put his house at my disposal. My wife is staying here, you know. We’re doing up the house in Portman Square, and she can’t stand the smell of paint.
Naturally. I don’t like it myself.
How is your wife, Mr. Swalecliffe? Well, I trust.
Thank you.
And the children?
Yes, thank you.
Now sit down and make yourselves comfortable, won’t you? Have you had tea?
Yes, thank you.
I took them into my club.
Will you have a drink? I can recommend my father-in-law’s whisky. I know it’s no good offering you one, Mr. Swalecliffe?
Boyce and I had a little drop of Scotch to our tea.
Then we’ll get to business at once, shall we?
I should like to say, before we go any further, that it is with the greatest regret that Mr. Ford and I have come up to London on such an errand.
There’s been a lot of gossip in Middlepool, and, well, we thought the shortest way to settle it was....
I personally don’t think this is a matter of which the committee ought to take any notice. A man’s private life is his private life, and....

That’s all very well, Colonel. Winter’s an old friend of mine. We’ve had business dealings together for the past twenty years. But ... well, it’s a question of winning the election or losing it. There’s never been much in it one way or another, and fifty votes more or less will make all the difference.

I want to tell you frankly, Mr. Winter, that I should feel it my duty to vote against you, if there were any truth in the reports that have been going about. And I should feel it my duty to advise my congregation to follow my example.

That’s clear enough in all conscience. Gentlemen, the best answer I can make to you is that I receive you in my father-in-law’s house. My wife is upstairs in her mother’s boudoir. I give you my word of honour that there is not the smallest shadow of truth in any single syllable that you have heard. I have issued a writ for libel against the
Surely that ought to satisfy anyone.
Well, it doesn’t satisfy me.
Perhaps you would like my father-in-law to tell you that every word I say is scrupulously true?
We don’t doubt your word, Mr. Winter, but we came to London with a particular object.
I must say I thought from the beginning it was open to the gravest question.
The committee discussed it at length, and the majority agreed that....
Of course, of course, Etchingham, will you give these gentlemen the assurance?
I think the whole thing’s damned impertinent.
That’s exactly what I said.
You’re only wasting time, Winter.
We made up our minds that we must have a certain assurance from the lips of Mrs. Winter. Then we can go back to Middlepool with comfortable minds.
D’you mean to say you wish to cross-examine my wife?
I merely wish her to answer the questions that were put to you in Colonel Boyce’s letter on behalf of the committee.

parts.direction: Pretending to fly into a violent passion.

parts.say: No decent woman would stand it. I refuse to ask my wife to expose herself to such a degradation.
That means that you don’t represent Middlepool in the next Parliament, George Winter.
I’d sooner lose my seat than expose a defenceless woman to such humiliation. You can go and tell that to your committee and be damned to you!
But we came up from Middlepool on the understanding that we were to see your wife, Mr. Winter.
My wife is in very delicate health.
We shan’t keep her more than five minutes. You’d be wise to let common sense get the better of your pretty sentiments.

lines.source:
[_There is a slight pause._ GEORGE WINTER _realizes that he cannot
     bluff them out of their determination: he goes over silently and
     rings the bell_.

parts.say: Very well.
I think it’s the best thing, you know.
But if my wife refuses to answer I warn you that I shall not say a word to persuade her. I think the whole thing’s a perfect scandal.
Tell Mrs. Winter that Lord Francis and I would be very much obliged if she’d come to the drawing-room for one moment.
Very good, sir.
I wish you to know that I have expressed myself very strongly all through against this proceeding.
Shut up, Boyce. When we want your opinion we’ll ask for it.

lines.source: [_They wait in silence. In a moment_ CATHERINE _comes in_.

parts.say: These are the gentlemen of whom I spoke to you. Gentlemen, here is my wife.
How d’you do, Mrs. Winter? Pleased to see you.
How d’you do?
We’ve not had the pleasure of welcoming you in Middlepool for some time.
I’ve not been very well lately.
Will you put the question to Mrs. Winter that we set in our letter to you of the day before yesterday?
No, sir. If you’re not ashamed to ask the question you may ask it yourself.
I am a stranger to Mrs. Winter. The matter requires some explanation.

It’s no use making any bones about it, Swalecliffe. Mrs. Winter, I’m sorry to put you in this position, but there it is, and it can’t be helped. There are busybodies everywhere, and Middlepool has its fair share of them. There’s been a lot of gossip about you and your good man, and if we don’t look out it’ll lose him the election.
What do you want me to say to you?
Well, we want to be able to go back to Middlepool and tell them we’ve had it from your own lips that there’s no truth in these reports.

lines.source:
[_There is a pause._ ETCHINGHAM _can hardly bear his anxiety_.
     BENNETT _is trying to hide his agitation_. GEORGE WINTER _looks at
     her with a smile_. CATHERINE _and_ JAMES FORD _confront one
     another, and she looks at him steadily_.

parts.say: That you may do.

lines.source:
[ETCHINGHAM _cannot prevent a little gasp of relief, but_ GEORGE
     WINTER _makes no sign_.

parts.say: You have no intention of divorcing your husband?
None whatever.
You’ve never had any intention?
Good lord, isn’t that enough for you?
Yes, yes, we won’t bother you any more. Thank you, very much! And I’m glad that you’ve put our minds at rest. George Winter, shake hands.
I’ll shake hands with you, but I can’t help saying that I could have expected more charity, more confidence in me from men who make a practice of belief in the Christian Church.
That’s all right.
I can understand your vexation, Mr. Winter. But we were in a very difficult position.
Anyhow, we must get along, and if we look sharp we’ll catch the 5.40 back to Middlepool. Good afternoon to you, Mrs. Winter. Good afternoon, gentlemen.
Mr. Bennett will show you out. Good-bye. Good-bye, Boyce. I shall be up at Middlepool in a day or two....
Oh, by the way, Boyce, a little bit of information for you--Robert Colby’s going to the War Office in the New Cabinet.

lines.source:
_The scene is a spacious sitting-room in the Palace Hotel at
     Middlepool. It is sumptuously furnished with the lack of taste
     peculiar to such apartments. Everything is large and rich and
     rather stiff. It is obvious that the decorations have been carried
     out on contract by a first-rate firm. They are calculated to give
     the business man who engages the room the impression that he is
     getting his money’s worth._

_On the left is a large French window, opening to the floor and
     looking on the square in front of the hotel. At the back is a door
     leading into_ GEORGE WINTER’S _bedroom. On the right are two doors;
     one leads into the passage, and the other is that of_ CATHERINE’S
     _room_. _There is a telephone on the table._

_It is some weeks later, between ten and eleven on the morning of
     the election._

_When the curtain rises there is an excited buzz of conversation._
     BOYCE _is at the telephone_.

parts.say: Yes, Colonel Boyce. Be sure you don’t make a mistake.
I can’t imagine what’s become of him. One would have thought....
If he’s not there, you’d better try somewhere else.
For goodness’ sake let me hear myself speak.

lines.source:
[_These speeches are said simultaneously, and immediately
     afterwards is heard the dull roar of a train passing through the
     station, and a long, shrill whistle._ ETCHINGHAM _starts
     nervously_.

parts.say: Oh, confound those trains.
I should have thought you’d got used to them by now.
Good Lord, I’ve not slept for a week. They go on all night.
They worried me a bit last night. And when I did get to sleep I heard them whistling away through my dreams.
They don’t seem to trouble Winter.
If they did I suppose he wouldn’t come to this hotel.

parts.direction: Nodding in the direction of_ GEORGE WINTER’S _room_.

parts.say: He sleeps next door, doesn’t he?
He told me he slept like a top last night.
He looked as fresh as paint this morning.
And his room’s practically on the line.
Oh, nonsense.
Yes, it is. You just walk down a flight of steps into the garden, and there you are within twenty feet of the line.
Worst place in Middlepool for a hotel. I told them so when they came to me about it. Wanted me to put money in it. Not me.

parts.direction: Breaking in before_ JAMES FORD _has finished_.

parts.say: Surely Mr. Winter ought to be here by now.
You won’t make him come any quicker by looking out of the window.
Every moment’s valuable. Something ought to be done at once.
Don’t you know where he is, Colonel?
He was booked to speak to the men at Parker and Gibbons at 10.30. But you know what he is. Half a dozen places at once. He’s about the most difficult person to catch I know.
Have you sent down to Parker and Gibbons?
Yes, of course I have; I’ve sent a dozen fellows after him to tell him to come to the hotel at once.
You’ve been careful? You’ve not ...?
You don’t think I’m a beginner at this game, do you?
Well, I didn’t know how you’d made him understand what had happened.
He’s not made him understand. When Winter’s told he’s expected at the Palace at once he’ll guess something’s in the wind.
You’re sure he won’t go to the Committee Rooms?
If he does he’ll be sent on. I thought it would cause a lot of gossip if we had a meeting there. That’s why I suggested the hotel.
I wish to goodness you wouldn’t look so depressed, Mr. Swalecliffe.
You’re a business man, Mr. Ford. D’you think there’s any truth in this article?
You’d better ask Lord Francis. He’s chairman of the new company; I’m only an investor.
Of course there’s nothing in it. The whole thing’s a malicious libel.
Well, we’ll hear what Winter’s got to say about it.
My Lord, I wish he’d come.
You don’t mean to say you think there’s anything in it?

I’ve applied for ten thousand shares. You don’t suppose I like it when an article comes out in a financial paper on the day of issue that the mine’s practically worked out, and Winter’s expert has reported that the ore’s not worth the cost of crushing.
Everybody who’s got a penny to spare in Middlepool has applied for shares.
George Winter told me it was the biggest thing he’d ever had.
He’s never let you down before. Why should he let you down now?
I don’t say he’s let me down. But he told me to put my shirt on it, and ... I don’t want ten thousand worthless shares.
The damnable thing is that it should happen on the day of the election.
It would be monstrous if people didn’t vote for him because of an article in a London newspaper.
You know what people are. They lose their heads. The seat has always been won and lost on the wobblers.
Oh, the first thing is to win the seat.
Well, we shan’t do that unless Mr. Winter comes at once and we make up our minds what to do.
Ring up the Committee Rooms, Boyce, and ask if anything’s been heard of him.
All right. I’ll do that.
I was never so taken aback as when Boyce showed me the telephone message from London.
When do the London papers get here, Mr. Ford?
They ought to be here by half-past ten.
Put me on 78, will you?
Why the devil don’t they bring them in?
Don’t worry. I’ve told a waiter to bring them as soon as they arrive.
I say, is that you, Masters? Has Mr. Winter been there? Well, send Rogers. Here. No, here, confound you! The Palace.
No, nothing’s been seen of him since early this morning.
I wonder what the other side are going to do when they hear this.
Oh, don’t you be afraid. They heard about the attack as soon as ever we did.
You ought to have held the line and prevented them from getting on to London.
Good God, one can’t think of everything at once.
It seems to me the whole thing has been about as disgracefully mismanaged as it could be.
If you’d ever tried to run an election you’d know it wasn’t so easy as all that.
I’m not an election agent. It’s not my business.
Come, come, gentlemen, it’s no good quarrelling about it.

lines.source: [_These three speeches are spoken at once._

parts.say: How is the polling going on?
Oh, I think we shall have the heaviest poll we’ve ever had.
Of course there’ll be some slackening off just now. A lot of working men voted when the polling stations opened.
There’ll be twice as many at the dinner-hour.
You don’t know what the Tories are doing, Colonel?
I should think I did know. They’re going to set up the article as soon as it comes in.
The whole article?
The whole confounded thing.
And placard the streets with it. They’ve made arrangements to print off a thousand, and they’ve got their bill stickers all ready and waiting.
It’s infamous.
Nonsense! It’s business. We’d have done the same if we’d had the luck to get such a stick as this to beat Morrison with the very morning of the election.
The comfort is, they don’t know Morrison and they do know Winter.
That’s the danger, too. They may know him too well.
I don’t know what the devil you mean by that. You seem to forget that you’re speaking of my son-in-law.
Oh, we’re not here to pay one another compliments.
If you’ll wait a minute or two he’ll be here himself and you can say to him anything you want to.
What I can’t make out is why he chose this particular day to bring out his company.
He didn’t think the election would take place just yet.
Every one’s been talking of a general election for the last two months.
You know it was sprung upon us at the end.
Couldn’t he have kept the issue back?
He’d got everything fixed up by then.
Of course he could. It was only his obstinacy. I told him it was a bad time to give an American issue to the public.
Well, you weren’t obliged to apply for shares, were you?
Tell me something I don’t know next, will you?
I can tell you there’s no harm in keeping a civil tongue in your head.
Thank you, I don’t want lessons in manners from you.
You won’t do yourselves much good by losing your tempers.
Why doesn’t Mr. Winter come?
I dare say he’s sent his car to take some one to the poll and he’s had to walk.
It seems to me that you’ve bungled everything you could.
I don’t know why the devil you should blame me.

lines.source: [_A waiter comes in with newspapers on a tray._

parts.say: Here they are at last.

lines.source:
[_They crowd round the waiter and take the papers from him. The
     waiter goes out._

parts.say: Thank God, now we shall know the worst.
No, that’s got nothing.
Here it is.
Give it me.

lines.source:
[_He takes the paper from_ BENNETT _and opens it_. ETCHINGHAM
     _watches him anxiously_.

parts.say: I wish to goodness I’d never thought of stocks and shares. I knew it was wrong. Oh, what a punishment!
We can’t all read the paper at once.
Spread it out on the table. That’s the best way.

lines.source: [BENNETT _and_ FORD _rapidly run their eyes down the article_.

parts.say: Steep, isn’t it?
If the Tories print this it’ll about bust us.
The whole thing’s a pack of lies. It’s scandalous that such methods should be used to influence an election.
D’you want to read it?
What does it say?
Merely what they phoned down from London.
But it puts it about as hot as I’ve ever seen a financial article.
D’you think it’ll interfere with the issue?
It’ll bust it.
Can’t something be done to find Winter?
All we can do is to wait.
Hang it all, we can’t go on waiting, and waiting, and waiting. Isn’t there one of you who can do something?
Keep your head, man, that’s about the best thing you can do.
It’s all right. I’ve got him.
Thank God.
I told him to hurry up. He was just going to speak to some fellows in a factory.
He’s coming?
Yes, rather. He said he’d be here in a jiffy.
Did he want to know what it was about?
There was no time for him to ask. And he was talking to a whole crowd when I found him.
He knows it’s important?
Don’t be afraid about that. If he says he’ll come at once, he’ll come.
Here he is.
At last.

lines.source:
[GEORGE WINTER _comes in and surveys them for a moment. He smiles
     sardonically._

parts.say: Quite a party.
We thought you were never coming.
What’s the trouble?
That’s the trouble.
has got an attack on the Campo del Oro.
Is that all?
It’s a good deal.
The Lewishams have got
in their pockets.
You read it.
They say there’s no gold in the mine.
What do they know about it? They’ve not been there and my expert has.
That’s just it. They say you’re floating it on the report the owners gave you when you bought it, and you’re holding back Macdonald’s.
It’s extraordinary what a lot the papers know.

parts.sound: The telephone rings.

parts.say: What is it?
London call. You’d better go and speak to them, Fred.
No, don’t connect with me. Mr. Bennett will come along.
It’s one of my brokers. Now let’s go on. As abuse I don’t really think very much of it. I could have said much unpleasanter things about myself.
You seem to take it very calmly.
I’ve not been fighting the Lewishams for ten years without getting some pretty hard words broken on my back.
D’you see that bit about where the money came from?
I didn’t see that.
I’ll read it you, shall I?

“It is stated that Mr. Winter paid eighty thousand pounds for this precious mine. It would perhaps be interesting to inquire how he was able to raise such a sum at a time not only of general stringency, but of peculiar difficulty in the Central American market. Perhaps Mr. Winter, like King Midas, is able to turn into gold everything he touches and he may have been able to change his office furniture into precious metal. Perhaps not.” Childish, isn’t it? Do they think I’m going to let out my little trade secrets to please them?
But where did you get the money?

lines.source:
[ETCHINGHAM _gives a slight start, but_ GEORGE WINTER _remains
     perfectly cool_.

parts.say: My dear fellow, you don’t suppose I stole it, do you? That’s where the born financier comes in. He makes money as a conjurer makes a white rabbit appear out of a silk handkerchief.
A very satisfactory explanation.

lines.source:
[_For an instant, hardly perceptible to the others, the eyes of_
     GEORGE WINTER _and_ JAMES FORD _meet_.

parts.say: But that’s hardly the point, is it?

lines.source:
[_During the rest of the scene_ JAMES FORD _is thinking the matter
     over. His eyes rest on_ GEORGE WINTER _as if he were trying to
     guess something_.

parts.say: Something must be done at once.
Have the Tories got hold of it?
They’re printing the article on posters.
Nuisance, isn’t it?

lines.source:
[_He pauses to reflect for a moment._ MR. SWALECLIFFE _breaks in
     upon his thoughts_.

parts.say: Is there any truth at all in that article, Mr. Winter?
Not a word.
It puts me in a very awkward position.
What’s the matter with you?
I thought the shares would go to a premium before they were issued.
Like the San José tramways, eh?
Mr. Ford says this will--bust the issue.
Nice of him.... Been having a little gamble, have you?
If it was a certainty I didn’t see there could be any harm in it.
Like playing with loaded dice? How many shares have you applied for?
Five hundred.
Sporting of you.
I didn’t mean to take them up, you understand. I haven’t got more than five hundred pounds in the world. I thought they were bound to go up half a crown and....
Five hundred half crowns are quite worth having, aren’t they?
It’s been a lesson to me. I’ll never do anything like it again. I shan’t have the chance. If I have to pay for the shares....
Get my cheque book, Teddie.
Yes, sir.
What are you going to do?
I don’t want anyone to come into this concern who doesn’t believe in it. Make out a cheque for five hundred pounds to Mr. Swalecliffe.

lines.source: [O’DONNELL _writes out a cheque during the next speeches_.

parts.say: That’s very generous of you.
Generous? Not a bit of it. You don’t think I mind having five hundred shares more, do you?
D’you think they’re worth it?
They’ll be worth ten pounds a piece in six months, or I’m a Dutchman.

lines.source:
[O’DONNELL _hands him the cheque-book and a pen_. GEORGE WINTER
     _signs his name and tears out a cheque_.

parts.say: That looks as if you had confidence in the mine.
Here you are.
D’you want me to buy your shares off you?
Not just yet, thank you.
But what’s the meaning of the article, then?
Why, it’s as plain as a pikestaff. The Lewishams were willing to give their eyes for the mine, but I was too much for them. Now they’re crabbing it. That’s all.

lines.source:
[_He says this with great assurance, as if it thoroughly explained
     the whole thing._

parts.say: But then....
Pay that into your bank and hand over the certificate to me when you get it.
D’you think they’ll go to a premium?
I’ve no doubt of it. I dare say the five hundred half-crowns will be just as useful to me as to you. But I shall hold on. I want a bigger profit than that.
But if they’re good enough for you, they’re good enough for me.
No, you’ve taken my cheque now. It’s too late.
There’s your cheque. You can have it back again. I’m going to keep the shares.

Well, I don’t mind. It won’t make much difference to me. But don’t sell them, whatever you read in the papers. What’s a profit of half a crown? Wait till you’ve got a profit of five pounds, and then you can think of selling them.
Five pounds? That would be two thousand five hundred.
Wait a minute. Get on to Bishop and Jones.
The printers?
We must answer this article. I’ve just been thinking what we’d better say.

lines.source:
[_He sits down and begins to write, while_ COLONEL BOYCE _goes to
     the telephone_.

parts.say: What’s their number, d’you know?
703, I think.
Is that the Exchange? Give me 703, will you? That is Bishop and Jones, the printers, isn’t it?
I’m going to make it hot and strong.
Isn’t there anything I can do?
Are you Bishop and Jones?
Tell them to have everything ready to print off a couple of thousand posters at once. You’re just coming round in the car.
Hulloa? Will you get everything ready to print off a couple of thousand posters at once. I’m just coming round. Colonel Boyce. Yes. That’s it.

parts.direction: Speaking through_ COLONEL BOYCE’S _instructions to the printers_.

parts.say: What d’you think of this, Ford?
Let’s have a look.
You see we’ve got the advantage that they have to print a whole article. And we only need a couple of sentences.
Yes, that seems all right.
Couldn’t be better.
Make a copy of it, Teddie. Hurry up.
We haven’t got any time to lose.
The car’s at the door.
I shan’t be a minute.
You can get hold of the bill-posters, can’t you?
Oh, yes, there’ll be no bother about that.
Here you are. That’s done.
Take it, Boyce. And hurry up.

parts.direction: Taking a copy of the reply.

parts.say: Trust me.

Teddie, jump into a cab and go round to the newspaper offices. And tell them to put that in their next edition. Biggest type they’ve got. Then go to the Committee Rooms and wait. I’ll ring you up there or come round.
All right.
And hustle, or I’ll sack you.

lines.source: [_He goes out, and as he does so_ BENNETT _comes in_.

parts.say: You’re taking it better than I expected.
What do you expect me to do; bang my head on the floor and tear out my hair? Can’t afford it. Takes me all my time to keep my hair on.
Here’s Bennett.
Well?
Nothing much has happened. They’re a bit excited in the City.
No bad drop in anything?
Nothing to speak of.
That’s a relief.
Everything is sound. No one would be such a fool as to do a bear.
I’m getting on to MacLaren and Hewitt.
That’s all right. I wanted them.
Are they brokers?
Yes. Look here, Ford. I’m due to speak in the Cattle Market now. I wish you’d go down and keep them going till I turn up. I shall only be ten minutes. You’ve got the line all right, Fred?
Yes.
Well, I don’t mind if I do that. There’s nothing I can do here, is there?
No, leave it all to me. Your interests are my interests.
I’ll make tracks.
That’s good.
Governor, I thought I’d better not say too much while he was there.
I saw something was up. That’s why I got rid of him.
Things are rotten.
Good Lord.
The Lewishams are going for us.
I thought they would as soon as I saw the article.
Who’s given it away, d’you think?
How do I know? That doesn’t matter. The only thing is to face it.
D’you mean our shares are falling, Mr. Bennett?
There’s a lot of selling.
I wish we could corner them. I’d like to give the bears a lesson.
If it goes on there’ll be a panic.
You’ve told the brokers to do all they can to prevent its going too far?
I’ve told them to buy, but carefully.
You must go up to London, Fred. There’s no one there with a head on his shoulders.
I thought that was the best thing myself. I’ve looked out the trains. I can just catch the express. I shall be there soon after one.
Then bolt at once. I give you a free hand.
If the slump can be stopped, I’ll stop it.
It’s not a matter of can. It must be stopped. And wire reassuring messages. We must hang on to the telephone for all we’re worth.
Good-bye.
And come back when the House closes. We must talk over things.
All right. Good luck.
Is it all up with us, George?
What the dickens are you talking about?
They’ve found out the truth. It’s there in black and white that the wretched mine’s worthless.
They can’t prove anything.
Ever since I knew I’ve scarcely closed my eyes at night. I wish I’d shot myself when you first told me.
My dear fellow, you’re much more comfortable here than you would be at Kensal Green.
And the worst of it is....
At first I was overcome with the horror of it. But little by little I’ve got used to it, used to your being a thief and a swindler.
You put things rather bluntly, don’t you?
And Bennett was a convict. It all seems quite natural now. And I can talk and laugh with you. And I eat by your side every day.
One can’t make a fortune without taking risks.
There are always those missing bonds. They’re in my thoughts day and night.
No one can make inquiries for three weeks. By that time we shall have gone to allotment, and the bonds will be safely back in the black box.
But will you be able to go to allotment?
Of course we shall. This article isn’t going to do us any harm. I shall win the seat. That’ll give these Middlepool people confidence.
George, I believe Ford is uneasy. I don’t trust him. Supposing he found out about the bonds?
It might be devilish expensive.
You’ll never buy him.
I never met the man yet who hadn’t his price. Flattery if he’s a fool, hard cash if he’s a wise man. But a price of some sort. There’s always a price.
Take care of Ford, George.
I’m not frightened.
Sometimes I’m afraid, you’re so confident. It’s impossible a thing like this can end well.

I believe in my star. I’ve been in tight corners before, but I’ve wriggled out of them. I’m stronger than ever I was. I’ve got ten times more brains than any of my competitors. The ball is at my feet and I’ve only got to set it rolling. What d’you think difficulties are to me? I’ve never been in better spirits, so alert, so buoyant, as during these last weeks when my neck has been in a noose and every policeman I passed might have a warrant in his pocket for my arrest. If there were ten times more difficulties I’d overcome them all. In ten years I shall be the richest man in London. In fifteen I shall be a peer. My God, I feel as if the world were an orange and I’d got my teeth into it, and I shall suck it dry.
I wonder how many ruined lives will be sacrificed to give you all you want. You walk over dead bodies and broken hearts.

Rot! I flutter the will-o’-the-wisp of gain before the covetous, and they follow. They want to make money without working for it. Well, I’m cleverer than they are. Swalecliffe gambles with his five hundred pounds. His five hundred pounds will find its way into my pocket. It’s his own look out. Each for himself and the devil take the hindmost.
By George, I’ve got an idea.... The Lewishams can’t attack my stocks without weakening their own. We’re in the same boat, and if one of us shakes it both’ll topple out.
What d’you mean?
Well, we’ll attack the Lewishams. I’ll get on to MacLaren’s at once. Go to the post office and wire to Bennett. He’s sure to call at the office.
He’ll twig. By George, that’s the ticket. Why didn’t I think of it before? We’ll make the Lewishams sorry they started this game.
But supposing ...?
Good God, man, don’t suppose, do as I tell you. Don’t you see we’ve got nothing to lose and everything to gain? I know my luck’s in. And I follow my luck. That’s genius.

lines.source:
[ETCHINGHAM _with a sigh and a shrug of the shoulders goes out to
     send the telegram_. GEORGE WINTER _begins to walk excitedly up and
     down_.

_The scene takes place in the sitting-room of the Palace Hotel, but
     it is eleven o’clock at night. Only a reading lamp is lit, the
     light of which falls on_ CATHERINE _and_ LADY FRANCIS. CATHERINE
     _is working at some embroidery_.

parts.say: Can you see, dear? Wouldn’t you like some more light?
No, the light hurts my eyes.
You’re looking very pale, darling.
I haven’t been sleeping very well here. We’re so near the trains, and they seem to run all night.
I wonder how George can stand it. His room is practically on the railway.
Thank heaven, it’s over. We shall know the result in half an hour, and to-morrow we can go.
What are you going to do?
What can I do? Nothing.
I’m afraid you’re very unhappy, Kate.
Please don’t think that, mother.
You’ve given up everything for our sake.

I wish I could think so. I gave up my divorce because--because I was afraid. I couldn’t risk the regret that Robert might feel later. I should always have been looking for it.... One must never forget that love is a woman’s whole life, but it’s never more than part of a man’s, never.
What did you tell him?
I wrote and said I found it impossible to go on with my action. I begged him not to try to move me. I told him I was very unhappy.
Poor child.
He wrote very kindly. He made it as easy for me as he could. And now it’s all over. I’ve lost my last chance of happiness. I’m bound to my husband for the rest of my life.
And do you still love Robert?
Yes. And I’m glad of what I’ve done. The only thing that helps me is the pride I take in all the great things he’s going to do. And it will have been me. I gave him the opportunity.

lines.source: [ANNE _comes in. She is wearing a coat and skirt and a hat._

parts.say: Well! You are strange people. How on earth can you sit there and sew while the counting’s going on? I’ve never been so excited in my life.
Why have you come back?
Well, it’s nearly finished now. Teddie said there’d be rather a scrummage when the result was known, and I’d better get out of the way.
Obedient creature.
It rather amuses me to be ordered about. Besides, I couldn’t help seeing that nobody wanted me. Teddie promised he’d bolt round as soon as the result was out. I say, let’s have some light, shall we?

lines.source:
[_She turns on the electricity, and the room is suddenly a glare of
     light._

parts.say: You’ll blind us.
I love an election. I’ve never had such a time in my life. I’ve enjoyed every minute of these three weeks. I hope Teddie’ll go into Parliament.
On four hundred a year?
Oh, George will give us a rise. He says Teddie’s awfully useful. George
good, isn’t he?
I’m glad you’re so happy, darling.

parts.direction: Abruptly, after a little, quick look at her.

parts.say: You’re not angry with us, Kate?
Good heavens, why should I be?
You know, it’s so dreadfully hard to pretend I haven’t got eyes in my head.... Why don’t you make it up with George, Katie?
I don’t know what makes you think there’s anything to make up.
Oh, my dear, what I didn’t guess for myself Teddie told me.
He would have been wiser to mind his own business.
It was rather....

If you knew how things were between George and myself, and you were willing to accept his favours what do you expect me to say? I didn’t ask you not to. I knew if I had you would only have refused. I’m cynical enough to know that in this world each of us takes care of his own interests.
My dear, don’t be so bitter.
One has to take people as one finds them; George has always been charming to me. If you’d only make allowances for him....

Oh, my dear, don’t. I’m not in the humour to stand that. Leave me to lead my own life without interference. Surely it’s enough that to bind me to him George should give you an income to marry on. You can’t want more from me than that.
Oh, my dear, I’m so sorry. I didn’t mean to say anything that would hurt you.
You haven’t. Forgive me. I didn’t mean to make a

lines.source: scene, but my nerves are a little upset. I’m a very weak, selfish woman,

parts.say: audit’s dreadfully hard to be half as angelic as you think me. I’m very glad that you’re going to marry Teddie. You’re in love with one another, and if you haven’t much money, what does it matter? I’m sure you’ll be tremendously happy.
You are a dear.

lines.source:
[FRANCIS ETCHINGHAM _comes in_. _He is wearing a dinner jacket and
     a black tie._ ANNE _springs up impulsively_.

parts.say: Is it over?
No, I was too anxious to stay any longer.
But George is going to get in?
Who can tell? The seat has always been lost or held by a handful of votes.
But how did it seem to be going?
Winter, Morrison, Winter, Morrison. One vote on one side, one vote on the other. It seemed interminable.
He won by seventy-five last time.
Who can tell the effect of all these rumours and suspicions and attacks? They may just have made the difference. Oh, it’s maddening.
Sit down, father, and rest. You look quite done up.
Even George is anxious. I know his face so well. He’s trying to appear as if he were certain.
No human being could help being anxious.
I thought I heard some shouting.
Oh, I wish I hadn’t come away.
Let’s open the window. Perhaps we shall hear something.

lines.source: [LADY FRANCIS _and_ ANNE _go to the window and open it_.

parts.say: No, I was mistaken.
Listen. I’m sure I hear cheering.

lines.source:
[_She goes out on to the balcony. She and_ LADY FRANCIS _are half
     hidden from view, so that it may be supposed the following scene
     between_ CATHERINE _and_ LORD FRANCIS _is not heard by them_.

parts.mic: In a low voice to_ CATHERINE.

parts.say: Oh, my dear, will you ever forgive me?
Oh, father, don’t. It was very noble of you not to tell me anything before I decided. Now that I know the whole truth....

The only hope we’ve got is to go on. If he gets in, if we can pull things together, we may get out of the muddle. He’s positive of it. The only thing that held me up was the thought of all of you. If I’d gone to the police there and then--or made away with myself, it would have meant the ruin of all of you.
And of all the unhappy people who’ve trusted everything they had to George.
You think I was right, Kate, don’t you? It wasn’t just cowardice on my part?
I hope you were right.
But if it was all in vain? If he’s not able to float the company and the truth comes out, then I shall have sacrificed you for nothing.
Oh, don’t think of it.
I believe if he wins the election he’ll be strong enough to force the issue on them.
But if the mine’s worthless?

We’re going to buy the shares in when the tide turns in Central America. Things are looking brighter already. He’s promised me that no one shall lose a farthing. When that’s done I go. Oh, how thankful I shall be!
Oh, I know, I know.
I had to tell some one, and I couldn’t tell your mother.
I’m glad you told me. It makes it easier to bear now we both know.
At last!... Father, father.

lines.source:
[_She comes back into the room, excitedly, and at the same time a
     vague, muffled shouting is heard in the distance._ ETCHINGHAM
     _springs to his feet_.

parts.say: Thank God. The suspense was awful.
There’s no mistaking it this time.
Is he in? Is he in?
Of course he’s in. I’ve never felt so confident in my life.
If it’s all right, then we’re safe. I’m sure it’s the beginning of the turn.
Why doesn’t Teddie make haste?
Listen to the shouting. Isn’t it splendid?

lines.source: [_More shouting is heard, this time a little louder._

parts.say: I expect they’re reading out the figures.

lines.source:
[TEDDIE O’DONNELL _rushes in, rather dishevelled, with his hat on
     the back of his head_.

parts.say: He’s in!
How ripping!

lines.source:
[FRANCIS ETCHINGHAM _sinks into a chair, too overcome to speak,
     trying to compose himself_. CATHERINE _puts her hand on his
     shoulder to show her sympathy_.

parts.say: What’s the majority?
Twenty-seven.
I say, what a squeak!
Just at the end I thought we were beaten. It was Morrison, Morrison, Morrison, until I almost screamed.
Well, he’s in at all events.
I am glad.

lines.source:
[_She throws her arms impulsively round_ O’DONNELL’S _neck and
     kisses him_.

parts.say: By Jove, it was a moment to live for when the figures were read out. You never heard such shouting.
Where is he now?
When I left he was making a speech to the crowd. But one couldn’t hear a word, because every one was shouting at the top of his voice. I simply bellowed.
Aren’t you glad, Kate?
Yes, very glad.
How can you take it so quietly!
Is he coming here?
Yes. I forgot to give you his message. He sent his love to Kate, and said he’d be here in two twos.
I wish he’d hurry up. Isn’t he a darling?

He’s the greatest man I’ve ever known. He’s a perfect stunner. I don’t know what there is about him, but you can’t help believing in him. And he was so splendid this morning about those confounded lies in the paper. All the rest of them were as frightened as rabbits, but he never turned a hair.
There’s a car.
That’s it, I bet you anything you like.
How jolly of him to come quickly!

parts.sound: She runs to the door and opens it.

parts.say: George, George!

lines.source:
[GEORGE WINTER _comes in boisterously and clasps_ ANNE _in his
     arms_.

parts.say: Isn’t it splendid!
Glorious victory, what!

lines.source:
[_He is followed by_ COLONEL BOYCE, JAMES FORD, MR. SWALECLIFFE,
     _and two other men_.

parts.say: Thank God!
You haven’t been worried about it? I knew I’d get in. I never had a moment’s doubt about it.
No one can say you don’t believe in yourself.
Hang it all, if you don’t believe in yourself, how can you expect other people to believe in you? Drinks, gentlemen!
Shall I ring?
I told the waiter on my way up. Here they are.

parts.direction: A couple of waiters come in with glasses and bottles of champagne.

parts.say: No teetotalism to-night, Mr. Swalecliffe. By Jove, I’m thirsty. Pour it out. Pour it out.
I never touch alcohol, Mr. Winter.
Poor is the heart that never rejoices. Have you all got glasses, gentlemen? Come on, Lady Francis. Don’t be backward, Anne.
Yes, please.
That’s right. Now then, Teddie. All ready? Gentlemen, I give you my wife, to whom this glorious victory is due.
Mrs. Winter, Mrs. Winter. Catherine.
Thank you very much.

lines.source:
[_There are shouts outside, cheers_: WINTER, WINTER, _For he’s a
     jolly good fellow_.

parts.say: Hulloa, they’ve come round to the hotel.
Just look at the crowd.
Shall I open the window?
Yes.

lines.source:
[_At his appearance the shouts break out more tumultuously. Cheer
     upon cheer is heard._ GEORGE WINTER _puts up his hand for silence_.

parts.say: Gentlemen, we’ve won a great fight. We’ve won in face of a campaign of lies, of misrepresentation, and of scandal. Truth always prevails. Honesty is the best policy. A glorious victory, gentlemen, and a triumph for English honesty, English plain dealing, and English integrity. Gentlemen, I drink your health.

lines.source:
[_He drinks his glass of champagne before the crowd. The cheering
     which has been going on all through the speech now grows louder and
     louder. There are shouts of_ MRS. WINTER.

parts.say: Kate, they want you.
No. Please not.
Come. No false modesty. Give them a bow, that won’t hurt you.

lines.source:
[_He takes her hand and draws her to the window. The crowd bursts
     out again into cheering._ GEORGE WINTER _comes back into the room_.

parts.say: My word, what a moment!
You must be dead beat.
I? Fresh as a daisy. Nothing can beat me.
By Jove, I had no idea it was so late.
I think I’ll be getting along.
Oh, nonsense! Why, the evening’s only just beginning.
I’m dog tired.
I must be getting away, too. My wife will be wanting to know all about it.
Well, if I can’t persuade you, I suppose I can’t. I hope you’ll all have as good a night as I mean to.
You think it’s all right about--about that matter?
Don’t you worry your head. It’s as right as rain. I tell you that nothing I touch can fail.
Then good-night.
Good-night.

lines.source:
[COLONEL BOYCE, SWALECLIFFE, _and the other two men who came in
     with them, go out_.

parts.say: You’re not going yet, Ford?
No. If you don’t mind I’d like to have a word with you when you can spare me a few minutes.
As many as you like. I’m ready now.
If you’re going to talk business, we’d better leave you.
I’m in no hurry, my lady.
It really is getting very late.
Aren’t you too tired for business now?

Tired? I don’t know what it is to be tired. When you write my biography, young man, you can say that after the hardest fought battle of the election, when the cheers of the multitude were still ringing in his ears, he sat down at midnight, fresh as paint, and talked business with the shrewdest man in Middlepool till break of day.
It’ll be more accurate if you say for ten minutes.
But so much less effective.
I’m sure you’ve been drinking too much champagne, George.
Nonsense. I could drink a gallon, and be as sober as a judge at the end of it.
Well, good-night.
Good-night, my chick. Have you named the happy day yet?
Good-night.
And you can add that I enveloped my mother-in-law in my arms.

parts.direction: With a smile, warding off his attempt to embrace her.

parts.say: I congratulate you. It’s been a great triumph.
Oh, it’s only the beginning. I’ve got the world at my feet. In ten years I shall be crying like Alexander because there are no more worlds to conquer.
You don’t want me any more, do you?
No, go to bed. You’re young, and you want your beauty sleep. I’ll be bound you’re not worried by the trains. Where’s your room?
It’s just above yours. But I sleep like a top.
That’s a good sign. You’ll be as great a man as I am one of these days.
Good-night.
And you’d better go off too, old man. You look tired out.
It’s been an exciting day for all of us.
It’s been one of the days that make life worth living.
Good-night.
I won’t say good-night to you just yet. If Mr. Ford is not going to keep you long I should like to speak to you afterwards.
It’ll be ten minutes at the utmost, Mrs. Winter.
I’m at your disposal, darling, now and always.

lines.source: [_With a slight bow to_ JAMES FORD, CATHERINE _goes out_.

parts.say: I told you I was justified in trusting my luck. Everything is coming out right. The Lewishams won’t be able to stand against me much longer. They’ll have to take me in. We’ll combine our interests, and then we shall hold Central America in the hollow of our hands. You’ll be in it too, James. You’re going to be a richer man than you guess. And when I’m in with the Lewishams I shall bide my time. Manny Lewisham can’t last much longer, and his sons are fools. When he’s gone I shall get the whole business in my hands. I’ve got ten times more brains than anyone in that market. There’s no one who can stand against me.
You haven’t forgotten that article in

Oh, is that what you want to talk to me about? I tell you that shan’t disturb my night’s rest. By the way, that reminds me: if I have won the election it was through no help of yours. I asked you to go down and speak in the Cattle Market, and when I got there I found there’d been no sign of you. It might have been devilish awkward.
Well, it so happens it didn’t matter.
Where did you get to after all?
I went up to London!

parts.direction: Indifferently, doing all he can to hide his suspicion.

parts.say: Did you?
I was struck by one of the paragraphs in the article. The one about where you got the money from.
I noticed that seemed to bother you a bit.
Things were pretty tight at that time.
A man in my position can always lay his hands on money.
It was a big sum.
Fair to moderate.

lines.source:
[_There is a very short pause. The two men, both shrewd, hard and
     keen, face one another like two duellists._

parts.say: It struck me that the Middlepool Investment Trust had got a large batch of bonds lying in the bank.

lines.source: [_He watches_ GEORGE WINTER _for the effect of this statement_.

parts.say: Well, they’re lying there still.
Will you take your oath on that?
Yes.
The more I thought of it, the more nervous I was. I went to the bank.

lines.source:
[GEORGE WINTER _gives him a rapid look, but otherwise makes no sign
     that he realizes his theft is discovered_.

parts.say: They showed me an order for delivery of the bonds signed by you, Etchingham, and Bennett.
Have a cigar, will you?
No.... What have you done with those bonds?
If they’re in their place when the auditor makes his examination no one has any question to ask.
You had no more right to touch them than my office boy has the right to take a sovereign from the petty cash.
What the devil d’you mean by that?
I’m a director of the Middlepool Investment Trust. I insist on the bonds being produced at once.
They shall be produced in a fortnight.
No, no, my friend, that won’t do.
Don’t be a fool, James, you know as well as I do that business is business.
Yes, and not theft.
How dare you speak to me like that!
It’s no good trying to bluster with me, George. I’ve seen you do it at shareholders’ meetings and very effective it is sometimes, but this isn’t the time for it.

lines.source:
[_There is a pause._ GEORGE WINTER _considers the position and
     determines to face it_.

parts.say: All right then.... I knew the mine was a good thing. I pledged the bonds to pay for it. I shall get them back as soon as the money comes in from the issue. Now you’ve got it.
It’s theft pure and simple.
I suppose you want to come in with me.

parts.direction: He does not notice_ JAMES FORD’S _instinctive movement of repulsion_.

parts.say: I’ll give you your shares for nothing. That means ten thousand pounds, and if you hold on to them they’ll be worth fifty thousand in a year.
Thank you. I’m not going to risk a lifetime’s honest work for a few thousand pounds.
Then what do you want?
Nothing.
You’ve been Mayor of Middlepool twice, and you’ve done a lot of work for the party. I can’t help thinking it’s almost time the Government showed some appreciation of your services.

You’ve mistaken your man, George Winter. I’ve worked like a nigger for thirty years. I’ve not let any chance slip by me, but I’ve never done anything that a man need be ashamed of. I’ve built up an honest business to leave to my sons, and an honest name. I’m too old to start being a rogue now.
I thought you wanted to talk business.
Right’s right, and wrong’s wrong. You can’t get over that. I couldn’t rest for a moment if I thought any act of mine wasn’t above board. It’s no credit of mine, I’m just made that way.

parts.direction: As if he were talking to a child.

parts.say: Come, James, we’ve been good friends for twenty years.
This afternoon, when I found out what you’d done--well, I could have cried.

lines.source:
[_There is a real anguish in his tone which startles_ GEORGE
     WINTER. _For the first time he realizes that the affair is serious.
     He begins to get frightened._

parts.say: But you don’t mean seriously....

How can I make you understand? You don’t seem to see that now I know what you’ve done I’m just filled with horror and loathing. If you’ve done this God knows what else you haven’t done. I don’t want to be hard on you. I must do my duty. I’m a director of the company. I put all my friends in it. I put my sister into it. And this mine. Is it true what that paper says? For all I know that’s a swindle too.
You’re not going to push me down now that I’m almost at the top of the tree? I’ve got the world at my feet. If you’ll only give me a month I can put everything straight.
Five minutes ago it was a fortnight. I don’t believe it. These things don’t come right. When a man has crossed the line that separates honesty from dishonesty he never gets back.
If you give me away now it’ll mean a general smash. The only chance of saving things is to go on. The money’s gone. You won’t get it back by giving me up to the police.
I must take my chance of that. After all, if I don’t speak it makes me a party to the crime. It can be proved that I went to the bank to-day.
Now you’re saying something I can understand. If I show you by plain figures that I can put everything right if you’ll only give me time....
I tell you I can’t. I’ve got my wife to think of, and my boys. It’s theft, it’s the money of orphans and widows that you’ve taken, and there’s only one course open to me.
What are you going to do?
My God, what can I do? I trusted you as I would have trusted my sons.
Out with it!
I must--I must consult the Chief Constable.
You wouldn’t do that? You don’t seriously mean that you’d go to the police? It’s madness. It’s so impractical. It’s stupid.
I could never respect myself again if I.... It’s a matter between my conscience and myself.... Oh, George, why have you put me in this position?

Look here, old man, I’ve done wrong. I admit it. I’ve done something that other men have done before me and it’s come out all right. At the time I thought the slump would only last a few days, and I thought I should be able to replace the bonds in a week. It’s the only slip I’ve made. Don’t be too hard on me....

parts.direction: With a break in his voice.

parts.say: Have mercy as you hope in your turn to have mercy shown to you. Don’t ruin me for this one mistake. Let it mean something to you that I’m humiliating myself before you.... It wasn’t a crime. It was only thoughtlessness. Give me another chance.

lines.source:
[JAMES FORD, _with his face between his hands, thinks it over. He
     is deeply moved by_ GEORGE WINTER’S _appeal_. GEORGE, _watching him
     keenly, thinks he is going to yield_.

parts.say: We’ve gone through bad times and good together. I’ve been a good friend to you. You’ve never had anything to reproach me with till now.
I can’t risk the money of all these poor people again.
Will it satisfy you if I give up the directorship of the Middlepool Trust? Give me six months to save my face and I’ll resign.

lines.source:
[JAMES FORD _looks up at him, wondering if he can put any trust in_
     GEORGE WINTER. GEORGE _waits for the decision with beating heart_.
     _He feels almost sick with fear._

parts.say: I’ll tell you what I’ll do. If the bonds are in their place by four o’clock to-morrow I’ll say nothing.
To-morrow? It can’t be done. It’s impossible.
That’s all I can do for you.

parts.direction: Hardly knowing what he is saying.

parts.say: But no one could get it. You know it’s impossible. Even if you gave me a week I couldn’t do it. I can’t, I can’t, I can’t. With the attack on us to-day we’re--we’re tottering. It’s as much as we shall be able to do to hold out till the tide turns. That’s not giving me a chance. Not a chance. To-morrow! It’s absurd!
That’s my last word.
You might as well send for the police at once. Oh, my God! It’s impossible.
If the money is not there by the time the bank closes I shall apply for a warrant.
D’you know what that means? It means a trial, and then--and then prison.
I can’t do more for you than I’ve offered.

lines.source:
[_The finality of this, the deep regret and the decision in_ FORD’S
     _tone, are like a blow in the face to_ GEORGE WINTER. _He gives a
     sudden start, and throwing off his humbleness, flies into
     ungovernable passion. He whips himself into a rage as he flings the
     scornful invective at_ JAMES FORD _and ends up on the last words in
     a positive scream of fury_.

parts.say: Oh, it’s infamous. It’s damned hypocrisy. You don’t care if I’ve taken the money or not. You’re afraid of your own skin. And you’re jealous of me. It’s envy. I knew you envied me all the time. D’you think I’ve been taken in by you? You were a little tin god in Middlepool till I came along. You didn’t fight me like a man. You just sided with me, waiting for your chance to trip me up. You think when I’m gone you’ll have the field to yourself. Why shouldn’t you be the member as well as I? It’s mean. It’s mean. You with your damned Christianity, your parrot cries of honesty. Damn you! Damn you! Damn you!

You see, you’ve gone too far. I shall never make you understand. You can’t realize that a man may be honest, even if he loses by it, just because he can’t help it, because he’s made straight as some men are made crooked.
It’s childish.
You’ve got through the world by knowing that nine men out of ten are rascals. You’ve forgotten that the tenth man must cross your path at last.

lines.source:
[_When he hears these words_ GEORGE WINTER _gives a start, and he
     looks at_ FORD _with staring, terrified eyes. He passes his hand
     over his forehead, trying to recall._

parts.say: Who said that to me before?
Good-bye, George. My promise holds.
It’s no good to me. I’m like a rat in a trap. You can get what fun you like out of seeing me wriggle.

lines.source:
[_For a moment_ JAMES FORD _looks at him, then silently goes out_.
     GEORGE WINTER _is seized with a horrible, convulsive trembling. He
     shakes as a man might shake in an ague. With his quick mind he sees
     that no subtlety will save him now; he is up against the blank wall
     of a character as strong as his own. In a moment_ CATHERINE _enters
     the room_.

parts.say: What the devil d’you want?
I heard Mr. Ford go. May I speak to you now?

lines.source: [GEORGE WINTER _makes an effort to appear composed_.

parts.say: Well?
Now that the election is over you can have no further use for me. I’ve carried out my part of the bargain scrupulously.

parts.direction: Putting his hand in a dazed way to his head.

parts.say: I don’t know what you’re talking about.
I understand that I’ve condoned all your offences towards me, and I’m helpless now to do anything. So you need have no fear that I shall interfere with you in any way.

parts.direction: He turns round and looks at her. He takes in at last what she is saying.

parts.say: But there’s no reason that I should expose myself any longer to a humiliation that I found unbearable. I’ve come to tell you that now I’ve done all you exacted I’m going to leave you, this time for good. I’m starting early to-morrow morning for the Continent with my friend Barbara Herbert, and I shall not return. You can devise whatever explanation you think necessary, and you may be quite sure I shan’t contradict it. I shall be gone by the time you get up. You will find in my room all the trinkets you’ve given me. I wish to take nothing with me that I have received from you.
Are you leaving your clothes?

parts.direction: With a shrug of the shoulders.

parts.say: I think there is nothing more to be said. Good-bye. I trust you to leave me in peace. I promise on my side to do nothing that can inconvenience you.

lines.source:
[_She waits for a moment to see if he has anything further to say,
     but as he remains silent she goes towards the door. As she is about
     to go out he bursts into a peal of laughter. She stops with a start
     and looks at him. His laughter grows, peal upon peal. It becomes
     wild and shrill and hysterical. He bellows with laughter. Already
     half frightened, not understanding_, CATHERINE _makes a step or two
     back into the room_.

parts.say: What’s the matter? George, George!

lines.source:
[_He laughs still, and then suddenly breaks into a sob. He gives
     way entirely, and bursts into uncontrolled weeping._

parts.say: George, what is it?
For God’s sake give me a drink.

lines.source:
[_She hurries to the half-empty bottle of champagne on the table
     and pours out a glass of wine. He drinks it at a gulp._

parts.say: That’s rich, that is. Rich.
What is it, George? It’s not because I’m going away?

Your going away doesn’t matter a damn to me. It means that I’ve been done in the eye. Those swindling rogues, the Lewishams, have got me at last. That article’s done the trick and I’m dished. You can go your own way now, Kate. You’ve got the better of me after all.
I don’t understand.
James Ford knows that the bonds have gone. And he’s going to Scotland Yard.
Oh! And father?
Oh, I can’t worry about your father now. He must look after his own skin. I’ve got enough to do to think of myself.
What shall I do?

He’ll give me till to-morrow to replace them, but I can’t. It’s impossible. And he knows I can’t. Damned hypocrite! I shouldn’t complain if I’d been beaten fairly; but it’s so childish. And just when I’d got the reins in my hand. He can’t countenance dishonesty. It’s childish. I always distrusted him. Sanctimonious prig! He’s jealous of me. He wants to kick me off my perch, so that he can take my place. And I know him. I know him inside out. He’ll do what he says.
It’s his duty.
Can’t we sell things? There’s my jewellery.
A drop in the ocean. How can I get eighty thousand pounds in a falling market.
D’you mean to say they’ll arrest you?

parts.direction: With a dull roar, like a wild beast at bay.

parts.say: No. D’you think I’m going to stand that, and a trial, and--and all the rest?
